これから<ruby>昼<rt>ひる</rt></ruby>ごはんを<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べる**ところ**です。<br>*I'm just about to have lunch.*

<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>昼<rt>ひる</rt></ruby>ごはんを<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べ**ているところ**です。<br>*I'm having lunch right now.*

<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>昼<rt>ひる</rt></ruby>ごはんを<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べ**たところ**です。<br>*I've just finished lunch.*

---

## ～ているところ · 食べるところ vs 食べているところ vs 食べたところ (cont.)

Nothing changes but the form of the verb, and the three sentences point at three different minutes. Learn them as a set: the same `ところ` is doing the same job in all three, and only the tense of the verb moves you along the timeline.

---

## ～ているところ · ～ているところ vs ～ている間に

> **Rule of thumb** - `ているところ` describes **the subject's own stage**, and usually ends the sentence. <code><ruby>間<rt>あいだ</rt></ruby></code> opens a **window** during which something else happens - and the `に` decides whether the other event fills the window or falls inside it.

The `に` is the entire difference, and it is worth slowing down for:

<ruby>母<rt>はは</rt></ruby>が<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>ている**<ruby>間<rt>あいだ</rt></ruby>**、ずっとそばにいました。<br>*I stayed beside my mother the whole time she was asleep.*

<ruby>母<rt>はは</rt></ruby>が<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>ている**<ruby>間<rt>あいだ</rt></ruby>に**、<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>い<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>ってきました。<br>*While my mother was asleep, I nipped out and did the shopping.*

---

## ～ているところ · ～ているところ vs ～ている間に (cont.)

Without `に`, the second clause must last as long as the window - hence `ずっと`, and hence verbs like <code><ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>っていた</code>, <code><ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>んでいた</code>. With `に`, the second clause is a one-off event that fits somewhere inside the window, and it is typically something finishable: going out, making a call, tidying up. Swap them and both sentences go wrong - ❌<code><ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>ている<ruby>間<rt>あいだ</rt></ruby>、<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>い<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>った</code> claims you shopped for the entire nap.

`ているところ` is doing something different again. It is not a time clause at all; it is a statement about where the subject has got to:

<ruby>母<rt>はは</rt></ruby>は<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>**ているところ**です。<br>*My mother is asleep just at the moment.*

---

## ～ているところ · Common mistakes

- ❌ <ruby>毎日<rt>まいにち</rt></ruby><ruby>運動<rt>うんどう</rt></ruby>しているところです。 → ✅ <ruby>毎日<rt>まいにち</rt></ruby><ruby>運動<rt>うんどう</rt></ruby>しています。<br>*A habit has no "stage". `ところ` only works for something happening at the moment of speaking.*

- ❌ <ruby>窓<rt>まど</rt></ruby>が<ruby>開<rt>あ</rt></ruby>いているところです。 → ✅ <ruby>窓<rt>まど</rt></ruby>が<ruby>開<rt>あ</rt></ruby>いています。<br>*This `ている` is a resulting state, not an action in progress, and `ところ` cannot attach to it.*

- ❌ <ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べるているところです。 → ✅ <ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べているところです。<br>*The `ている` is built on the て-form, not the dictionary form. The dictionary form goes straight onto `ところ` and means "about to".*

- ❌ <ruby>父<rt>ちち</rt></ruby>は<ruby>十年<rt>じゅうねん</rt></ruby><ruby>前<rt>まえ</rt></ruby>から<ruby>同<rt>おな</rt></ruby>じ<ruby>会社<rt>かいしゃ</rt></ruby>で<ruby>働<rt>はたら</rt></ruby>いているところです。 → ✅ …<ruby>働<rt>はたら</rt></ruby>いています。<br>*Ten years is not a stage you are standing in. Long-running situations take plain `ている`.*

---

## ～ているところ · Practice 1

**1.** 「もうレポートを<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>しましたか。」「いいえ、<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>い____ところです。」

{reveal}
いいえ、<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>い**ている**ところです。

{reveal}
The writing is under way at this moment, which is exactly the stage `ところ` picks out. <code><ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>くところです</code> would mean you have not started yet, and <code><ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>いたところです</code> would mean it is already done - a very different answer to give your boss.

---

## ～ているところ · Practice 2

**2.** <ruby>毎朝<rt>まいあさ</rt></ruby><ruby>新聞<rt>しんぶん</rt></ruby>を（<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>んでいます・<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>んでいるところです）。

{reveal}
<ruby>毎朝<rt>まいあさ</rt></ruby><ruby>新聞<rt>しんぶん</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>んでいます**。

{reveal}
<code><ruby>毎朝<rt>まいあさ</rt></ruby></code> makes this a habit, and `ところ` cannot express a habit - it names a single stage in a single action. Drop <code><ruby>毎朝<rt>まいあさ</rt></ruby></code> and put <code><ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby></code> there instead, and the other option becomes the right one.

---

## ～ているところ · Practice 3

**3.** Translate into Japanese: "I'm just checking now, so could you wait a moment?"

{reveal}
<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>**<ruby>確認<rt>かくにん</rt></ruby>しているところ**ですので、<ruby>少々<rt>しょうしょう</rt></ruby>お<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ちいただけますか。

{reveal}
This is the standard status report. `ているところです` tells the other person the work is actually in motion, which is why it is the polite alternative to a bare `まだです`.

---

## ～ているところ · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: <ruby>姉<rt>あね</rt></ruby>は<ruby>三年<rt>さんねん</rt></ruby><ruby>前<rt>まえ</rt></ruby>から<ruby>大阪<rt>おおさか</rt></ruby>に<ruby>住<rt>す</rt></ruby>んでいるところです。

{reveal}
✅ <ruby>姉<rt>あね</rt></ruby>は<ruby>三年<rt>さんねん</rt></ruby><ruby>前<rt>まえ</rt></ruby>から<ruby>大阪<rt>おおさか</rt></ruby>に<ruby>住<rt>す</rt></ruby>んでいます。

{reveal}
<code><ruby>住<rt>す</rt></ruby>んでいる</code> is a state, not an action in progress, and three years is not a moment. As it stands the sentence would also be misread as "the place where my sister lives", since `ところ` still means "place".

---

## ～ているところ · Practice 5

**5.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) <ruby>姉<rt>あね</rt></ruby>が<ruby>料理<rt>りょうり</rt></ruby>をしている<ruby>間<rt>あいだ</rt></ruby>、<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>皿<rt>さら</rt></ruby>を<ruby>洗<rt>あら</rt></ruby>っていました。 (b) <ruby>姉<rt>あね</rt></ruby>が<ruby>料理<rt>りょうり</rt></ruby>をしている<ruby>間<rt>あいだ</rt></ruby>に、<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>い<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きました。

---

## ～ているところ · Practice 5 — answer

(a) has no `に`, so the two activities are the same length: for the whole time your sister was cooking, you were at the sink. Both clauses describe stretches, and neither has a single point attached to it.

(b) has `に`, which turns the cooking into a **window** and puts a one-off event inside it. The shopping trip started and finished somewhere in the middle of the cooking; it did not last the whole time and nobody claims it did.

That one syllable is the whole distinction. A verb that goes on (<code><ruby>洗<rt>あら</rt></ruby>っていた</code>, <code><ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>っていた</code>) wants <code><ruby>間<rt>あいだ</rt></ruby></code>; a verb that finishes (<code><ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>った</code>, <code><ruby>電話<rt>でんわ</rt></ruby>した</code>) wants <code><ruby>間<rt>あいだ</rt></ruby>に</code>.

---

# ～ところ

**Meaning** · about to do; on the point of doing

With a verb in the **dictionary form**, `ところ` names the stage just *before* the action: you have not started, and you are about to. The same construction in the past - `～ところだった` - becomes one of the most useful sentences in the language: "I very nearly did."

---

## ～ところ · Formation

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Verb | **dictionary form** + ところだ | <ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>る → <ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>るところだ |
| Polite | dictionary form + ところです | <ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>るところです |
| Past - "nearly" | dictionary form + ところだった | <ruby>遅<rt>おく</rt></ruby>れるところだった |
| Past polite | dictionary form + ところでした | <ruby>忘<rt>わす</rt></ruby>れるところでした |
| More imminent still | ようとしている + ところ | <ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>かけようとしているところ |
| Interrupted | ところ + に／へ | <ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>るところに<ruby>電話<rt>でんわ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>た |
| Typical companions | これから、<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>から、ちょうど、もう<ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>しで | ちょうど<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めるところ |
| Casual contraction | とこ | <ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>るとこ |
| ❌ ます-form | ❌<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きますところ | ✅<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くところ |

---

## ～ところ · Formation (cont.)

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| ❌ Distant future | ❌<ruby>来月<rt>らいげつ</rt></ruby><ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くところです | ✅<ruby>来月<rt>らいげつ</rt></ruby><ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く<ruby>予定<rt>よてい</rt></ruby>です |

> **Rule of thumb** - the dictionary form in front of `ところ` means the action has **not begun**. Not "I am doing it", not "I have done it" - the foot is still in the air.

> **Note** - in this sense `ところ` normally ends the sentence with `だ`／`です`, or carries on with `に`／`へ` to introduce an interruption. It is not a free subordinate clause: to say "the phone rang as I was about to go to bed" you need <code><ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>るところに</code>, not a bare <code><ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>るところ</code> followed by a comma.

---

## ～ところ · Examples

<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>から<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>かける**ところ**です。<br>*I'm just heading out now.*

これから<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>まる**ところ**です。<br>*The meeting is about to start.*

あぶない! もう<ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>しで<ruby>転<rt>ころ</rt></ruby>ぶ**ところ**だった。<br>*Careful! I nearly went over.*

お<ruby>風呂<rt>ふろ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>入<rt>はい</rt></ruby>る**ところ**だったので、<ruby>電話<rt>でんわ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>られませんでした。<br>*I was about to get in the bath, so I couldn't pick up.*

---

## ～ところ · Examples (cont.)

<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>る**ところ**に<ruby>友<rt>とも</rt></ruby>だちから<ruby>電話<rt>でんわ</rt></ruby>がかかってきた。<br>*Just as I was going to bed, a friend rang.*

<ruby>危<rt>あや</rt></ruby>うく<ruby>終電<rt>しゅうでん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>逃<rt>のが</rt></ruby>す**ところ**でした。<br>*I very nearly missed the last train.*

ちょうど<ruby>家<rt>いえ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>る**ところ**なので、あと<ruby>十分<rt>じゅっぷん</rt></ruby>くらいで<ruby>着<rt>つ</rt></ruby>くと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います。<br>*I'm walking out the door right now, so I should be there in about ten minutes.*

<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>を<ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>かずに<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>る**ところ**でしたが、<ruby>同僚<rt>どうりょう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>教<rt>おし</rt></ruby>えてくれて<ruby>助<rt>たす</rt></ruby>かりました。<br>*I was about to go home without hearing the explanation, but a colleague filled me in - a lucky escape.*

---

## ～ところ · Nuance & register

In its present-tense use, `ところです` is a status report about the very near future, and it is the natural answer to <code><ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>してる?</code> or <code>もう<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>た?</code>. In casual speech it contracts to `とこ` and drops the copula: <code><ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>るとこ</code>. Both registers are extremely common; what you will not hear is this pattern in a formal written notice, where a schedule would be stated with times instead.

The past form is where the real value is. `～ところだった` means *it nearly happened and it didn't*, and it almost always carries relief. It collects a fixed set of adverbs - <code>もう<ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>しで</code>, <code><ruby>危<rt>あや</rt></ruby>うく</code>, `あぶなく` - and it is how Japanese says all of these:

---

## ～ところ · Nuance & register (cont.)

- <code><ruby>忘<rt>わす</rt></ruby>れるところでした</code> - "I almost forgot."
- <code><ruby>遅刻<rt>ちこく</rt></ruby>するところだった</code> - "I nearly ended up late."
- <code><ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>ってしまうところだった</code> - "I almost bought it."

Note that the verb stays in the **dictionary form** even though the sentence is about the past. The past lives in `だった`／`でした` at the end; the verb has to stay un-happened, because the whole point is that it never happened.

One thing this pattern does **not** do is announce plans. It has a horizon of a few minutes. For anything further out, the words are `つもり` and <code><ruby>予定<rt>よてい</rt></ruby></code>.

---

## ～ところ · 出るところ vs 出たところ

> **Rule of thumb** - the form of the verb walks you across the event. Dictionary form: **not started**. た-form: **just finished**. The `ところ` is identical in both.

<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>、<ruby>家<rt>いえ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>る**ところ**です。<br>*I'm just about to leave the house.*

<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>、<ruby>家<rt>いえ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>た**ところ**です。<br>*I've just left the house.*

---

## ～ところ · 出るところ vs 出たところ (cont.)

Said into a phone, these two put you in completely different places: still indoors, or already on the street. The middle member of the set - <code><ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>ているところ</code> - is built on `ている` and covers the stretch in between.

This is why the form in front of `ところ` deserves more care than any other choice on this page. The word never changes; the verb carries all the information.

---

## ～ところ · ～ところだ vs ～つもり・～予定

> **Rule of thumb** - `ところ` reaches a few **minutes** into the future. `つもり` is an **intention** and <code><ruby>予定<rt>よてい</rt></ruby></code> is a **schedule**, and both stretch as far as you like.

<ruby>来月<rt>らいげつ</rt></ruby>、<ruby>京都<rt>きょうと</rt></ruby>へ<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く**つもり**です。<br>*I'm planning to go to Kyoto next month.*

<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>駅<rt>えき</rt></ruby>へ<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く**ところ**です。<br>*I'm on my way to the station this minute.*

❌<code><ruby>来月<rt>らいげつ</rt></ruby><ruby>京都<rt>きょうと</rt></ruby>へ<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くところです</code> is wrong, and audibly so: `ところ` claims you are on the very brink of the action, and you cannot be on the brink of something a month away.

---

## ～ところ · ～ところだ vs ～つもり・～予定 (cont.)

The reverse substitution is not an error so much as a loss. <code><ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くつもりです</code> reports your intention and leaves open whether you have moved; <code><ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くところです</code> says you are already on your feet.

---

## ～ところ · ～ところだった vs ～そうになった

> **Rule of thumb** - both mean "almost". `ところだった` is a whole **situation** you narrowly avoided; `そうになった` is a **physical event** that nearly happened to you.

もう<ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>しで<ruby>遅刻<rt>ちこく</rt></ruby>する**ところ**でした。<br>*I very nearly ended up late.*

<ruby>階段<rt>かいだん</rt></ruby>で<ruby>転<rt>ころ</rt></ruby>び**そうになり**ました。<br>*I almost fell on the stairs.*

---

## ～ところ · ～ところだった vs ～そうになった (cont.)

The mechanics differ too: `そうになる` attaches to the **ます-stem** (<code><ruby>転<rt>ころ</rt></ruby>び</code>, <code><ruby>落<rt>お</rt></ruby>ち</code>, <code><ruby>泣<rt>な</rt></ruby>き</code>), while `ところ` takes the dictionary form. And their coverage differs. `そうになる` wants something on the verge of physically occurring - falling, dropping, crying, crashing. `ところだった` is happy with outcomes you avoided by *deciding differently*: <code><ruby>危<rt>あや</rt></ruby>うく<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>いほうを<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>うところだった</code>, "I almost bought the expensive one." `そうになる` cannot say that.

---

## ～ところ · Common mistakes

- ❌ <ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>かけ**ますところ**です。 → ✅ <ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>かけ**る**ところです。<br>*`ところ` is a noun, and a noun takes the plain form in front of it. The politeness is already there in `です`.*

- ❌ <ruby>来年<rt>らいねん</rt></ruby>、アメリカに<ruby>留学<rt>りゅうがく</rt></ruby>する**ところ**です。 → ✅ <ruby>来年<rt>らいねん</rt></ruby>、アメリカに<ruby>留学<rt>りゅうがく</rt></ruby>する**<ruby>予定<rt>よてい</rt></ruby>**です。<br>*A year is far outside the range of this pattern. Distant plans take <code><ruby>予定<rt>よてい</rt></ruby></code> or `つもり`.*

- ❌ もう<ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>しで<ruby>財布<rt>さいふ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>忘<rt>わす</rt></ruby>れ**たところ**でした。 → ✅ もう<ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>しで<ruby>財布<rt>さいふ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>忘<rt>わす</rt></ruby>れ**るところ**でした。<br>*The verb stays in the dictionary form: the forgetting never happened. Only `でした` moves into the past.*

---

## ～ところ · Common mistakes (cont.)

- ❌ <ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べ**ているところ**だったので、<ruby>後<rt>あと</rt></ruby>で<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きます。（meaning "I was about to eat"） → ✅ <ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べ**るところ**だったので…<br>*`ている` puts you in the middle of the meal. If the food is untouched, the dictionary form is the one you want.*

---

## ～ところ · Practice 1

**1.** あぶない! もう<ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>しで<ruby>車<rt>くるま</rt></ruby>にぶつかる____だった。

{reveal}
もう<ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>しで<ruby>車<rt>くるま</rt></ruby>にぶつかる**ところ**だった。

{reveal}
<code>もう<ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>しで</code> is the giveaway: it introduces something that came close to happening and then did not, and the pattern for that is `～るところだった`. Note that the verb stays in the dictionary form because the collision never took place.

---

## ～ところ · Practice 2

**2.** ちょうど<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>、<ruby>会社<rt>かいしゃ</rt></ruby>を（<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>る・<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>た）ところです。これから<ruby>向<rt>む</rt></ruby>かいます。

{reveal}
ちょうど<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>、<ruby>会社<rt>かいしゃ</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>る**ところです。

{reveal}
The second sentence - "I'll head over now" - tells you the journey has not started yet, so you are still on the office side of the door. That is the dictionary form. <code><ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>たところ</code> would put you outside already.

---

## ～ところ · Practice 3

**3.** Translate into Japanese: "I was just about to phone you."

{reveal}
ちょうど<ruby>電話<rt>でんわ</rt></ruby>する**ところ**でした。

{reveal}
The call had not been made, so the verb is in the dictionary form, and the past sits in `でした`. This is a very common thing to say when someone contacts you first, and it is friendlier than <code><ruby>電話<rt>でんわ</rt></ruby>しようと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>っていました</code> because it claims you were already in motion.

---

## ～ところ · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: <ruby>来月<rt>らいげつ</rt></ruby>、<ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>引<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>っ<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>すところです。

{reveal}
✅ <ruby>来月<rt>らいげつ</rt></ruby>、<ruby>東京<rt>とうきょう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>引<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>っ<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>す**<ruby>予定<rt>よてい</rt></ruby>**です。（or <ruby>引<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>っ<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>す**つもり**です）

{reveal}
`ところ` means you are on the brink of the action, within minutes. A move next month is a plan, so it needs <code><ruby>予定<rt>よてい</rt></ruby></code> for a fixed arrangement or `つもり` for an intention.

---

## ～ところ · Practice 5

**5.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) <ruby>財布<rt>さいふ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>忘<rt>わす</rt></ruby>れるところでした。 (b) <ruby>財布<rt>さいふ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>忘<rt>わす</rt></ruby>れてしまいました。

{reveal}
(a) is a near miss with a happy ending: the wallet is in your pocket. You noticed in time, and the sentence is coloured by relief - this is what you say as you turn back from the door with it in your hand.

{reveal}
(b) is the disaster itself. The wallet is on the kitchen table and you are on the train. `てしまう` reports a completed action you regret, where `ところでした` reports one that never happened at all.

---

# ～たところ

**Meaning** · have just done it - standing at the moment immediately after

With the verb in the **た-form**, `ところ` names the stage right after the action finished. The emphasis is on *right*: this is a claim about the clock, not about how fresh the event feels. Minutes ago, not last month.

---

## ～たところ · Formation

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Verb | **た-form** + ところだ | <ruby>着<rt>つ</rt></ruby>く → <ruby>着<rt>つ</rt></ruby>いたところだ |
| Verb (voiced た-form) | だ-form + ところだ | <ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>む → <ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>んだところだ |
| Polite | た-form + ところです | <ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わったところです |
| Past reference | た-form + ところだった | <ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>たところだった |
| Followed by an event | たところ + に／へ／で | <ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>たところに<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>った |
| Typical companions | <ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>、たった<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>、ちょうど | たった<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>ったところ |
| Casual contraction | たとこ | <ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>着<rt>つ</rt></ruby>いたとこ |
| ❌ Modifying a noun | ❌<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>ったところの<ruby>車<rt>くるま</rt></ruby> | ✅<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>ったばかりの<ruby>車<rt>くるま</rt></ruby> |
| ❌ Distant past | ❌<ruby>去年<rt>きょねん</rt></ruby><ruby>結婚<rt>けっこん</rt></ruby>したところです | ✅<ruby>去年<rt>きょねん</rt></ruby><ruby>結婚<rt>けっこん</rt></ruby>したばかりです |

---

## ～たところ · Formation (cont.)

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| ❌ Negative | ❌<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べなかったところ | ✅まだ<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べていません |

> **Rule of thumb** - `たところ` pins you to the moment immediately after the action. If you can put <code>たった<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby></code> in front of the sentence, it fits. If you would have to put <code><ruby>先月<rt>せんげつ</rt></ruby></code> there, it does not.

---

## ～たところ · Formation (cont.)

> **Note** - `～たところ` has a second, unrelated life as a **connective**, and you will meet it in reading before you produce it: <code><ruby>店<rt>みせ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>電話<rt>でんわ</rt></ruby>したところ、もう<ruby>閉<rt>し</rt></ruby>まっていました</code> - "when I rang the shop, it turned out to be closed." That version has no `だ`, sits at a comma, and belongs to formal writing. The last contrast section below separates the two.

---

## ～たところ · Examples

たった<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>うちに**<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>ったところ**です。<br>*I've literally just got home.*

<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>**<ruby>起<rt>お</rt></ruby>きたところ**なので、まだ<ruby>顔<rt>かお</rt></ruby>も<ruby>洗<rt>あら</rt></ruby>っていません。<br>*I've only just woken up - I haven't even washed my face yet.*

ちょうど<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>が**<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わったところ**です。<br>*The meeting has just this minute finished.*

メールは<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>**<ruby>送<rt>おく</rt></ruby>ったところ**ですので、<ruby>確認<rt>かくにん</rt></ruby>してみてください。<br>*I've just sent the email, so please check for it.*

---

## ～たところ · Examples (cont.)

<ruby>駅<rt>えき</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>たところ**で、<ruby>高校<rt>こうこう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>友<rt>とも</rt></ruby>だちにばったり<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>った。<br>*I'd just come out of the station when I ran straight into an old school friend.*

お<ruby>湯<rt>ゆ</rt></ruby>が**わいたところ**だから、お<ruby>茶<rt>ちゃ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>入<rt>い</rt></ruby>れましょうか。<br>*The water's just boiled - shall I make some tea?*

<ruby>引<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>っ<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>しの<ruby>荷物<rt>にもつ</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>運<rt>はこ</rt></ruby>び<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わったところ**に、<ruby>大家<rt>おおや</rt></ruby>さんが<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>ました。<br>*The landlord turned up just as we'd finished carrying in the boxes.*

さっき<ruby>銀行<rt>ぎんこう</rt></ruby>から<ruby>戻<rt>もど</rt></ruby>って、<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>やっと<ruby>書類<rt>しょるい</rt></ruby>を<ruby>全部<rt>ぜんぶ</rt></ruby>**<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>したところ**です。<br>*I got back from the bank a while ago, and I've only just now handed in all the paperwork.*

---

## ～たところ · Nuance & register

`たところです` is the polite way to report that something is done *this instant*, and it is a workplace staple. Asked whether you have sent the file, <code><ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>送<rt>おく</rt></ruby>ったところです</code> is better than <code><ruby>送<rt>おく</rt></ruby>りました</code> because it tells the other person to look now. In casual speech it shortens to `たとこ`: <code>ごめん、<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>起<rt>お</rt></ruby>きたとこ</code>.

The construction is **objective**. It is measured against the clock, and it will not stretch. That is its whole personality, and it is exactly what separates it from `たばかり`, which is measured against how the speaker feels. Because of that, `たところ` has no emotional colour of its own: it neither excuses nor boasts, it just reports where on the timeline you are standing.

---

## ～たところ · Nuance & register (cont.)

Two structural limits follow from the same fact. `たところ` cannot modify a noun - there is no ❌<code><ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>ったところの<ruby>料理<rt>りょうり</rt></ruby></code> - because it describes a moment rather than a property of the thing. And it has no negative form: "I haven't eaten yet" is <code>まだ<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べていません</code>, never ❌<code><ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べなかったところです</code>.

For narration in the past, use `たところだった`: <code><ruby>部屋<rt>へや</rt></ruby>に<ruby>入<rt>はい</rt></ruby>ったとき、<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>電話<rt>でんわ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>切<rt>き</rt></ruby>ったところだった</code>.

---

## ～たところ · ～たところ vs ～たばかり

> **Rule of thumb** - `たところ` measures with a **clock**; `たばかり` measures with a **feeling**. Both translate as "just", and only one of them will stretch to last year.

<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>駅<rt>えき</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>着<rt>つ</rt></ruby>いたところ**です。<br>*I've just arrived at the station.*

<ruby>去年<rt>きょねん</rt></ruby><ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>たばかり**です。<br>*I only came to Japan last year.*

---

## ～たところ · ～たところ vs ～たばかり (cont.)

The second sentence is impossible with `ところ`: ❌<code><ruby>去年<rt>きょねん</rt></ruby><ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>たところです</code>. A year is not a moment. `ばかり` survives it because the speaker is not reporting the clock - they are saying the arrival is still recent *as far as they are concerned*, which is why it works as an excuse for not knowing their way around.

The second difference is structural and easy to test. `ばかり` modifies nouns freely; `ところ` does not:

<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>った**ばかりの**パソコンが<ruby>壊<rt>こわ</rt></ruby>れてしまった。<br>*The computer I'd only just bought has broken.*

---

## ～たところ · ～たところ vs ～たばかり (cont.)

❌<code><ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>ったところのパソコン</code> is not Japanese. If a noun follows, `ばかり` is your only option.

---

## ～たところ · ～たところ vs ～たあとで

> **Rule of thumb** - `たところ` is a **statement about now** and ends the sentence. `～たあとで` is a **connector** and always has another clause after it.

<ruby>仕事<rt>しごと</rt></ruby>が**<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わったところ**です。<br>*I've just finished work.*

<ruby>仕事<rt>しごと</rt></ruby>が<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わった**あとで**、<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>みに<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きます。<br>*After work I'm going out for a drink.*

The first sentence is complete; the second would be unfinished without its second half. And they carry different information: `あとで` says nothing at all about how recent the event is, while `たところ` says nothing about what happens next.

---

## ～たところ · ～たところ vs ～たあとで (cont.)

When you do want to hang a following clause on `たところ`, it needs a particle - `に`, `へ` or `で` - and the meaning becomes "just as I had done X, Y happened": <code><ruby>席<rt>せき</rt></ruby>に<ruby>座<rt>すわ</rt></ruby>ったところに<ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>入<rt>はい</rt></ruby>ってきた</code>.

---

## ～たところ · ～たところだ vs ～たところ、…

> **Rule of thumb** - with `だ`／`です` it means **"just finished"**. Standing at a comma with no copula, it is a formal connective meaning **"when I did X, it turned out that Y"**.

<ruby>課長<rt>かちょう</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>いたところ**です。<br>*I've just this minute asked the section chief.*

<ruby>課長<rt>かちょう</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>いたところ**、<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>になったそうです。<br>*I asked the section chief, and apparently the meeting has been cancelled.*

---

## ～たところ · ～たところだ vs ～たところ、… (cont.)

The connective version has three tells: no `だ`, a comma, and a second clause that reports something **discovered** as a result. It belongs to written and formal Japanese - reports, business email, news - and in speech people say <code><ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>いてみたら</code> instead. You need to recognise it so that a sentence like the second one does not read to you as "I have just asked."

---

## ～たところ · Common mistakes

- ❌ <ruby>去年<rt>きょねん</rt></ruby>この<ruby>会社<rt>かいしゃ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>入<rt>はい</rt></ruby>ったところです。 → ✅ <ruby>去年<rt>きょねん</rt></ruby>この<ruby>会社<rt>かいしゃ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>入<rt>はい</rt></ruby>った**ばかり**です。<br>*A year ago is not "just now" on any clock. Subjective recency is `ばかり`'s job.*

- ❌ これは<ruby>先週<rt>せんしゅう</rt></ruby><ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>った**ところの**<ruby>自転車<rt>じてんしゃ</rt></ruby>です。 → ✅ これは<ruby>先週<rt>せんしゅう</rt></ruby><ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>った**ばかりの**<ruby>自転車<rt>じてんしゃ</rt></ruby>です。<br>*`ところ` cannot modify a noun. When a noun follows, only `ばかり` works.*

- ❌ <ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>昼<rt>ひる</rt></ruby>ごはんを<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べる**ところ**です。（meaning "I've just eaten"） → ✅ <ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>昼<rt>ひる</rt></ruby>ごはんを<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べ**た**ところです。<br>*The dictionary form means you have not started. One character decides whether the food is gone.*

---

## ～たところ · Common mistakes (cont.)

- ❌ まだ<ruby>返事<rt>へんじ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>なかったところです。 → ✅ まだ<ruby>返事<rt>へんじ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>ていません。<br>*There is no negative version of this pattern. "Not yet" is `まだ～ていません`.*

---

## ～たところ · Practice 1

**1.** 「もう<ruby>昼<rt>ひる</rt></ruby>ごはんを<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べましたか。」「ええ、<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べ____ところです。」

{reveal}
ええ、<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べ**た**ところです。

{reveal}
The た-form places you immediately after the meal, which is what <code><ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby></code> and the question both call for. <code><ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べるところです</code> would mean the food is still untouched, and would answer the question with a flat no.

---

## ～たところ · Practice 2

**2.** <ruby>三年<rt>さんねん</rt></ruby><ruby>前<rt>まえ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>大学<rt>だいがく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>卒業<rt>そつぎょう</rt></ruby>した（ところ・ばかり）です。

{reveal}
<ruby>三年<rt>さんねん</rt></ruby><ruby>前<rt>まえ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>大学<rt>だいがく</rt></ruby>を<ruby>卒業<rt>そつぎょう</rt></ruby>した**ばかり**です。

{reveal}
Three years cannot be squeezed into `ところ`, which is measured on the clock. `ばかり` reports how recent it feels to the speaker - here, that they still count as a new graduate.

---

## ～たところ · Practice 3

**3.** Translate into Japanese: "The train has just left, so the next one is in ten minutes."

{reveal}
<ruby>電車<rt>でんしゃ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>**<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>たところ**なので、<ruby>次<rt>つぎ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>十分<rt>じゅっぷん</rt></ruby><ruby>後<rt>ご</rt></ruby>です。

{reveal}
The departure happened seconds ago and the sentence is about the clock, so `たところ` is exactly right. <code><ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>たばかり</code> would also be understood but would sound like a complaint about your luck rather than a timetable fact.

---

## ～たところ · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: これは<ruby>先月<rt>せんげつ</rt></ruby><ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>したところのテレビです。

{reveal}
✅ これは<ruby>先月<rt>せんげつ</rt></ruby><ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>した**ばかりの**テレビです。

{reveal}
Two problems, one fix. `ところ` cannot sit in front of a noun, and last month is too far back for it anyway. `ばかり` handles both: it takes `の` before a noun and it stretches to cover anything the speaker still thinks of as recent.

---

## ～たところ · Practice 5

**5.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>たところです。 (b) <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>たばかりです。

{reveal}
(a) means you have this moment arrived - you are at the airport, or you have just walked out of it, and the suitcase is still in your hand. It is a statement about the clock and it will not stretch past a few minutes.

{reveal}
(b) means you are new here. It might be a week, it might be six months; what it reports is that the arrival is still recent from where you stand. This is the one you use to explain why your Japanese is shaky or why you got lost, and (a) would be strange in that role.

---

# ～たばかり

**Meaning** · only just did it - recent as far as the speaker is concerned

`たばかり` also translates as "just", but it is measuring something quite different from `たところ`. `ところ` reads the clock. `ばかり` reads the **speaker**: it says the event is still recent *to them*, and that judgement stretches. Five minutes, five weeks, sometimes five years - as long as the speaker still feels new to it.

---

## ～たばかり · Formation

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Verb | **た-form** + ばかりだ | <ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>る → <ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>たばかりだ |
| Verb (voiced た-form) | だ-form + ばかりだ | <ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>む → <ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>んだばかりだ |
| Polite | た-form + ばかりです | <ruby>着<rt>つ</rt></ruby>いたばかりです |
| **Before a noun** | た-form + ばかり + **の** + Noun | <ruby>焼<rt>や</rt></ruby>いたばかりのパン |
| Giving a reason | たばかりなので／たばかりで | <ruby>入<rt>はい</rt></ruby>ったばかりなので… |
| Past reference | たばかりだった | <ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めたばかりだった |
| Casual | ばっかり／ばっか | <ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>たばっかり |
| Different sense: "only" | Noun + ばかり | ゲームばかりしている |
| Different sense: "nothing but" | て-form + ばかり + いる | <ruby>遊<rt>あそ</rt></ruby>んでばかりいる |

---

## ～たばかり · Formation (cont.)

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| ❌ Dictionary form | ❌<ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>るばかりです | ✅<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>たばかりです |

> **Rule of thumb** - recency here is **relative to the thing**. A bus that left five minutes ago, a job started last month and a building put up five years ago can all take `ばかり`, because "new" means something different for each. That flexibility is exactly what `たところ` refuses.

> **Note** - the noun-modifying form is the practical reason to learn this pattern. <code><ruby>生<rt>う</rt></ruby>まれたばかりの<ruby>赤<rt>あか</rt></ruby>ちゃん</code>, <code><ruby>習<rt>なら</rt></ruby>ったばかりの<ruby>漢字<rt>かんじ</rt></ruby></code>, <code><ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>ったばかりの<ruby>靴<rt>くつ</rt></ruby></code> - all completely ordinary, and none of them can be built with `ところ`. Do not drop the `の`.

---

## ～たばかり · Examples

さっき<ruby>昼<rt>ひる</rt></ruby>ごはんを<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べた**ばかり**です。<br>*I only had lunch a little while ago.*

この<ruby>会社<rt>かいしゃ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>入<rt>はい</rt></ruby>った**ばかり**で、まだ<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>もわかりません。<br>*I've only just joined this company, so I don't know anything yet.*

<ruby>焼<rt>や</rt></ruby>いた**ばかり**のパンはやっぱりおいしいね。<br>*Bread straight out of the oven really is good, isn't it.*

<ruby>生<rt>う</rt></ruby>まれた**ばかり**の<ruby>赤<rt>あか</rt></ruby>ちゃんは、<ruby>一日<rt>いちにち</rt></ruby><ruby>中<rt>じゅう</rt></ruby><ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>ています。<br>*A newborn baby sleeps all day long.*

---

## ～たばかり · Examples (cont.)

<ruby>習<rt>なら</rt></ruby>った**ばかり**の<ruby>漢字<rt>かんじ</rt></ruby>を、もう<ruby>忘<rt>わす</rt></ruby>れてしまいました。<br>*I've already forgotten the kanji I only just learned.*

<ruby>去年<rt>きょねん</rt></ruby><ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>った**ばかり**のパソコンなのに、もう<ruby>動<rt>うご</rt></ruby>かなくなった。<br>*I only bought this computer last year and it's already stopped working.*

この<ruby>町<rt>まち</rt></ruby>に<ruby>引<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>っ<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>してきた**ばかり**なので、この<ruby>辺<rt>へん</rt></ruby>のことはまだよく<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>らないんです。<br>*I've only just moved to this town, so I don't really know the area yet.*

<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>た**ばかり**のころは、コンビニで<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>い<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>をするだけでも<ruby>緊張<rt>きんちょう</rt></ruby>しました。<br>*When I'd only just arrived in Japan, even shopping in a convenience store made me nervous.*

---

## ～たばかり · Nuance & register

`たばかり` is register-neutral, and its most characteristic job is **explaining yourself**. `～たばかりなので` is how Japanese excuses inexperience, disorder or ignorance without apologising outright: <code><ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めたばかりなので、まだ<ruby>下手<rt>へた</rt></ruby>です</code>, <code><ruby>引<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>っ<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>したばかりで、<ruby>部屋<rt>へや</rt></ruby>が<ruby>片付<rt>かたづ</rt></ruby>いていません</code>. It buys the speaker some room, and because the recency is subjective, nobody argues with it.

In casual speech it lengthens rather than shortens: `ばっかり` and `ばっか` are both extremely common - <code><ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>起<rt>お</rt></ruby>きたばっかりだよ</code> - and both are firmly spoken-only.

---

## ～たばかり · Nuance & register (cont.)

Be aware that the same word `ばかり` has a much more frequent meaning, "only, nothing but": <code><ruby>肉<rt>にく</rt></ruby>ばかり<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べる</code>, <code><ruby>文句<rt>もんく</rt></ruby>ばかり<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>う</code>, <code><ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>てばかりいる</code>. The two are told apart by what comes in front. A **た-form** gives you "just did"; a **noun** or a **て-form** gives you "nothing but". Getting this wrong produces a sentence that means the opposite of what you intended, so it is worth a moment's care.

---

## ～たばかり · ～たばかり vs ～たところ

> **Rule of thumb** - `ところ` is measured on the **clock**; `ばかり` is measured by the **speaker**. In the few minutes after an event both are available; outside that window only `ばかり` survives.

<ruby>入学<rt>にゅうがく</rt></ruby>した**ばかり**なので、<ruby>友<rt>とも</rt></ruby>だちがまだ<ruby>少<rt>すく</rt></ruby>ないです。<br>*I've only just started at the school, so I don't have many friends yet.*

<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby><ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わった**ところ**です。<br>*The meeting finished just now.*

---

## ～たばかり · ～たばかり vs ～たところ (cont.)

Try swapping them. ❌<code><ruby>入学<rt>にゅうがく</rt></ruby>したところなので</code> would claim you enrolled minutes ago, which makes nonsense of the excuse. And <code><ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わったばかりです</code>, while perfectly grammatical, shifts the emphasis from the timetable to how it feels - closer to "it's barely over" than to "it finished at 3.02".

The second difference is the one that decides most sentences in practice: only `ばかり` can sit in front of a noun. <code><ruby>届<rt>とど</rt></ruby>いたばかりの<ruby>荷物<rt>にもつ</rt></ruby></code> is normal; ❌<code><ruby>届<rt>とど</rt></ruby>いたところの<ruby>荷物<rt>にもつ</rt></ruby></code> does not exist.

---

## ～たばかり · ～たばかり vs ばかり ("only, nothing but")

> **Rule of thumb** - look left. **た-form** + ばかり = "just did". **Noun** + ばかり, or **て-form** + ばかり + いる = "nothing but".

<ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>は<ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しいゲームを<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>った**ばかり**だ。<br>*My little brother has only just bought the new game.*

<ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>はゲーム**ばかり**している。<br>*My little brother does nothing but play games.*

---

## ～たばかり · ～たばかり vs ばかり ("only, nothing but") (cont.)

Same four syllables, and the two sentences do not even share a topic: the first is about when, the second about proportion. The `ている` version is the one to watch, because it looks so close to the pattern on this page: <code><ruby>泣<rt>な</rt></ruby>いてばかりいる</code> means "does nothing but cry", while <code><ruby>泣<rt>な</rt></ruby>いたばかりだ</code> would mean "has only just cried".

---

## ～たばかり · ～たばかり vs 最近

> **Rule of thumb** - <code><ruby>最近<rt>さいきん</rt></ruby></code> is an adverb about a **period**; `たばかり` attaches to a **single completed event**. They combine happily, but they are not substitutes.

**<ruby>最近<rt>さいきん</rt></ruby>**、よく<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>を<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きます。<br>*I've been going to the cinema a lot lately.*

この<ruby>店<rt>みせ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>先月<rt>せんげつ</rt></ruby><ruby>開<rt>ひら</rt></ruby>いた**ばかり**です。<br>*This shop only opened last month.*

---

## ～たばかり · ～たばかり vs 最近 (cont.)

<code><ruby>最近<rt>さいきん</rt></ruby></code> can cover a habit spread over weeks, which `ばかり` cannot do at all - there is no single event for it to attach to. Conversely `ばかり` pins the recency to one thing that happened, which is why it, and not <code><ruby>最近<rt>さいきん</rt></ruby></code>, can go in front of a noun.

Putting them together is completely normal and adds emphasis: <code><ruby>最近<rt>さいきん</rt></ruby><ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めたばかりの<ruby>趣味<rt>しゅみ</rt></ruby>です</code>, "it's a hobby I've only recently taken up."

---

## ～たばかり · Common mistakes

- ❌ <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>る**ばかり**です。 → ✅ <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>**た**ばかりです。<br>*This pattern is built on the た-form. The dictionary form gives you an entirely different, much rarer construction.*

- ❌ <ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>ったばかり<ruby>車<rt>くるま</rt></ruby>を<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>せてください。 → ✅ <ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>ったばかり**の**<ruby>車<rt>くるま</rt></ruby>を<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>せてください。<br>*In front of a noun, `ばかり` needs `の`. Leaving it out is the single most common slip with this pattern.*

- ❌ <ruby>兄<rt>あに</rt></ruby>は<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>た**ばかり**います。 → ✅ <ruby>兄<rt>あに</rt></ruby>は<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>**て**ばかりいます。<br>*"Does nothing but sleep" is built on the て-form plus `いる`. With the た-form the sentence would mean he had only just fallen asleep.*

---

## ～たばかり · Common mistakes (cont.)

- ❌ <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>**て**ばかりです。（meaning "I've only just come to Japan"） → ✅ <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>**た**ばかりです。<br>*The て-form pushes you into the "nothing but" meaning, which here would be something like "all I do is come to Japan".*

---

## ～たばかり · Practice 1

**1.** この<ruby>町<rt>まち</rt></ruby>に<ruby>引<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>っ<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>して<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>____ばかりなので、まだ<ruby>道<rt>みち</rt></ruby>がよくわかりません。

{reveal}
<ruby>引<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>っ<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>して<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>**た**ばかりなので…

{reveal}
The pattern needs the た-form. Note what the sentence is doing: the move might have been a month ago, and `ばかり` is being used to excuse not knowing the streets yet - a job the clock-bound `たところ` could not do.

---

## ～たばかり · Practice 2

**2.** これは<ruby>五年<rt>ごねん</rt></ruby><ruby>前<rt>まえ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>建<rt>た</rt></ruby>った（ところ・ばかり）のビルです。

{reveal}
これは<ruby>五年<rt>ごねん</rt></ruby><ruby>前<rt>まえ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>建<rt>た</rt></ruby>った**ばかり**のビルです。

{reveal}
Two reasons, and either one settles it. Five years is far outside `ところ`'s range, and `ところ` cannot modify a noun in the first place. For a building, five years old genuinely counts as new - which is exactly the kind of judgement `ばかり` is built to express.

---

## ～たばかり · Practice 3

**3.** Translate into Japanese: "These are cakes I've just baked - please help yourself."

{reveal}
<ruby>焼<rt>や</rt></ruby>いた**ばかりの**ケーキです。どうぞ<ruby>召<rt>め</rt></ruby>し<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がってください。

{reveal}
A noun follows, so the form must be `たばかりの` with the `の` in place. This is the everyday way to say "freshly made", and it is one of the commonest uses of the pattern.

---

## ～たばかり · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: <ruby>息子<rt>むすこ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>しないで、<ruby>遊<rt>あそ</rt></ruby>んだばかりいます。

{reveal}
✅ <ruby>息子<rt>むすこ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>しないで、<ruby>遊<rt>あそ</rt></ruby>**んで**ばかりいます。

{reveal}
"Does nothing but play" is the *other* `ばかり`, and it is built on the て-form plus `いる`. With the た-form the sentence would say he had only just started playing, which is not a complaint at all.

---

## ～たばかり · Practice 5

**5.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) <ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>仕事<rt>しごと</rt></ruby>を<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めたばかりです。 (b) <ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>仕事<rt>しごと</rt></ruby>を<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めたところです。

{reveal}
(a) says you are new to the job. It could be your third day or your third month; what the sentence claims is that you have not settled in yet, and it usually leads into an explanation - you are still learning, you cannot answer that question without asking someone.

{reveal}
(b) reads the clock. It says the starting happened moments ago, which for a job is odd unless you are describing this morning: "I've just this minute started." Native speakers would understand it as the literal instant, and would probably have expected (a).

---

# N4 - Doing things for each other, and asking favours

- ～てあげる
- ～てくれる
- ～てもらう
- ～てやる
- ～てほしい
- ～てもらえませんか・～てくれませんか
- ～ていただけませんか
- ～てすみません

---

# N4 - Doing things for each other, and asking favours (cont.)

- ～てよかった

---

# ～てあげる

**Meaning** · do something *for* someone - the action itself is the gift, and it travels away from the speaker

At N5 you learned that `あげる` hands an **object** to someone outside your circle. `～てあげる` hands over an **action** instead. The direction rule is identical; what is new is that naming an act as a favour puts it on the record, and that can be generous or it can be smug, depending on who you say it to.

---

## ～てあげる · Formation

Attach `あげる` to the て-form. `あげる` then conjugates as an ordinary る-verb.

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Verb | て-form + あげる | <ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>る → <ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>ってあげる |
| Verb (polite) | て-form + あげます | <ruby>貸<rt>か</rt></ruby>す → <ruby>貸<rt>か</rt></ruby>してあげました |
| Verb (offering) | て-form + あげよう／あげましょうか | <ruby>運<rt>はこ</rt></ruby>ぶ → <ruby>運<rt>はこ</rt></ruby>んであげましょうか |
| To someone above you (humble) | て-form + さしあげる | <ruby>案内<rt>あんない</rt></ruby>する → <ruby>案内<rt>あんない</rt></ruby>してさしあげる |
| To someone below you / an animal | て-form + やる | <ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>う → <ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>ってやる |

The particle on the person who benefits is **not** decided by `あげる`. It is decided by the verb underneath, exactly as it would be without `あげる` attached:

---

## ～てあげる · Formation (cont.)

| Underlying verb frame | Particle | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Verb already takes <ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>に | に | <ruby>友<rt>とも</rt></ruby>だち**に**<ruby>道<rt>みち</rt></ruby>を<ruby>教<rt>おし</rt></ruby>えてあげる |
| Verb already takes <ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>を | を | <ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>ども**を**<ruby>迎<rt>むか</rt></ruby>えに<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>ってあげる |
| Verb acts on the person's possession | の | <ruby>母<rt>はは</rt></ruby>**の**<ruby>荷物<rt>にもつ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>ってあげる |

> **Rule of thumb** - the benefit must land **outside** the speaker. There is no ❌<code><ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>に<ruby>教<rt>おし</rt></ruby>えてあげる</code>. If the favour comes toward you or your family, the verb you need is <code><ruby>教<rt>おし</rt></ruby>えてくれる</code>.

---

## ～てあげる · Examples

<ruby>妹<rt>いもうと</rt></ruby>に<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>んであげた**。<br>*I read my little sister a book.*

<ruby>荷物<rt>にもつ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>重<rt>おも</rt></ruby>そうだったので、**<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>ってあげました**。<br>*The bags looked heavy, so I carried them for her.*

お<ruby>母<rt>かあ</rt></ruby>さんに**<ruby>電話<rt>でんわ</rt></ruby>してあげて**。<ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>してるよ。<br>*Give your mum a call. She's worried.*

<ruby>道<rt>みち</rt></ruby>が<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>からないと<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>うので、<ruby>駅<rt>えき</rt></ruby>まで**<ruby>案内<rt>あんない</rt></ruby>してあげた**。<br>*He said he didn't know the way, so I walked him to the station.*

---

## ～てあげる · Examples (cont.)

<ruby>息子<rt>むすこ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>自転車<rt>じてんしゃ</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>してあげたら**、とても<ruby>喜<rt>よろこ</rt></ruby>んだ。<br>*When I fixed my son's bike for him, he was delighted.*

<ruby>留学生<rt>りゅうがくせい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>漢字<rt>かんじ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>み<ruby>方<rt>かた</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>教<rt>おし</rt></ruby>えてあげる**<ruby>約束<rt>やくそく</rt></ruby>をしました。<br>*I promised to teach the exchange student how to read kanji.*

<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>ってきたから、<ruby>隣<rt>となり</rt></ruby>のおばあさんの<ruby>洗濯物<rt>せんたくもの</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>取<rt>と</rt></ruby>り<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>んであげました**。<br>*It started raining, so I brought in the laundry for the old lady next door.*

<ruby>自分<rt>じぶん</rt></ruby>で<ruby>考<rt>かんが</rt></ruby>えさせたほうがいいので、<ruby>答<rt>こた</rt></ruby>えは**<ruby>教<rt>おし</rt></ruby>えてあげません**でした。<br>*It's better to make him think for himself, so I didn't give him the answer.*

---

## ～てあげる · Nuance & register

**`～てあげる` announces the favour.** That is its entire function, and it is why the pattern needs handling. <code><ruby>荷物<rt>にもつ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>ちましょうか</code> is a plain offer to carry a bag. <code><ruby>荷物<rt>にもつ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>ってあげましょうか</code> adds "…as a kindness to you", and the person hearing it now has a debt on the table they did not ask for. Between friends this is warm. Aimed at a stranger, a customer or anyone senior, it lands as condescending.

The safe habit: **do not say `～てあげる` to the person receiving the favour.** Say it *about* the favour afterwards, or to a third party.

---

## ～てあげる · Nuance & register (cont.)

- To the person: <ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>いましょうか。／お<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>いしましょうか。
- About it later: <ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>、<ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんの<ruby>引<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>っ<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>しを<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>ってあげた。

`さしあげる` does **not** rescue the situation. It is grammatically the humble form, but announcing to a superior that you have bestowed something on them is worse, not better - the humility is in the word and the presumption is in the construction. Real Japanese reaches for the honorific-humble frame instead: お<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>ちします, ご<ruby>案内<rt>あんない</rt></ruby>します, お<ruby>貸<rt>か</rt></ruby>しします. Keep `さしあげる` for narrating in the third person （<ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>にお<ruby>土産<rt>みやげ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>ってさしあげた）and even there it is slightly stiff.

---

## ～てあげる · Nuance & register (cont.)

`～てやる` is the downward member of the family - for animals, plants, small children, one's own younger siblings - and it is blunter and more male-marked.

There is a second, sharper `～てあげる`: said with a flat tone about something the listener does not want, it turns sarcastic or threatening. <ruby>本当<rt>ほんとう</rt></ruby>のことを<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>ってあげようか - "shall I *do you the favour* of telling you the truth?" The mechanism is the same: you are insisting that this is a kindness when both of you know it is not.

In casual speech the contraction is `～たげる`: <ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>ってあげる → <ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>ったげる, <ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>ておいてあげる → <ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>といたげる. Common in the Kansai area and in relaxed speech generally; never write it.

---

## ～てあげる · ～てあげる vs ～てくれる

> **Rule of thumb** - same event, opposite direction. `～てあげる` when the favour leaves your side; `～てくれる` when it arrives at your side.

The subject of both is the person **doing** the action. What changes is where the benefit ends up relative to the うち／そと line you learned at N5.

<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>が<ruby>山田<rt>やまだ</rt></ruby>さんの<ruby>仕事<rt>しごと</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>ってあげた**。<br>*I helped Yamada with his work.*

<ruby>山田<rt>やまだ</rt></ruby>さんが<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>の<ruby>仕事<rt>しごと</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>ってくれた**。<br>*Yamada helped me with my work.*

---

## ～てあげる · ～てあげる vs ～てくれる (cont.)

The line is your family, not just your body. If a teacher explains something to your daughter, that favour has come toward your side, so it is <ruby>娘<rt>むすめ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>してくださいました - never ❌してあげました, which would push your own daughter into the そと group.

---

## ～てあげる · ～てあげる vs the plain verb

> **Rule of thumb** - the plain verb reports *what happened*. `～てあげる` reports *who it was for*. If the beneficiary is not the point, leave it off.

<ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>、<ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>の<ruby>部屋<rt>へや</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>片<rt>かた</rt></ruby>づけました**。<br>*I tidied my brother's room yesterday.*

<ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>、<ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>の<ruby>部屋<rt>へや</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>片<rt>かた</rt></ruby>づけてあげました**。<br>*I tidied my brother's room for him yesterday.*

Both are correct. The second one is the version you say when you want credit, or when you are complaining that you had to. This is not a subtlety learners can skip: overusing `～てあげる` is one of the clearest markers of a foreign speaker, because English "for him" is neutral and Japanese `～てあげる` is not.

---

## ～てあげる · ～てあげる vs ～させてあげる

> **Rule of thumb** - `～てあげる` means you *did* it for them. `～させてあげる` means you *let them* do it, as a kindness.

English "let him" and "did it for him" are far apart; in Japanese they are one suffix apart, and learners reach for the wrong one.

<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>どもに<ruby>絵<rt>え</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>描<rt>か</rt></ruby>いてあげた**。<br>*I drew a picture for my child.*

<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>どもに<ruby>自由<rt>じゆう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>絵<rt>え</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>描<rt>か</rt></ruby>かせてあげた**。<br>*I let my child draw whatever they liked.*

---

## ～てあげる · ～てあげる vs ～させてあげる (cont.)

The causative `～させてあげる` is extremely common with permission （<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>ませてあげる, <ruby>遊<rt>あそ</rt></ruby>ばせてあげる）and carries the same warmth - and the same risk of sounding lofty about your own generosity.

---

## ～てあげる · Common mistakes

- ❌ <ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんが<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>に<ruby>地図<rt>ちず</rt></ruby>を<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>いて**あげました**。 → ✅ <ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんが<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>に<ruby>地図<rt>ちず</rt></ruby>を<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>いて**くれました**。<br>*A favour arriving at the speaker can never be `～てあげる`. This is the N5 あげる／くれる rule, unchanged.*

- ❌ <ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>、この<ruby>資料<rt>しりょう</rt></ruby>をコピーして**さしあげましょうか**。 → ✅ <ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>、この<ruby>資料<rt>しりょう</rt></ruby>をコピー**しましょうか**。／お<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>ちしましょうか。<br>*Offering a superior a *labelled* favour is presumptuous even in the humble form. Drop the giving verb and use the plain offer or the お～します frame.*

- ❌ <ruby>友<rt>とも</rt></ruby>だち**に**<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>ってあげました。 → ✅ <ruby>友<rt>とも</rt></ruby>だち**を**<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>ってあげました。<br>*`あげる` does not assign the particle. <code><ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>う</code> takes <ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>を, so the person keeps `を`.*

---

## ～てあげる · Common mistakes (cont.)

- ❌ <ruby>傘<rt>かさ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>貸<rt>か</rt></ruby>し**あげます**。 → ✅ <ruby>傘<rt>かさ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>貸<rt>か</rt></ruby>し**てあげます**。<br>*`あげる` attaches to the て-form, not the ます-stem.*

- ❌ <ruby>母<rt>はは</rt></ruby>が<ruby>妹<rt>いもうと</rt></ruby>にセーターを<ruby>編<rt>あ</rt></ruby>んで**あげました**。（telling an outsider）→ ✅ <ruby>母<rt>はは</rt></ruby>が<ruby>妹<rt>いもうと</rt></ruby>にセーターを<ruby>編<rt>あ</rt></ruby>んで**くれました**。<br>*Both are inside your family, so from your chair the favour landed on your side. `あげる` here would sound as though neither of them were related to you.*

---

## ～てあげる · Practice 1

**1.** <ruby>荷物<rt>にもつ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>多<rt>おお</rt></ruby>かったので、<ruby>後輩<rt>こうはい</rt></ruby>のかばんを<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>っ____。

{reveal}
<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>っ**てあげました**。

{reveal}
The favour goes from the speaker outward to a junior colleague, so `～てあげる` is the right direction. Note the `の` on <code><ruby>後輩<rt>こうはい</rt></ruby></code>: the verb acts on the bag, and the owner of the bag is marked with `の`.

---

## ～てあげる · Practice 2

**2.** Choose: <ruby>課長<rt>かちょう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しいやり<ruby>方<rt>かた</rt></ruby>を<ruby>教<rt>おし</rt></ruby>えて（あげました・くださいました）。

{reveal}
<ruby>課長<rt>かちょう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しいやり<ruby>方<rt>かた</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>教<rt>おし</rt></ruby>えてくださいました**。

{reveal}
The section chief is the one acting and the benefit reaches the speaker, so the verb must be the toward-me one, in its honorific form. `あげました` would reverse the direction and put the speaker above the boss.

---

## ～てあげる · Practice 3

**3.** Translate into Japanese: "I'll look after the dog for you while you're away."

{reveal}
<ruby>留守<rt>るす</rt></ruby>の<ruby>間<rt>あいだ</rt></ruby>、<ruby>犬<rt>いぬ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>世話<rt>せわ</rt></ruby>を**してあげるよ**。

{reveal}
Said to a close friend this is warm and normal. To an acquaintance you would drop the giving verb - <ruby>犬<rt>いぬ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>世話<rt>せわ</rt></ruby>をしておきますよ - because announcing the favour to its recipient is what makes `～てあげる` sound self-satisfied.

---

## ～てあげる · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>、<ruby>重<rt>おも</rt></ruby>そうですね。<ruby>荷物<rt>にもつ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>ってあげましょうか。

{reveal}
✅ <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>、<ruby>重<rt>おも</rt></ruby>そうですね。お<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>ち**しましょうか**。

{reveal}
The grammar is fine and the effect is rude: you are informing your teacher that you are about to be generous to them. Swapping in `さしあげましょうか` does not help. The natural offer upward is the humble お + ます-stem + します frame.

---

## ～てあげる · Practice 5

**5.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) <ruby>窓<rt>まど</rt></ruby>を<ruby>開<rt>あ</rt></ruby>けました。 (b) <ruby>窓<rt>まど</rt></ruby>を<ruby>開<rt>あ</rt></ruby>けてあげました。

{reveal}
(a) is a neutral report of an action: the window got opened, and nothing is said about who wanted it open.

{reveal}
(b) frames the same action as a service performed for somebody - you opened it *for* them, because they were hot or could not reach. It implies a specific beneficiary who is not you, and depending on tone it can carry either kindness or a hint of "and you're welcome". If the beneficiary is the person you are speaking to, (a) is almost always the better choice.

---

# ～てくれる

**Meaning** · someone does something for me, or for my side - and I am grateful for it

`～てくれる` is the action counterpart of the `くれる` you met at N5. Someone else performs the verb, and the good of it arrives at the speaker's うち. Unlike `～てあげる`, this one is not risky to say: marking a favour that came *to* you is simply politeness, and leaving it off can sound cold.

---

## ～てくれる · Formation

Attach `くれる` to the て-form. The doer is the subject; the beneficiary - usually <code><ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby></code> - is normally left unsaid, because the verb has already said it.

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Verb | て-form + くれる | <ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>う → <ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>ってくれる |
| Verb (polite) | て-form + くれます | <ruby>送<rt>おく</rt></ruby>る → <ruby>送<rt>おく</rt></ruby>ってくれました |
| Verb (negative) | て-form + くれない | <ruby>返事<rt>へんじ</rt></ruby>する → <ruby>返事<rt>へんじ</rt></ruby>してくれない |
| From someone above you (honorific) | て-form + くださる → くださいます | <ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>す → <ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>してくださいました |
| Casual request | て-form + くれない？／くれる？ | <ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>つ → <ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ってくれない? |

---

## ～てくれる · Formation (cont.)

The sentence frame is <code>Aが（<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>に）～てくれる</code>. As with plain `くれる`, the particle on the beneficiary comes from the underlying verb - <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>に<ruby>教<rt>おし</rt></ruby>えてくれる but <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>を<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ってくれる.

> **Rule of thumb** - `～てくれる` can never have the speaker as the doer. There is no ❌<code><ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>が<ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんに<ruby>貸<rt>か</rt></ruby>してくれた</code>. Nothing can move toward you while you are the one doing it.

> **Note** - the ます-form of `くださる` is irregular: **くださいます**, not ❌くださります. And the `ください` you have used since your first week is nothing more than the imperative of this verb - <code><ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ってください</code> is literally "give me the favour of waiting".

---

## ～てくれる · Examples

<ruby>父<rt>ちち</rt></ruby>が<ruby>駅<rt>えき</rt></ruby>まで**<ruby>送<rt>おく</rt></ruby>ってくれました**。<br>*My dad drove me to the station.*

だれが<ruby>窓<rt>まど</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>閉<rt>し</rt></ruby>めてくれた**の?<br>*Who closed the window for me?*

<ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>作文<rt>さくぶん</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>してくださいました**。<br>*My teacher kindly corrected my essay.*

<ruby>同<rt>おな</rt></ruby>じ<ruby>課<rt>か</rt></ruby>の<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>が<ruby>仕事<rt>しごと</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>代<rt>か</rt></ruby>わってくれて**、<ruby>助<rt>たす</rt></ruby>かりました。<br>*Someone in my section covered my shift, which was a real help.*

---

## ～てくれる · Examples (cont.)

だれも**<ruby>教<rt>おし</rt></ruby>えてくれなかった**から、<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>変<rt>か</rt></ruby>わったのを<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>らなかった。<br>*Nobody told me, so I didn't know the meeting time had changed.*

<ruby>妻<rt>つま</rt></ruby>が<ruby>毎朝<rt>まいあさ</rt></ruby>お<ruby>弁当<rt>べんとう</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>ってくれる**ので、<ruby>昼<rt>ひる</rt></ruby>ごはんに<ruby>困<rt>こま</rt></ruby>りません。<br>*My wife makes me a packed lunch every morning, so lunch is never a problem.*

<ruby>息子<rt>むすこ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>熱<rt>ねつ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>したとき、<ruby>隣<rt>となり</rt></ruby>の<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>が<ruby>病院<rt>びょういん</rt></ruby>まで<ruby>車<rt>くるま</rt></ruby>で**<ruby>運<rt>はこ</rt></ruby>んでくださいました**。<br>*When my son had a fever, our neighbour was kind enough to drive us to the hospital.*

<ruby>忙<rt>いそが</rt></ruby>しいのに<ruby>最後<rt>さいご</rt></ruby>まで<ruby>話<rt>はなし</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>いてくれて**、<ruby>本当<rt>ほんとう</rt></ruby>にありがとう。<br>*Thank you so much for hearing me out to the end even though you were busy.*

---

## ～てくれる · Nuance & register

`～てくれる` is **gratitude built into the grammar**. Japanese has no polite way to report a favour received without it. If a colleague fixes your spreadsheet and you tell someone <ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんが<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>しました, you have described an event; add `くれました` and you have acknowledged a kindness. Omitting it where it belongs sounds ungrateful in a way that has no English equivalent, so learners should err toward using it.

The single most useful frame built on it is `～てくれて、ありがとう` - the standard way to thank someone for an **action**（<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>てくれてありがとう）, as opposed to `～をありがとう` for a thing. Polite version: `～てくださって、ありがとうございます`. Also common: <code>～てくれて<ruby>助<rt>たす</rt></ruby>かりました</code>, "you saved me."

---

## ～てくれる · Nuance & register (cont.)

The **negative** is where the emotion flips. `～てくれない` / `～てくれなかった` is a complaint, not a neutral report: it says the favour was owed and did not arrive. <ruby>誰<rt>だれ</rt></ruby>も<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>ってくれなかった means "nobody would help me", with the resentment audible. Compare the bare <ruby>誰<rt>だれ</rt></ruby>も<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>いませんでした, which is a flat statement of fact.

In the **question** form `～てくれない?` the same negative becomes a soft casual request - the first rung of the request ladder that runs on up through `～てくれませんか`, `～てもらえませんか` and `～ていただけませんか`.

---

## ～てくれる · Nuance & register (cont.)

Register notes: `くれる` is plain, `くれます` polite, `くださる` honorific. `くださる` is used for a superior's kindness toward you and is completely standard in business speech. The plain imperative `くれ`（<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ってくれ）is rough, male-marked and abrupt - fine among close male friends, never to a stranger. In fast speech `～てくれる` reduces to `～てくれ` + rising tone or, very casually, <ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>せてくんない? Do not write that.

One extension worth knowing: `～てくれる` can be used with things and weather by personification, and it is warm rather than childish - <ruby>天気<rt>てんき</rt></ruby>が<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>ってくれてよかった, "thankfully the weather held out for us."

---

## ～てくれる · ～てくれる vs ～てもらう

> **Rule of thumb** - one event, two chairs. `～てくれる` seats the **doer** as subject; `～てもらう` seats the **beneficiary** as subject.

<ruby>友<rt>とも</rt></ruby>だちが<ruby>引<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>っ<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>しを**<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>ってくれました**。<br>*My friend helped me move.*

<ruby>友<rt>とも</rt></ruby>だちに<ruby>引<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>っ<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>しを**<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>ってもらいました**。<br>*I got my friend to help me move.*

Both are natural and describe the same afternoon. The difference is initiative and warmth. `くれる` presents the friend as acting of his own accord and reads as thanks. `もらう` presents the speaker as having arranged it, which is why it is the form you use when you asked, hired, or requested. Notice the particle flip on the friend: `が` as subject, `に` as source.

---

## ～てくれる · ～てくれる vs ～てくださる

> **Rule of thumb** - `くださる` is `くれる` with a status gap. Use it when the person doing you the favour is above you, or is a customer.

<ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>空港<rt>くうこう</rt></ruby>まで**<ruby>迎<rt>むか</rt></ruby>えに<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>てくださいました**。<br>*The department head came to meet me at the airport.*

Using plain `くれました` about a superior is grammatical but flat, and in front of that superior or their colleagues it sounds disrespectful. In private grumbling to a friend it is perfectly normal - the choice tracks the audience as much as the person.

---

## ～てくれる · ～てくれる vs ～てあげる

> **Rule of thumb** - `くれる` is safe to say to anyone; `あげる` is not.

They are mirror images grammatically, but not socially. Thanking someone with <code><ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>ってくれてありがとう</code> is warm. Telling that same person <code><ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>ってあげたよ</code> is smug, because you are the one naming your own act a favour.

<ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんが<ruby>会場<rt>かいじょう</rt></ruby>まで<ruby>地図<rt>ちず</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>いてくれた**。<br>*Tanaka drew me a map to the venue.*

<ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんに<ruby>会場<rt>かいじょう</rt></ruby>までの<ruby>地図<rt>ちず</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>いてあげた**。<br>*I drew Tanaka a map to the venue.*

---

## ～てくれる · Common mistakes

- ❌ <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>が<ruby>友<rt>とも</rt></ruby>だちに<ruby>自転車<rt>じてんしゃ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>貸<rt>か</rt></ruby>して**くれました**。 → ✅ <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>が<ruby>友<rt>とも</rt></ruby>だちに<ruby>自転車<rt>じてんしゃ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>貸<rt>か</rt></ruby>して**あげました**。<br>*`くれる` cannot take the speaker as the doer. When the favour leaves you, it is `あげる`.*

- ❌ <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>して**くださりました**。 → ✅ <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>して**くださいました**。<br>*`くださる` has an irregular ます-form, like おっしゃる → おっしゃいます.*

- ❌ <ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>てくれて**ありがとうを<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>います**。 → ✅ <ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>てくれて**ありがとう**。<br>*Thanks for an action is expressed with `～てくれてありがとう` directly; there is no need to build a sentence around the word ありがとう.*

---

## ～てくれる · Common mistakes (cont.)

- ❌ <ruby>母<rt>はは</rt></ruby>が<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>に<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>った<ruby>料理<rt>りょうり</rt></ruby>はおいしいです。 → ✅ <ruby>母<rt>はは</rt></ruby>が<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>ってくれた<ruby>料理<rt>りょうり</rt></ruby>はおいしいです。<br>*Not ungrammatical, but a Japanese speaker would hear the missing `くれる` as oddly detached about their own mother's cooking.*

- ❌ <ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>って**くれ**、お<ruby>願<rt>ねが</rt></ruby>いします。 → ✅ <ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>って**ください**。／<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>って**くれない**?<br>*Bare `くれ` is a rough male command and clashes with a polite frame.*

---

## ～てくれる · Practice 1

**1.** <ruby>友<rt>とも</rt></ruby>だちが<ruby>空港<rt>くうこう</rt></ruby>まで<ruby>迎<rt>むか</rt></ruby>えに<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>て____ので、タクシーに<ruby>乗<rt>の</rt></ruby>らずにすみました。

{reveal}
<ruby>迎<rt>むか</rt></ruby>えに<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>て**くれた**ので…

{reveal}
The friend acted and the benefit reached the speaker, so `くれる` is required. It also does real work in the sentence: it is what tells the listener the trip to the airport was a kindness rather than a coincidence.

---

## ～てくれる · Practice 2

**2.** Choose: <ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>推薦状<rt>すいせんじょう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>いて（くれました・くださいました）。You are telling a colleague at work.

{reveal}
<ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>推薦状<rt>すいせんじょう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>いて**くださいました**。

{reveal}
A department head is above you, and you are speaking in a workplace register, so the honorific `くださる` is the expected choice. `くれました` is not wrong Japanese, but about a superior at work it sounds careless.

---

## ～てくれる · Practice 3

**3.** Translate into Japanese: "Thank you for waiting."

{reveal}
**<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>っていてくれて、ありがとう**。／ polite: **お<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ちくださって、ありがとうございます**。

{reveal}
Thanks for an *action* is built on `～てくれて`, not on a noun. Note the `ていて`: the person was in the state of waiting, so <code><ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>っていて</code> is more natural than the bare <code><ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>って</code>.

---

## ～てくれる · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: <ruby>山田<rt>やまだ</rt></ruby>さんは<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>に<ruby>日本語<rt>にほんご</rt></ruby>を<ruby>教<rt>おし</rt></ruby>えてあげました。

{reveal}
✅ <ruby>山田<rt>やまだ</rt></ruby>さんは<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>に<ruby>日本語<rt>にほんご</rt></ruby>を<ruby>教<rt>おし</rt></ruby>えて**くれました**。

{reveal}
The teaching arrives at the speaker, so the direction verb must be `くれる`. As written, the sentence claims Yamada did the speaker a favour *away from* the speaker, which is impossible.

---

## ～てくれる · Practice 5

**5.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) <ruby>誰<rt>だれ</rt></ruby>も<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>いませんでした。 (b) <ruby>誰<rt>だれ</rt></ruby>も<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>ってくれませんでした。

{reveal}
(a) is a neutral fact: no help occurred. It could describe a task nobody was expected to join.

{reveal}
(b) adds the speaker's stake. Because `くれる` frames help as something that should have come toward them, its negative says the help was owed and withheld - "nobody would lift a finger for me." It is a complaint, and native listeners hear the resentment clearly.

---

# ～てもらう

**Meaning** · get someone to do something for you; have something done for your benefit

`～てもらう` describes the same favour as `～てくれる`, but from the receiving chair. The person who benefits becomes the **subject** of the sentence, and the person who actually does the work is demoted to a `に` phrase. That re-arrangement is the whole difficulty: English "I had my hair cut" hides the hairdresser, and Japanese puts them back in with `に`.

---

## ～てもらう · Formation

Attach `もらう` to the て-form. The frame is `Bは Aに ～てもらう` - B receives, A does.

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Verb | て-form + もらう | <ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>す → <ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>してもらう |
| Verb (polite) | て-form + もらいます | <ruby>送<rt>おく</rt></ruby>る → <ruby>送<rt>おく</rt></ruby>ってもらいました |
| From someone above you (humble) | て-form + いただく | <ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>る → <ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>ていただきました |
| Potential (used for requests) | て-form + もらえる／いただける | <ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>る → <ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>てもらえますか |
| Negative potential (polite request) | て-form + もらえませんか | <ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>つ → <ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ってもらえませんか |

> **Rule of thumb** - the doer takes `に`. Not `が`, which would make them the receiver, and not `を`, which is reserved for the thing acted on.

---

## ～てもらう · Formation (cont.)

`から` is possible instead of `に` when the favour is information or an object moving from a source, and it is preferred when the giver is an organisation: <ruby>大学<rt>だいがく</rt></ruby>**から**<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>してもらいました. With most action verbs, `に` is the default.

> **Note** - the beneficiary is normally the speaker or the speaker's side, exactly as with `くれる`. <ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんは<ruby>山田<rt>やまだ</rt></ruby>さんに<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>ってもらった is fine when you are narrating about a third party, but it quietly puts you in Tanaka's camp for the length of the sentence.

---

## ～てもらう · Examples

<ruby>友<rt>とも</rt></ruby>だちに<ruby>写真<rt>しゃしん</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>撮<rt>と</rt></ruby>ってもらった**。<br>*I got a friend to take a photo of me.*

<ruby>駅員<rt>えきいん</rt></ruby>さんに<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>き<ruby>方<rt>かた</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>教<rt>おし</rt></ruby>えてもらいました**。<br>*I had the station attendant tell me how to get there.*

パソコンが<ruby>動<rt>うご</rt></ruby>かなくなったので、<ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>てもらった**。<br>*My laptop stopped working, so I got my brother to take a look at it.*

<ruby>来週<rt>らいしゅう</rt></ruby>、<ruby>美容院<rt>びよういん</rt></ruby>で<ruby>髪<rt>かみ</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>切<rt>き</rt></ruby>ってもらう**<ruby>予定<rt>よてい</rt></ruby>です。<br>*I'm getting my hair cut at the salon next week.*

---

## ～てもらう · Examples (cont.)

<ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>書類<rt>しょるい</rt></ruby>にサインを**していただきました**。<br>*I had the department head sign the documents.*

<ruby>引<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>っ<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>しの<ruby>日<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>後輩<rt>こうはい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>車<rt>くるま</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>してもらう**つもりです。<br>*I'm planning to get a junior colleague to lend me his car on moving day.*

<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>き<ruby>方<rt>かた</rt></ruby>が<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>からなかったので、<ruby>窓口<rt>まどぐち</rt></ruby>の<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>にゆっくり**<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>していただきました**。<br>*I didn't know how to fill it in, so I had the clerk at the counter explain it slowly.*

<ruby>自分<rt>じぶん</rt></ruby>で<ruby>決<rt>き</rt></ruby>められないなら、<ruby>一度<rt>いちど</rt></ruby><ruby>専門家<rt>せんもんか</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>相談<rt>そうだん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>乗<rt>の</rt></ruby>ってもらった**ほうがいいですよ。<br>*If you can't decide on your own, you'd do better to get a specialist to talk it through with you.*

---

## ～てもらう · Nuance & register

**`～てもらう` implies the receiver had a hand in it.** Not always a spoken request - sometimes just consent, or having gone somewhere for the service - but the event is not a bolt from the blue. That is why <ruby>髪<rt>かみ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>切<rt>き</rt></ruby>ってもらった is the normal way to say you had a haircut: you went to the salon and asked. Compare <ruby>急<rt>きゅう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>がやんでくれた, where nothing was arranged, and only `くれる` works.

Because the receiver is the subject, `～てもらう` is also the natural frame for **planning and arranging**: <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>、<ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんに<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>てもらいます means "I'll have Tanaka come" - the speaker is organising it. Said about a person present, this can sound managerial, so it belongs downward or sideways, not upward.

---

## ～てもらう · Nuance & register (cont.)

`～ていただく` is the humble form and is one of the workhorses of business Japanese. Whole registers of office speech are built on it: ご<ruby>確認<rt>かくにん</rt></ruby>いただけますでしょうか, <ruby>少々<rt>しょうしょう</rt></ruby>お<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ちいただきます. Note the honorific frame `お／ご + stem + いただく` （お<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ちいただく, ご<ruby>記入<rt>きにゅう</rt></ruby>いただく）, which is politer still than <code><ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>っていただく</code> and very common on signs and announcements.

The potential forms are where this pattern earns its keep in daily life. `もらえる` means "can receive the favour", which is exactly what a request is:

---

## ～てもらう · Nuance & register (cont.)

- `～てもらえる?` - casual, to a friend
- `～てもらえますか` - polite, everyday
- `～てもらえませんか` - politer; the negative leaves room to refuse
- `～ていただけませんか` - humble, business standard
- `～ていただけないでしょうか` - the top of the ladder

Register: `もらう` is neutral in plain and polite speech alike, with no male/female marking. `いただく` belongs to formal and business situations; using it with close friends sounds like you are being funny on purpose. Casually `もらえる?` often contracts in speech to `もらえん?` in western dialects - regional, not standard.

---

## ～てもらう · ～てもらう vs ～てくれる

> **Rule of thumb** - `～てもらう` says *I got them to*; `～てくれる` says *they did it for me*. Initiative sits with the subject.

<ruby>近所<rt>きんじょ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>に<ruby>留守<rt>るす</rt></ruby>の<ruby>間<rt>あいだ</rt></ruby><ruby>猫<rt>ねこ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>世話<rt>せわ</rt></ruby>を**してもらいました**。<br>*I got a neighbour to look after the cat while I was away.*

<ruby>近所<rt>きんじょ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>が<ruby>留守<rt>るす</rt></ruby>の<ruby>間<rt>あいだ</rt></ruby><ruby>猫<rt>ねこ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>世話<rt>せわ</rt></ruby>を**してくれました**。<br>*A neighbour looked after the cat for me while I was away.*

---

## ～てもらう · ～てもらう vs ～てくれる (cont.)

The first says you arranged it. The second says they stepped in - and it carries more warmth, which is why thanks are almost always phrased with `くれる`: <ruby>世話<rt>せわ</rt></ruby>をしてくれてありがとう. してもらってありがとう is occasionally heard in casual speech, but it is not the standard shape: gratitude points at what the other person did, so the giving verb is the one that belongs there.

There is a hard limit on `もらう`. If the doer acted entirely on their own and the event was not arranged, `もらう` is unnatural: <ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>らない<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>が<ruby>財布<rt>さいふ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>拾<rt>ひろ</rt></ruby>ってくれた - a stranger picked up my dropped wallet - cannot become ❌<ruby>拾<rt>ひろ</rt></ruby>ってもらった unless you had asked them to.

---

## ～てもらう · ～てもらう vs the causative ～させる

> **Rule of thumb** - both are English "have someone do it". `～てもらう` is *asking* and the doer is willing; `～させる` is *making* and the speaker has authority.

<ruby>息子<rt>むすこ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>い<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>ってもらいました**。<br>*I got my son to go and do the shopping (and thanks, son).*

<ruby>息子<rt>むすこ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>い<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かせました**。<br>*I made my son go and do the shopping.*

---

## ～てもらう · ～てもらう vs the causative ～させる (cont.)

Because `もらう` builds in gratitude, it softens an instruction; because `させる` asserts power, it is unusable upward and sounds harsh even downward. Combining both is how you ask for permission politely: <code><ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>させていただきます</code>, "allow me to explain."

---

## ～てもらう · ～てもらう vs ～てほしい

> **Rule of thumb** - `～てもらう` reports a favour that happened or is arranged; `～てほしい` states a wish that has not.

<ruby>来週<rt>らいしゅう</rt></ruby>までに<ruby>返事<rt>へんじ</rt></ruby>を**もらいたい**んですが。<br>*I'd like to get an answer by next week.*

<ruby>来週<rt>らいしゅう</rt></ruby>までに<ruby>返事<rt>へんじ</rt></ruby>を**してほしい**んですが。<br>*I'd like you to answer by next week.*

The desiderative `～てもらいたい` sits between them: it is a wish expressed through the receiving frame, and it is a shade more indirect - and therefore softer - than `～てほしい`, because it talks about what you would receive rather than about what the other person should do.

---

## ～てもらう · Common mistakes

- ❌ <ruby>友<rt>とも</rt></ruby>だち**が**<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>ってもらいました。 → ✅ <ruby>友<rt>とも</rt></ruby>だち**に**<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>ってもらいました。<br>*With `もらう` the doer takes `に`. `が` would make the friend the one receiving the favour.*

- ❌ <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>推薦状<rt>すいせんじょう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>いて**もらいました**。（in a formal report）→ ✅ <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>推薦状<rt>すいせんじょう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>いて**いただきました**。<br>*Receiving a favour from someone above you takes the humble `いただく` in any formal setting.*

- ❌ <ruby>助<rt>たす</rt></ruby>けてもらって**ありがとうございました**。 → ✅ <ruby>助<rt>たす</rt></ruby>けて**くださって**ありがとうございました。<br>*Thanks point at the *giver's* act, so the giving verb is the one that fits.*

---

## ～てもらう · Common mistakes (cont.)

- ❌ <ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>らない<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>に<ruby>道<rt>みち</rt></ruby>を<ruby>教<rt>おし</rt></ruby>えてもらった。（when they volunteered）→ ✅ <ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>らない<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>が<ruby>道<rt>みち</rt></ruby>を<ruby>教<rt>おし</rt></ruby>えてくれた。<br>*Unrequested help is `くれる` territory. `もらう` implies you asked.*

- ❌ <ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>てもらいます。（said to the department head）→ ✅ <ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>にご<ruby>出席<rt>しゅっせき</rt></ruby>いただけますでしょうか。<br>*Arranging a superior's actions out loud sounds managerial. Turn it into a request with the humble potential.*

---

## ～てもらう · Practice 1

**1.** カメラを<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>っていなかったので、<ruby>通<rt>とお</rt></ruby>りかかった<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>____<ruby>撮<rt>と</rt></ruby>ってもらいました。

{reveal}
<ruby>通<rt>とお</rt></ruby>りかかった<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>**に**<ruby>撮<rt>と</rt></ruby>ってもらいました。

{reveal}
The doer of the favour is marked with `に` in a `もらう` sentence. The subject slot belongs to the speaker, who is the one receiving the service.

---

## ～てもらう · Practice 2

**2.** Choose: <ruby>荷物<rt>にもつ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>届<rt>とど</rt></ruby>かないので、お<ruby>店<rt>みせ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>電話<rt>でんわ</rt></ruby>して<ruby>調<rt>しら</rt></ruby>べて（もらいました・くれました）。

{reveal}
お<ruby>店<rt>みせ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>電話<rt>でんわ</rt></ruby>して<ruby>調<rt>しら</rt></ruby>べて**もらいました**。

{reveal}
The speaker rang up and asked, so the favour was arranged, and the shop is marked with `に` as the doer. `くれました` would need the shop as the `が`-subject and would suggest they checked without being asked.

---

## ～てもらう · Practice 3

**3.** Translate into Japanese: "Could I have you explain it once more?" (to a client)

{reveal}
もう<ruby>一度<rt>いちど</rt></ruby>ご<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>**いただけますでしょうか**。／もう<ruby>一度<rt>いちど</rt></ruby><ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>して**いただけませんか**。

{reveal}
Upward, `もらう` becomes `いただく`, and the potential `いただける` in a negative or でしょうか question is what turns the receiving frame into a polite request. The お／ご + noun + いただく version is the more formal of the two.

---

## ～てもらう · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: <ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>、<ruby>友<rt>とも</rt></ruby>だちが<ruby>宿題<rt>しゅくだい</rt></ruby>を<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>ってもらいました。

{reveal}
✅ <ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>、<ruby>友<rt>とも</rt></ruby>だち**に**<ruby>宿題<rt>しゅくだい</rt></ruby>を<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>ってもらいました。 （or ✅ <ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>、<ruby>友<rt>とも</rt></ruby>だちが<ruby>宿題<rt>しゅくだい</rt></ruby>を<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>って**くれました**。）

{reveal}
