| With the tail kept | ＋ いけない／だめ | <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かなきゃいけない／<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かなきゃだめ |
| With the tail dropped | nothing after it | <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かなきゃ。／<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かなくちゃ。 |
| Emphatic variant | なくちゃ → なくっちゃ | <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かなくっちゃ |

---

## ～なくちゃ・～なきゃ · Formation (cont.)

> **Rule of thumb** - the two contractions come from different parents and do not mix. `なくては` → **なくちゃ**; `なければ` → **なきゃ**. There is no ❌`なくきゃ` and no ❌`なけちゃ`.

---

## ～なくちゃ・～なきゃ · Examples

もう**<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>なきゃ**。<br>*I've got to go to bed.*

あ、<ruby>電気<rt>でんき</rt></ruby><ruby>消<rt>け</rt></ruby>さ**なきゃ**。<br>*Oh - I need to turn the light off.*

<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby><ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>いから、そろそろ**<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>らなくちゃ**。<br>*I've got an early start, so I should be heading home.*

<ruby>宿題<rt>しゅくだい</rt></ruby>、<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby><ruby>中<rt>じゅう</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わらせなきゃいけない**んだ。<br>*The thing is, I've got to get the homework finished today.*

---

## ～なくちゃ・～なきゃ · Examples (cont.)

<ruby>冷蔵庫<rt>れいぞうこ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>空<rt>から</rt></ruby>っぽだ。<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>い<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かなきゃ**。<br>*The fridge is empty. I need to go shopping.*

<ruby>傘<rt>かさ</rt></ruby>、<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>って**<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かなくちゃだめだよ**。<ruby>午後<rt>ごご</rt></ruby>から<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>だって。<br>*You've got to take an umbrella - apparently it's raining from the afternoon.*

<ruby>来週<rt>らいしゅう</rt></ruby><ruby>友<rt>とも</rt></ruby>だちの<ruby>結婚式<rt>けっこんしき</rt></ruby>だから、<ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>服<rt>ふく</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>わなきゃ**いけないなあ。<br>*My friend's wedding is next week, so I'm going to have to buy something new to wear.*

<ruby>部屋<rt>へや</rt></ruby>がこんなに<ruby>散<rt>ち</rt></ruby>らかっているのに、**<ruby>片付<rt>かたづ</rt></ruby>けなくちゃ**と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>うだけで<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>もしていない。<br>*The room is in this state and all I do is think I ought to tidy it, without ever actually starting.*

---

## ～なくちゃ・～なきゃ · Nuance & register

Casual. That is the whole point, and it is also the whole restriction. `なくちゃ` and `なきゃ` belong in speech among friends, family and close colleagues, and in writing only where writing imitates speech - messages, chat, blogs, dialogue in manga and novels. They do not appear in reports, emails to clients, exam answers or announcements.

They are **not** sloppy or uneducated, and they are not gender-marked: adults of every age and both sexes use them constantly. What they are is *unguarded*. Saying <code><ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>らなきゃ</code> lets the listener see you making a decision, which is exactly right with a friend and wrong in front of a customer.

---

## ～なくちゃ・～なきゃ · Nuance & register (cont.)

`なきゃ` is the more frequent of the two in everyday Tokyo speech. `なくちゃ` is a touch lighter and rounder, and it turns up often when someone is talking to a child or being deliberately breezy; a few speakers hear it as slightly cuter than `なきゃ`, but nobody would call it a different level of politeness. The stretched `なくっちゃ` adds emphasis - <code>これは<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>なくっちゃ</code>「this I've *got* to see」.

---

## ～なくちゃ・～なきゃ · Nuance & register (cont.)

The tail is normally dropped. When it is kept, it stays in plain form: `なきゃいけない`, `なきゃだめ`, and in very casual Tokyo speech `なきゃなんない` (from `ならない`). Attaching a polite tail is the classic learner error - you cannot half-contract a sentence, and ❌<code><ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かなきゃいけません</code> mixes two registers inside one predicate. If you need politeness, expand the whole thing back out to `なければなりません`.

One more thing that catches people out in listening: because the ending is missing, these forms often end an utterance on a rising or trailing intonation and sound unfinished. <code>あ、<ruby>洗濯<rt>せんたく</rt></ruby>しなきゃ…</code> is a complete thought. Do not wait for the rest of it.

---

## ～なくちゃ・～なきゃ · ～なきゃ vs ～なくちゃ

> **Rule of thumb** - the same word twice over. Choose by ear, not by meaning; `なきゃ` is the more common default.

そろそろ**<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>なきゃ**。<br>*I'd better get going.*

そろそろ**<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>なくちゃ**。<br>*I'd better get going.*

There is no difference of meaning, obligation strength or politeness to report, and a page that invented one would be lying. The only observable tendencies are that `なきゃ` is heard more often overall, `なくちゃ` sounds slightly softer and is common in speech directed at children, and only `なくちゃ` has the emphatic stretched form `なくっちゃ`.

---

## ～なくちゃ・～なきゃ · ～なきゃ vs ～ないと

> **Rule of thumb** - both are casual spoken obligation. `ないと` is neutral and usable slightly further up the politeness scale; `なきゃ` is more informal and more self-directed.

<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>資料<rt>しりょう</rt></ruby>、<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>ら**ないと**いけませんね。<br>*We'll need to put the meeting materials together, won't we.*

うわ、<ruby>資料<rt>しりょう</rt></ruby><ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>ら**なきゃ**。<br>*Ugh - I've got to make the handouts.*

---

## ～なくちゃ・～なきゃ · ～なきゃ vs ～ないと (cont.)

`ないと` survives being made polite: <code><ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かないといけません</code> is fine at work. `なきゃ` does not. And `なきゃ` leans towards things the speaker is telling *themselves*, which is why it so often follows あ or うわ and precedes nothing at all.

---

## ～なきゃ as obligation vs ～なきゃ as plain "unless"

> **Rule of thumb** - `なきゃ` is just contracted `なければ`. If a consequence follows it, it is an ordinary conditional and has nothing to do with obligation.

<ruby>自分<rt>じぶん</rt></ruby>で**<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>なきゃ**わからないよ。<br>*You won't know unless you look for yourself.*

<ruby>自分<rt>じぶん</rt></ruby>で**<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>なきゃ**。<br>*I've got to go and look for myself.*

The first is "if you don't look, you won't understand" - the `いけない` is not implied and never was. The second has nothing after it, so the listener fills in the missing "that won't do" and hears an obligation.

---

## ～なきゃ as obligation vs ～なきゃ as plain "unless" (cont.)

The same holds for `なくちゃ`, and it explains a shape you will meet often: <code><ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>くなきゃ<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>わない</code>「I won't buy it unless it's cheap」, <code><ruby>君<rt>きみ</rt></ruby>じゃなきゃだめだ</code>「it has to be you」.

---

## ～なくちゃ・～なきゃ · Common mistakes

- ❌ <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>か**なきゃです**。 → ✅ <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>か**なきゃ**。／<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>か**なければなりません**。<br>*There is no polite version of a contraction. `です` cannot be bolted onto `なきゃ`; if you need politeness, expand the form.*

- ❌ <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く**なきゃ** → ✅ <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>か**なきゃ**<br>*The contraction still starts from the ない-form. Build <code><ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かない</code> first, then squeeze.*

- ❌ <ruby>急<rt>いそ</rt></ruby>が**なくきゃ** → ✅ <ruby>急<rt>いそ</rt></ruby>が**なくちゃ**／<ruby>急<rt>いそ</rt></ruby>が**なきゃ**<br>*The two contractions have different parents and cannot be blended. `なくては`→`なくちゃ`, `なければ`→`なきゃ`.*

---

## ～なくちゃ・～なきゃ · Common mistakes (cont.)

- ❌ <ruby>会員<rt>かいいん</rt></ruby>**だなきゃ**だめです。 → ✅ <ruby>会員<rt>かいいん</rt></ruby>**じゃなきゃ**だめだよ。<br>*Nouns negate to `じゃない`, so the contracted conditional is `じゃなきゃ`. Note the ending changed too - `だめです` after `じゃなきゃ` is a register mismatch.*

- ❌（in an email to a client）<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>までに<ruby>送<rt>おく</rt></ruby>ら**なきゃ**いけません。 → ✅ <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>までに<ruby>送<rt>おく</rt></ruby>ら**なければなりません**。<br>*Contractions do not belong in written business Japanese, however polite the tail you attach to them.*

---

## ～なくちゃ・～なきゃ · Practice 1

**1.** やばい、<ruby>電車<rt>でんしゃ</rt></ruby><ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>っちゃう。<ruby>走<rt>はし</rt></ruby>ら____。

{reveal}
<ruby>走<rt>はし</rt></ruby>ら**なきゃ**。（also fine: <ruby>走<rt>はし</rt></ruby>ら**なくちゃ**。）

{reveal}
The situation is urgent, spoken and self-directed, which is the natural home of the contracted forms with the ending dropped. Anything longer would sound like the speaker had time to think.

---

## ～なくちゃ・～なきゃ · Practice 2

**2.** <ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>に（<ruby>報告<rt>ほうこく</rt></ruby>しなきゃいけません・<ruby>報告<rt>ほうこく</rt></ruby>しなければなりません）。

{reveal}
<ruby>報告<rt>ほうこく</rt></ruby>し**なければなりません**。

{reveal}
`なきゃ` is a casual contraction and `いけません` is a polite ending; putting them in one predicate mixes registers inside a single word. Pick one level - fully contracted for speech among friends, fully expanded when you are being polite.

---

## ～なくちゃ・～なきゃ · Practice 3

**3.** Translate into Japanese, as something you say to yourself on remembering it: "Oh no, I have to return the library books today."

{reveal}
あ、<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby><ruby>図書館<rt>としょかん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby><ruby>返<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>さ**なきゃ**。

{reveal}
Muttered self-obligation drops the `いけない` and drops the particles too. The interjection at the front is part of the pattern: these forms almost always follow a moment of realisation.

---

## ～なくちゃ・～なきゃ · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: この<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>、<ruby>絶対<rt>ぜったい</rt></ruby><ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>るなきゃ。

{reveal}
✅ この<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>、<ruby>絶対<rt>ぜったい</rt></ruby><ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>**なきゃ**。（emphatic: <ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>**なくっちゃ**。）

{reveal}
`なきゃ` replaces `なければ`, which is built on the ない-form - <code><ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>ない</code> → <code><ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>なければ</code> → <code><ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>なきゃ</code>. The dictionary form never appears in front of it.

---

## ～なくちゃ・～なきゃ · Practice 5

**5.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) <ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く**<ruby>予約<rt>よやく</rt></ruby>しなきゃ**<ruby>席<rt>せき</rt></ruby>がなくなるよ。 (b) <ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く**<ruby>予約<rt>よやく</rt></ruby>しなきゃ**。

{reveal}
(a) is not an obligation sentence at all. `なきゃ` here is simply contracted `なければ` working as an ordinary conditional, and the second half states the consequence: book early, or the seats will be gone.

{reveal}
(b) leaves the consequence out. Because the missing half is understood to be "that won't do", the whole utterance is heard as the speaker realising they have to act. The contraction is identical in both; what decides the reading is whether anything follows it.

---

# ～なくてもいい

**Meaning** · you don't have to; it's fine not to

`～なくてもいい` is the exact negative counterpart of `～てもいい`. Same shape, same `も` of concession, same verdict `いい` - only the thing being conceded is now a *non*-action: "even if you don't do it, that's fine." It does not tell anyone to stop. It removes a requirement and leaves the choice open.

---

## ～なくてもいい · Formation

Negate first, swap the final `い` of `ない` for `くても`, then finish with `いい`.

---

## ～なくてもいい · Formation (cont.)

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Verb (う-verb) | ない-form − い + くてもいい | <ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>つ → <ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>たなくてもいい |
| Verb (る-verb) | ない-form − い + くてもいい | <ruby>着<rt>き</rt></ruby>る → <ruby>着<rt>き</rt></ruby>なくてもいい |
| Verb (する) | しなくてもいい | <ruby>予約<rt>よやく</rt></ruby>する → <ruby>予約<rt>よやく</rt></ruby>しなくてもいい |
| Verb (<ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>る) | <ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>なくてもいい | <ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>る → <ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>なくてもいい |
| い-adjective | ～くない → ～くなくてもいい | <ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい → <ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しくなくてもいい |
| な-adjective | drop だ + でなくてもいい | <ruby>完璧<rt>かんぺき</rt></ruby>だ → <ruby>完璧<rt>かんぺき</rt></ruby>でなくてもいい |
| Noun | noun + でなくてもいい | スーツ → スーツでなくてもいい |
| Polite | いい → いいです | <ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>たなくてもいいです |
| Asking | ～なくてもいいですか | <ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>たなくてもいいですか |

---

## ～なくてもいい · Formation (cont.)

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Softer / politer | いい → かまいません, <ruby>大丈夫<rt>だいじょうぶ</rt></ruby>です | <ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>たなくてもかまいません |
| Casual (も dropped) | ～なくていい | <ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>たなくていいよ |

> **Rule of thumb** - the particle carries the whole meaning. `～なくて**は**いけない` = must; `～なくて**も**いい` = needn't. Everything else in the two patterns is shared scaffolding.

---

## ～なくてもいい · Examples

<ruby>靴<rt>くつ</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>脱<rt>ぬ</rt></ruby>がなくてもいいです**。<br>*You don't have to take your shoes off.*

<ruby>急<rt>いそ</rt></ruby>が**なくてもいい**よ。<br>*There's no need to rush.*

<ruby>返事<rt>へんじ</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>かなくてもいいです**か。<br>*Is it all right if I don't write back?*

<ruby>服装<rt>ふくそう</rt></ruby>はスーツ**でなくてもいい**そうです。<br>*I hear it doesn't have to be a suit.*

---

## ～なくてもいい · Examples (cont.)

<ruby>部屋<rt>へや</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>広<rt>ひろ</rt></ruby>くなくてもいい**けど、<ruby>駅<rt>えき</rt></ruby>に<ruby>近<rt>ちか</rt></ruby>いほうがいい。<br>*The flat doesn't have to be big, but I'd rather it were near a station.*

そんなに**<ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>しなくてもいい**んじゃない？<br>*Don't you think you're worrying more than you need to?*

<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>仕事<rt>しごと</rt></ruby>が<ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わったので、<ruby>残業<rt>ざんぎょう</rt></ruby>は**しなくてもいい**ことになりました。<br>*Work finished early today, so it turns out we don't have to stay late.*

レポートは<ruby>手書<rt>てが</rt></ruby>きでも<ruby>印刷<rt>いんさつ</rt></ruby>でもよくて、<ruby>表紙<rt>ひょうし</rt></ruby>は**つけなくてもかまいません**。<br>*The report may be handwritten or printed, and you needn't add a cover page.*

---

## ～なくてもいい · Nuance & register

The pattern itself is neutral; `いいです` makes it polite in form. What is not neutral is the **social act**. Saying "you don't have to" means you are in a position to lift the requirement, and that is a position of authority. Between equals it is generous. Aimed upward it is presumptuous: telling your manager <code><ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>なくてもいいですよ</code> sounds like you are giving them permission to skip work.

Upward, the same content goes through different wording: <code>ご<ruby>無理<rt>むり</rt></ruby>なさらないでください</code>, <code>お<ruby>気<rt>き</rt></ruby>になさらないでください</code>, <code>そのままで<ruby>結構<rt>けっこう</rt></ruby>です</code>. Note that <code><ruby>結構<rt>けっこう</rt></ruby>です</code> is genuinely ambiguous - it can mean "that's fine as it is" or "no thank you" - and tone and context are the only things separating them.

---

## ～なくてもいい · Nuance & register (cont.)

In speech the `も` disappears constantly: <code><ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かなくていいよ</code>, <code><ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>たなくていいから</code>. This is not a different pattern and carries no change in meaning; it is simply what fast Japanese does to the phrase. Learners who have only seen `なくてもいい` in a textbook often fail to recognise `なくていい` in conversation. The more emphatic casual variant is `なくたっていい` (<code><ruby>謝<rt>あやま</rt></ruby>らなくたっていいよ</code>).

Three neighbours worth knowing, in rising order of formality: <code>なくても<ruby>大丈夫<rt>だいじょうぶ</rt></ruby></code> (warm, spoken), `なくてもかまいません`「it doesn't matter if you don't」(neutral, business), <code>なくても<ruby>結構<rt>けっこう</rt></ruby>です</code>「it is not required」(formal, institutional). `かまわない` is the one to reach for when you want to sound like you truly do not mind.

---

## ～なくてもいい · Nuance & register (cont.)

Finally, the pattern is not only about other people. `～なくてもいい` about yourself reports relief or a decision: <code><ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は<ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>起<rt>お</rt></ruby>きなくてもいいから、<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>でも<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>よう</code>.

---

## ～なくてもいい · ～なくてもいい vs ～てもいい

> **Rule of thumb** - `～てもいい` opens a door: you *may* do it. `～なくてもいい` closes a duty: you *needn't* do it. Neither one pushes you in either direction.

<ruby>写真<rt>しゃしん</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>撮<rt>と</rt></ruby>ってもいい**ですか。<br>*Is it okay if I take photos?*

<ruby>写真<rt>しゃしん</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>撮<rt>と</rt></ruby>らなくてもいい**ですか。<br>*Is it okay if I don't take photos?*

The first asks whether the action is permitted; the second asks whether the action is required. In a museum you would ask the first; on a job where photographing is part of your task, you would ask the second.

---

## ～なくてもいい · ～なくてもいい vs ～てもいい (cont.)

They pair up into a neat square with the obligation forms. `てもいい` may, `てはいけない` must not, `なくてはいけない` must, `なくてもいい` needn't. Permission and prohibition are built on the て-form; obligation and exemption on the negative stem.

---

## ～なくてもいい · ～なくてもいい vs ～ないでください

> **Rule of thumb** - "you don't have to" is not "please don't". `なくてもいい` leaves the action available; `ないでください` takes it away.

<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>わ**なくてもいいですよ**。<br>*You don't have to help.*

<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>わ**ないでください**。<br>*Please don't help.*

---

## ～なくてもいい · ～なくてもいい vs ～ないでください (cont.)

English blurs these - "you don't have to help" is often *meant* as a polite refusal - but Japanese does not. The first sentence releases someone who was offering; the second turns them away, and would be startling from a colleague. When you want to decline an offer kindly, the natural wording is <code><ruby>大丈夫<rt>だいじょうぶ</rt></ruby>です、ありがとうございます</code>, not either of these.

---

## ～なくてもいい vs ～なくてもかまいません・～なくても大丈夫

> **Rule of thumb** - same exemption, three temperatures. <code><ruby>大丈夫<rt>だいじょうぶ</rt></ruby></code> is warm, `いい` is neutral, `かまいません` is businesslike.

<ruby>無理<rt>むり</rt></ruby>に<ruby>全部<rt>ぜんぶ</rt></ruby>**<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べなくても<ruby>大丈夫<rt>だいじょうぶ</rt></ruby>だよ**。<br>*Honestly, you don't have to finish it all.*

<ruby>当日<rt>とうじつ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>印鑑<rt>いんかん</rt></ruby>を**お<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>ちにならなくてもかまいません**。<br>*You do not need to bring a personal seal on the day.*

---

## ～なくてもいい vs ～なくてもかまいません・～なくても大丈夫 (cont.)

<code><ruby>大丈夫<rt>だいじょうぶ</rt></ruby></code> says *don't worry about it* and belongs in speech between people who know each other. `かまいません` says *it makes no difference to us* and belongs in counters, forms and customer service. Plain `いい` sits between them and is never wrong, which is why it is the form to learn first.

---

## ～なくてもいい · Common mistakes

- ❌ <ruby>払<rt>はら</rt></ruby>わ**なくてはいい**です。 → ✅ <ruby>払<rt>はら</rt></ruby>わ**なくても**いいです。<br>*`なくては` pairs with `いけない`; `なくても` pairs with `いい`. Mixing them produces a pattern that does not exist.*

- ❌ <ruby>学生<rt>がくせい</rt></ruby>**だなくても**いいです。 → ✅ <ruby>学生<rt>がくせい</rt></ruby>**でなくても**いいです。<br>*Nouns and な-adjectives negate through `で(は)ない`, so the join is `でなくても`.*

- ❌ <ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい**じゃなくても**いい。 → ✅ <ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>し**くなくても**いい。<br>*<code><ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい</code> is an い-adjective, so its negative is `くない` and the join is `くなくても`.*

---

## ～なくてもいい · Common mistakes (cont.)

- ❌（meaning "you don't have to come tomorrow"）<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は<ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>**ないでください**。 → ✅ <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は<ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>**なくてもいいですよ**。<br>*Straight from English. The `ないでください` version instructs the person to stay away, which is a completely different message.*

- ❌ <ruby>課長<rt>かちょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>出席<rt>しゅっせき</rt></ruby>し**なくてもいいですよ**。 → ✅ <ruby>課長<rt>かちょう</rt></ruby>、ご<ruby>都合<rt>つごう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>悪<rt>わる</rt></ruby>ければ、ご<ruby>欠席<rt>けっせき</rt></ruby>でも<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>ございません。<br>*Releasing someone from a duty implies you had the authority to impose it. Upward, state the situation instead of granting an exemption.*

---

## ～なくてもいい · Practice 1

**1.** このレストランは<ruby>予約<rt>よやく</rt></ruby>し____いいですよ。いつも<ruby>空<rt>す</rt></ruby>いていますから。

{reveal}
<ruby>予約<rt>よやく</rt></ruby>し**なくても**いいですよ。

{reveal}
The restaurant is always empty, so booking is not required - the exemption reading. Note the particle: `なくても` with `いい`, never `なくては`.

---

## ～なくてもいい · Practice 2

**2.** <ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>のとき、ネクタイを（しなくてもいいです・しないでください）。

{reveal}
Either is grammatical, but they say different things. **しなくてもいいです** means a tie is optional; **しないでください** instructs people not to wear one. For a normal dress-code announcement the first is what is meant.

---

## ～なくてもいい · Practice 3

**3.** Translate into Japanese, politely: "You don't need to bring anything."

{reveal}
<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>も**<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>って<ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>なくてもいいですよ**。 （more formal: <ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>も**お<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>ちいただかなくてもかまいません**。）

{reveal}
The `よ` matters: without it the sentence can read as a flat instruction, whereas telling a guest not to trouble themselves should sound warm. <code><ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>る</code> takes the irregular negative stem <code><ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby></code>.

---

## ～なくてもいい · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>のパーティーは<ruby>正式<rt>せいしき</rt></ruby>な<ruby>服<rt>ふく</rt></ruby>だなくてもいいです。

{reveal}
✅ <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>のパーティーは<ruby>正式<rt>せいしき</rt></ruby>な<ruby>服<rt>ふく</rt></ruby>**でなくてもいいです**。

{reveal}
`だ` never survives in front of a negative join. A noun negates as <code><ruby>服<rt>ふく</rt></ruby>ではない</code>, and the exemption form built on that is <code><ruby>服<rt>ふく</rt></ruby>でなくてもいい</code>.

---

## ～なくてもいい · Practice 5

**5.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) <ruby>全部<rt>ぜんぶ</rt></ruby><ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>ま**なくてもいいです**。 (b) <ruby>全部<rt>ぜんぶ</rt></ruby><ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>ま**なくてはいけません**。

{reveal}
(a) removes a requirement: reading all of it is optional, and the listener may read as much or as little as they like. One particle - `も` - is doing that work.

{reveal}
(b) imposes one: all of it has to be read, and there is no choice in the matter. The `は` closes off the alternative that `も` opens. Because the two sentences differ by a single kana in the middle of a long predicate, they are easy to mishear and worth saying aloud a few times.

---

# ～必要がある

**Meaning** · there is a need to do it; it is necessary to do it

Read <ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>. <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby></code> is a noun meaning *necessity*, and `ある` is the ordinary verb of existence - so the pattern literally says *a need to do X exists*. That is why it feels cooler than the obligation forms: it does not push anybody, it states a fact about the situation.

---

## ～必要がある · Formation

The verb in front stays in the **dictionary form**. Nouns join with `の`.

---

## ～必要がある · Formation (cont.)

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Verb | dictionary form + <ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がある | <ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>つ → <ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>つ<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がある |
| Verb (する) | dictionary form + <ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がある | <ruby>登録<rt>とうろく</rt></ruby>する → <ruby>登録<rt>とうろく</rt></ruby>する<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がある |
| Noun | noun + の + <ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がある | <ruby>修理<rt>しゅうり</rt></ruby> → <ruby>修理<rt>しゅうり</rt></ruby>の<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がある |
| Negative | <ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>はない／<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がない | <ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>つ<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>はない |
| Polite | <ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>があります／ありません | <ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>つ<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>があります |
| Past | <ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>があった／なかった | <ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>つ<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>はなかった |
| Question | <ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がありますか | <ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>つ<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がありますか |
| Formal negative | <ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>はございません | <ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>つ<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>はございません |
| い-adjective / な-adjective | not available | <ruby>静<rt>しず</rt></ruby>かだ → ❌<ruby>静<rt>しず</rt></ruby>かな<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がある |

---

## ～必要がある · Formation (cont.)

> **Rule of thumb** - the negative flips the particle. Affirmative <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>が**ある**</code>, negative <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>は**ない**</code>. The `は` is doing what `は` always does with a negative: marking the thing being denied. <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がない</code> is possible, but `は` is the everyday choice.

> **Note** - the negation goes on `ある`, never on the verb in front. "You don't need to go" is <code><ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>はない</code>, not ❌<code><ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かない<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がある</code>, which would mean something like "there is a need for you not to go."

---

## ～必要がある · Examples

パスポートを<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>せる**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>があります**。<br>*You need to show your passport.*

<ruby>急<rt>いそ</rt></ruby>ぐ**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>はありません**。<br>*There's no need to hurry.*

もう<ruby>一度<rt>いちど</rt></ruby><ruby>確認<rt>かくにん</rt></ruby>する**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がある**。<br>*We need to check it one more time.*

この<ruby>書類<rt>しょるい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>翻訳<rt>ほんやく</rt></ruby>の**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がありますか**。<br>*Does this document need translating?*

---

## ～必要がある · Examples (cont.)

<ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>する**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>はない**よ。<ruby>全部<rt>ぜんぶ</rt></ruby>うまくいっているから。<br>*You've no need to worry - everything's going fine.*

<ruby>海外<rt>かいがい</rt></ruby>で<ruby>働<rt>はたら</rt></ruby>くには、ビザを<ruby>申請<rt>しんせい</rt></ruby>する**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>があります**。<br>*To work abroad, you need to apply for a visa.*

<ruby>去年<rt>きょねん</rt></ruby><ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>った<ruby>資料<rt>しりょう</rt></ruby>なので、<ruby>数字<rt>すうじ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しいものに<ruby>直<rt>なお</rt></ruby>す**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>があります**。<br>*These materials are from last year, so the figures need updating.*

<ruby>会員<rt>かいいん</rt></ruby>カードをお<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>ちの<ruby>方<rt>かた</rt></ruby>は、<ruby>受付<rt>うけつけ</rt></ruby>で<ruby>住所<rt>じゅうしょ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>く**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>はございません**。<br>*Members do not need to write their address at reception.*

---

## ～必要がある · Nuance & register

<code>～<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がある</code> is the **objective** member of the family. It describes a requirement as a property of the situation, with nobody's authority behind it, which makes it the default in manuals, instructions, application guidance, business email and academic writing. If you have ever read a Japanese form, you have read this pattern.

That neutrality has a practical use: it lets you tell someone what has to happen without telling *them* what to do. <code>ご<ruby>確認<rt>かくにん</rt></ruby>いただく<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がございます</code> is still direct, but <code><ruby>三月<rt>さんがつ</rt></ruby>までに<ruby>提出<rt>ていしゅつ</rt></ruby>する<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>があります</code> said about a shared deadline points at the deadline, not at the listener.

---

## ～必要がある · Nuance & register (cont.)

The flip side is that it sounds stiff about small personal errands. Nobody says <code><ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>い<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>をする<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がある</code> to a friend - that is <code><ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>い<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby><ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かないと</code> territory. Using the formal pattern for a trip to the supermarket sounds like reading from a report.

The negative is the half you will use most, and it is unusually warm for such a formal pattern. <code><ruby>謝<rt>あやま</rt></ruby>る<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>はないよ</code>「you don't need to apologise」 and <code><ruby>気<rt>き</rt></ruby>にする<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>はありません</code>「there's no need to worry about it」 are everyday reassurances. In casual speech `が` drops out altogether: <code>そんなに<ruby>急<rt>いそ</rt></ruby>ぐ<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>ない</code>.

---

## ～必要がある · Nuance & register (cont.)

At the formal end, `ある` is replaced by its humble-polite equivalents: <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がございます</code> and <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>はございません</code>, which is what shop staff and official notices use.

---

## ～必要がある · ～必要がある vs ～なければならない

> **Rule of thumb** - <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がある</code> reports that a need exists; `なければならない` says the alternative is unacceptable. The first describes, the second compels.

この<ruby>薬<rt>くすり</rt></ruby>は<ruby>毎日<rt>まいにち</rt></ruby><ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>む**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>があります**。<br>*This medicine needs to be taken every day.*

この<ruby>薬<rt>くすり</rt></ruby>は<ruby>毎日<rt>まいにち</rt></ruby>**<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>まなければなりません**。<br>*You must take this medicine every day.*

---

## ～必要がある · ～必要がある vs ～なければならない (cont.)

Both are correct and a doctor might say either. The first sounds like an explanation of how the treatment works; the second sounds like an instruction being issued to you. When the requirement comes from a rule with force behind it - a law, a contract, a school regulation - `なければならない` is the stronger fit. When it comes from the nature of the task, <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がある</code> is.

There is also a grammatical difference worth noticing: `なければならない` attaches to a *negative* stem, while <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がある</code> attaches to a plain dictionary form. That makes the second much easier to build under time pressure.

---

## ～必要がある · ～必要はない vs ～なくてもいい

> **Rule of thumb** - `なくてもいい` grants an exemption; <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>はない</code> denies that a requirement ever existed.

<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>なくてもいいですよ**。<br>*You don't have to come in tomorrow.*

<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>る<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>はありません**。<br>*There is no need for you to come in tomorrow.*

The first is a person releasing another person, which is why it needs `よ` or a smile to sound kind. The second is a statement about the schedule, and because it does not position the speaker as the one granting permission, it is often the safer thing to say upward or to a stranger.

---

## ～必要がある · ～必要はない vs ～なくてもいい (cont.)

In their negative-reassurance use they come very close: <code><ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>しなくてもいい</code> and <code><ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>する<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>はない</code> are near-synonyms, the second slightly firmer, as if arguing the worry away rather than waving it off.

---

## ～必要がある · ～必要がある vs ～が必要だ

> **Rule of thumb** - <code>する<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がある</code> needs an **action**; <code>が<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>だ</code> needs a **thing**.

ここで<ruby>靴<rt>くつ</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>脱<rt>ぬ</rt></ruby>ぐ<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>があります**。<br>*You need to take your shoes off here.*

ここでは<ruby>上<rt>うわ</rt></ruby>ばきが**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>です**。<br>*You need indoor shoes here.*

---

## ～必要がある · ～必要がある vs ～が必要だ (cont.)

The two are often interchangeable in translation and never in grammar. A verb before <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby></code> requires the dictionary form and the `が…ある` frame; a noun before it takes `が` and the plain な-adjective predicate <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>だ／です</code>. A noun can also be forced into the `ある` frame with `の` - <code><ruby>修理<rt>しゅうり</rt></ruby>の<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がある</code> - which sounds distinctly more formal than <code><ruby>修理<rt>しゅうり</rt></ruby>が<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>だ</code>.

---

## ～必要がある · Common mistakes

- ❌ <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>き**ます**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>があります。 → ✅ <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>があります。<br>*The verb in front of <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby></code> is plain and non-past. `ます` cannot appear inside the sentence; politeness goes on `あります` at the end.*

- ❌ <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>か**ない**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>があります。 → ✅ <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>は**ありません**。<br>*To say there is no need, negate `ある`, not the verb. Negating the verb creates a need *not* to go, which is a different and much rarer idea.*

- ❌ ビザ<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>があります。 → ✅ ビザ**の**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>があります。／ビザ**が**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>です。<br>*A noun cannot sit straight against <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby></code>. Either link it with `の` or switch to the <code>が<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>だ</code> pattern.*

---

## ～必要がある · Common mistakes (cont.)

- ❌ <ruby>部屋<rt>へや</rt></ruby>が<ruby>静<rt>しず</rt></ruby>か**な**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>があります。 → ✅ <ruby>部屋<rt>へや</rt></ruby>は<ruby>静<rt>しず</rt></ruby>か**でなければなりません**。<br>*Adjectives do not take this pattern at all. Requirements about qualities go through the obligation forms.*

- ❌（to a friend）そろそろ<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>る<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がある。 → ✅ そろそろ<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>らないと。<br>*Not wrong, just wrongly dressed. For your own small obligations in conversation, the `ないと` / `なきゃ` end of the family is what people actually use.*

---

## ～必要がある · Practice 1

**1.** この<ruby>申込書<rt>もうしこみしょ</rt></ruby>には、はんこを<ruby>押<rt>お</rt></ruby>す____ありますか。

{reveal}
はんこを<ruby>押<rt>お</rt></ruby>す**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>が**ありますか。

{reveal}
The verb stays in the dictionary form, and the question is about whether a requirement exists - exactly what this pattern is for. On a form, it is more natural than asking <code><ruby>押<rt>お</rt></ruby>さなくてもいいですか</code>.

---

## ～必要がある · Practice 2

**2.** <ruby>課長<rt>かちょう</rt></ruby>に（<ruby>報告<rt>ほうこく</rt></ruby>する<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>があります・<ruby>報告<rt>ほうこく</rt></ruby>しなきゃ）と<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>で<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>った。

{reveal}
<ruby>報告<rt>ほうこく</rt></ruby>する**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>があります**。

{reveal}
A meeting is a formal setting and the sentence is stating what the situation requires, not muttering a personal chore. `なきゃ` is a casual contraction and would sound out of place in front of colleagues.

---

## ～必要がある · Practice 3

**3.** Translate into Japanese, as a line of written guidance: "Applicants need to submit two photographs."

{reveal}
<ruby>申込者<rt>もうしこみしゃ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>写真<rt>しゃしん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>二枚<rt>にまい</rt></ruby><ruby>提出<rt>ていしゅつ</rt></ruby>する**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>があります**。

{reveal}
Written guidance wants the impersonal pattern: it states what the process requires without addressing anyone. <code><ruby>提出<rt>ていしゅつ</rt></ruby>しなければならない</code> would also fit a rulebook, but it sounds more like a command than an instruction sheet.

---

## ～必要がある · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は<ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>ない<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がありません。

{reveal}
✅ <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は<ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>る**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>はありません**。

{reveal}
Two things went wrong. The verb must be affirmative and in the dictionary form, and the negation belongs on `ある`. Note also the particle flip: negatives of this pattern normally take `は`.

---

## ～必要がある · Practice 5

**5.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) <ruby>返事<rt>へんじ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>く**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>はありません**。 (b) <ruby>返事<rt>へんじ</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>かなくてもいいです**。

{reveal}
(a) states that the process does not call for a reply. The speaker is describing how things work, which makes it neutral and slightly formal - the wording of a notice or of someone explaining a procedure.

{reveal}
(b) tells the listener they are released from writing one. It implies the speaker is in a position to decide, so it sounds more personal and, depending on who is speaking to whom, either kind or presumptuous.

---

# 必要

**Meaning** · necessary; needed - the word itself, not the pattern

Read <ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>. It is a noun that behaves as a な-adjective: something <code>が<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>だ</code>「is needed」, and a <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>な</code> thing is a required one. The verb pattern <code>～<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がある</code> is built out of this word, but the word does plenty of work on its own, and getting its particles right is what stops learners writing English with Japanese vocabulary in it.

---

## 必要 · Formation

The thing that is needed takes `が`, not `を` - <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby></code> is not a verb and has no object.

---

## 必要 · Formation (cont.)

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Noun (predicate) | Noun + が + <ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>だ／です | ビザ → ビザが<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>です |
| Before a noun | <ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby> + な + Noun | <ruby>道具<rt>どうぐ</rt></ruby> → <ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>な<ruby>道具<rt>どうぐ</rt></ruby> |
| Purpose | Noun + に + <ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>な + Noun | <ruby>生活<rt>せいかつ</rt></ruby> → <ruby>生活<rt>せいかつ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>なもの |
| Negative (casual) | <ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>ない／<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>じゃない | それは<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>ない |
| Negative (polite) | <ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>ありません／<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>ではありません | それは<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>ありません |
| Past | <ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>だった／<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>なかった | <ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>だった |
| Becoming | <ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>になる | お<ruby>金<rt>かね</rt></ruby>が<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>になった |
| Verb instead of noun | dictionary form + <ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がある | <ruby>申<rt>もう</rt></ruby>し<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>む<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がある |
| Formal verb | Noun + を + <ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>とする | <ruby>助<rt>たす</rt></ruby>けを<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>とする<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby> |

---

## 必要 · Formation (cont.)

> **Rule of thumb** - <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby></code> is a な-adjective, so it never takes `くない` or `かった`. The negative is <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>じゃない</code>／<code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>ない</code>, and the past is <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>だった</code>.

> **Note** - the written antonym is <code><ruby>不要<rt>ふよう</rt></ruby></code>, which you will meet on forms and labels rather than in speech: <code><ruby>記入<rt>きにゅう</rt></ruby><ruby>不要<rt>ふよう</rt></ruby></code>「no entry required」, <code><ruby>返却<rt>へんきゃく</rt></ruby><ruby>不要<rt>ふよう</rt></ruby></code>「no need to return this」.

---

## 必要 · Examples

パスポートが**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>です**。<br>*You'll need your passport.*

**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>な**ものだけ<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>って<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>てください。<br>*Please bring only what you need.*

その<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>ない**よ。<br>*That explanation isn't necessary.*

<ruby>申<rt>もう</rt></ruby>し<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>みに**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>な**<ruby>書類<rt>しょるい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>三<rt>みっ</rt></ruby>つです。<br>*There are three documents required for the application.*

---

## 必要 · Examples (cont.)

<ruby>急<rt>きゅう</rt></ruby>に<ruby>現金<rt>げんきん</rt></ruby>が**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>になった**。<br>*I suddenly found myself needing cash.*

この<ruby>仕事<rt>しごと</rt></ruby>に<ruby>経験<rt>けいけん</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>ではありません**。<br>*No experience is required for this job.*

<ruby>一人<rt>ひとり</rt></ruby><ruby>暮<rt>ぐ</rt></ruby>らしを<ruby>始<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めるとき、<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>っていたより<ruby>多<rt>おお</rt></ruby>くのものが**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>だった**。<br>*When I started living on my own, I needed more things than I had expected.*

<ruby>災害<rt>さいがい</rt></ruby>のときに<ruby>本当<rt>ほんとう</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>な**のは、<ruby>水<rt>みず</rt></ruby>と<ruby>情報<rt>じょうほう</rt></ruby>だと<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>われています。<br>*What you really need in a disaster, they say, is water and information.*

---

## 必要 · Nuance & register

<code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby></code> is a Sino-Japanese word, and like most of them it leans formal and slightly abstract. It is completely ordinary in polite speech, business email, notices and writing. In casual conversation, though, Japanese usually reaches for the plain verb `いる` instead: a friend asks <code><ruby>袋<rt>ふくろ</rt></ruby>いる？</code>, not <code><ruby>袋<rt>ふくろ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>ですか</code>. At a convenience store counter you will hear both, because staff speech is formal.

The negatives are worth separating. <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>ない</code> is short, everyday and can sound abrupt - <code>そんなの<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>ない</code> is close to "we don't need that rubbish." <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>ありません</code> is the neutral polite version and the one to use with strangers. <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>ではありません</code> is stiffer again and belongs in writing. As a refusal at a shop counter, the standard phrase is not any of these but <code><ruby>大丈夫<rt>だいじょうぶ</rt></ruby>です</code> or <code><ruby>結構<rt>けっこう</rt></ruby>です</code>.

---

## 必要 · Nuance & register (cont.)

<code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>とする</code> is a genuine verb and a register marker: it appears in journalism, official documents and formal description - <code><ruby>支援<rt>しえん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>としている<ruby>地域<rt>ちいき</rt></ruby></code>「areas that require assistance」. Using it in conversation would sound like reading a press release.

One more thing to notice: <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby></code> describes what a *purpose* demands. It carries no warmth. That is why it is the right word for documents, tools, time and money, and the wrong word for people - see the contrast below.

---

## 必要 · 必要 vs いる

> **Rule of thumb** - same meaning, different word class and different register. `いる` is a verb and casual; <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby></code> is a な-adjective and formal.

レシート、**いる**？<br>*D'you want the receipt?*

レシートは**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>ですか**。<br>*Would you like a receipt?*

---

## 必要 · 必要 vs いる (cont.)

Both take their object with `が` (or with no particle at all in speech), which is the one thing they share structurally. `いる` - written <ruby>要<rt>い</rt></ruby>る, though usually left in kana - is a う-verb: `いります`, `いらない`, `いった`. Beware that its past and て-forms collide with <code><ruby>入<rt>はい</rt></ruby>る</code>, <code><ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く</code> and the existence verb `いる`, which is why it is far more common in the non-past.

`いる` is also limited to things. For an *action* you need <code>～<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がある</code> or one of the obligation forms: there is no ❌<code><ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くがいる</code>.

---

## 必要 · 必要 vs 大切・大事

> **Rule of thumb** - <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby></code> = required for a purpose. <code><ruby>大切<rt>たいせつ</rt></ruby></code>／<code><ruby>大事<rt>だいじ</rt></ruby></code> = important, precious, valued. Do not use <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby></code> about people.

<ruby>家族<rt>かぞく</rt></ruby>はとても**<ruby>大切<rt>たいせつ</rt></ruby>です**。<br>*My family means a great deal to me.*

この<ruby>仕事<rt>しごと</rt></ruby>には<ruby>集中力<rt>しゅうちゅうりょく</rt></ruby>が**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>です**。<br>*This job requires concentration.*

---

## 必要 · 必要 vs 大切・大事 (cont.)

Swap them and both sentences go wrong in interesting ways. <code><ruby>家族<rt>かぞく</rt></ruby>が<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>です</code> sounds like you are shopping for one - the word treats its object as a resource. And <code><ruby>集中力<rt>しゅうちゅうりょく</rt></ruby>が<ruby>大切<rt>たいせつ</rt></ruby>です</code> is fine but says something milder: concentration *matters*, rather than the job being impossible without it.

<code><ruby>大事<rt>だいじ</rt></ruby></code> is the more conversational of the two importance words; <code><ruby>大切<rt>たいせつ</rt></ruby></code> is a shade warmer and more careful. Both are な-adjectives, like <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby></code> itself.

---

## 必要 · 必要だ vs 必要がある

> **Rule of thumb** - a **noun** is needed → <code>が<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>だ</code>. An **action** is needed → <code>～する<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がある</code>.

<ruby>予約<rt>よやく</rt></ruby>が**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>です**。<br>*A reservation is required.*

<ruby>予約<rt>よやく</rt></ruby>する**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>があります**。<br>*You need to make a reservation.*

The information is the same and the framing is not. The first names a thing the situation demands, and would suit a sign on a door. The second describes something the listener has to do, and suits an explanation.

---

## 必要 · 必要だ vs 必要がある (cont.)

A noun can be pushed into the `ある` frame with `の` (<code><ruby>予約<rt>よやく</rt></ruby>の<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>があります</code>), which sounds noticeably more bureaucratic. A verb, on the other hand, cannot use the `だ` frame at all - there is no ❌<code><ruby>予約<rt>よやく</rt></ruby>するが<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>です</code>.

---

## 必要 · Common mistakes

- ❌ <ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>**の**<ruby>書類<rt>しょるい</rt></ruby> → ✅ <ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>**な**<ruby>書類<rt>しょるい</rt></ruby><br>*<code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby></code> is a な-adjective when it modifies a noun. `の` looks tempting because the word is also a noun, but it is not how the phrase is built.*

- ❌ パスポート**を**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>です。 → ✅ パスポート**が**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>です。<br>*There is no verb here, so there is no object. The needed thing is the subject and takes `が`.*

- ❌ この<ruby>靴<rt>くつ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>**くない**。 → ✅ この<ruby>靴<rt>くつ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>**じゃない**。<br>*Only い-adjectives negate with `くない`. <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby></code> takes `じゃない`, `ではない`, or bare `ない`.*

- ❌ <ruby>病院<rt>びょういん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く**が**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>です。 → ✅ <ruby>病院<rt>びょういん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>があります**。<br>*A verb cannot be marked with `が`. To say an action is needed, switch to the <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>がある</code> frame.*

---

## 必要 · Common mistakes (cont.)

- ❌（to a friend, about a plastic bag）<ruby>袋<rt>ふくろ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>ですか。 → ✅ <ruby>袋<rt>ふくろ</rt></ruby>いる？<br>*Grammatical and oddly formal. Among friends the everyday word for needing a thing is `いる`.*

---

## 必要 · Practice 1

**1.** この<ruby>手続<rt>てつづ</rt></ruby>きに____な<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>を<ruby>全部<rt>ぜんぶ</rt></ruby><ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>って<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>ました。

{reveal}
この<ruby>手続<rt>てつづ</rt></ruby>きに**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>**な<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>を<ruby>全部<rt>ぜんぶ</rt></ruby><ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>って<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>ました。

{reveal}
Modifying a noun, <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby></code> behaves as a な-adjective, so the connector is `な`. The `に` marks the purpose the things are needed *for*.

---

## 必要 · Practice 2

**2.** ペン、（いる・<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>でいらっしゃいますか）？ - said to a close friend.

{reveal}
ペン、**いる**？

{reveal}
Between friends the plain verb is what people use; the honorific version is not merely over-polite, it is comic. <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby></code> itself is not rude here, but it still sounds like a form rather than a question about a pen.

---

## 必要 · Practice 3

**3.** Translate into Japanese, as a line on a website: "A credit card is not required."

{reveal}
クレジットカードは**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>ありません**。

{reveal}
<code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>ありません</code> is the standard polite negative and the usual wording on notices. <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>ない</code> would be too blunt for a public-facing page, and <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>ではございません</code> would be stiffer than most sites go.

---

## 必要 · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は<ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>起<rt>お</rt></ruby>きるが<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>です。

{reveal}
✅ <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は<ruby>早<rt>はや</rt></ruby>く<ruby>起<rt>お</rt></ruby>きる**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>があります**。

{reveal}
`が` can only mark a noun. When what is needed is an action, the dictionary form attaches straight to <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby></code> and the sentence closes with `ある`.

---

## 必要 · Practice 5

**5.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) この<ruby>会社<rt>かいしゃ</rt></ruby>には<ruby>君<rt>きみ</rt></ruby>が**<ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby>だ**。 (b) この<ruby>会社<rt>かいしゃ</rt></ruby>にとって<ruby>君<rt>きみ</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>大切<rt>たいせつ</rt></ruby>な<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>だ**。

{reveal}
(a) says the company cannot function without you. <code><ruby>必要<rt>ひつよう</rt></ruby></code> frames a person as something the organisation requires, so the compliment is real but cool - it is about what you produce. In a film this is the line a boss says to stop someone resigning.

{reveal}
(b) says you are valued. <code><ruby>大切<rt>たいせつ</rt></ruby></code> is about worth rather than utility, and it is the word you would use about a person if you wanted the sentence to sound warm. Both are natural Japanese; only one of them is affectionate.

---

# N4 - Thinking, wondering, and asking

- ～と思う
- って
- かどうか
- かもしれない
- はずだ
- はずがない
- かな
- かしら

---

# N4 - Thinking, wondering, and asking (cont.)

- かい
- じゃないか

---

# ～と思う

**Meaning** · I think (that) … - <code><ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う</code> is "think", and `と` is the string that ties a whole sentence into a parcel for it to carry

`と` is a **quotation marker**. It takes an entire sentence, wraps it up, and hands it to a verb of thinking or saying. <code>と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う</code> is therefore not "think about" - it reports a complete thought, word for word, as your opinion. The parcel is always tied in **plain form**, no matter how polite the sentence around it is.

---

## ～と思う · Formation

`と` follows the plain form of the quoted clause. Nouns and な-adjectives keep their `だ`.

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Verb | plain form + と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う | <ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>る → <ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>ると<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う |
| Verb (past) | た-form + と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う | <ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わった → <ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わったと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う |
| Verb (negative) | ない-form + と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う | <ruby>間<rt>ま</rt></ruby>に<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>わない → <ruby>間<rt>ま</rt></ruby>に<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>わないと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う |
| い-adjective | plain form + と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う | <ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>い → <ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>いと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う |
| な-adjective | + だ + と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う | <ruby>無理<rt>むり</rt></ruby> → <ruby>無理<rt>むり</rt></ruby>だと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う |
| Noun | + だ + と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う | <ruby>冗談<rt>じょうだん</rt></ruby> → <ruby>冗談<rt>じょうだん</rt></ruby>だと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う |
| Volitional - "I'm thinking of…" | よう-form + と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う | <ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>もう → <ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>もうと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う |
| Somebody else's opinion | plain form + と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>っている | <ruby>正<rt>ただ</rt></ruby>しい → <ruby>正<rt>ただ</rt></ruby>しいと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>っている |

---

## ～と思う · Formation (cont.)

> **Rule of thumb** - nothing polite goes in front of `と`. ❌<code><ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きますと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います</code> → ✅<code><ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います</code>. The politeness of the whole sentence is carried by the **final** verb and nowhere else.

> **Note** - the `だ` that disappears before `でしょう` stays before `と`. It is <code><ruby>大丈夫<rt>だいじょうぶ</rt></ruby>でしょう</code> but <code><ruby>大丈夫<rt>だいじょうぶ</rt></ruby>だと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います</code>.

---

## ～と思う · Examples

あの<ruby>店<rt>みせ</rt></ruby>はもう<ruby>閉<rt>し</rt></ruby>まっている**と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う**。<br>*I think that shop has already closed.*

この<ruby>傘<rt>かさ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>山田<rt>やまだ</rt></ruby>さんのだ**と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います**。<br>*I think this umbrella is Yamada's.*

<ruby>試験<rt>しけん</rt></ruby>はそんなに<ruby>難<rt>むずか</rt></ruby>しくない**と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う**よ。<br>*I don't think the test will be all that hard.*

<ruby>今年<rt>ことし</rt></ruby>の<ruby>冬<rt>ふゆ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>去年<rt>きょねん</rt></ruby>より<ruby>暖<rt>あたた</rt></ruby>かい**と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>いませんか**。<br>*Don't you think this winter is milder than last year's?*

---

## ～と思う · Examples (cont.)

<ruby>来月<rt>らいげつ</rt></ruby>から<ruby>自転車<rt>じてんしゃ</rt></ruby>で<ruby>通<rt>かよ</rt></ruby>おう**と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>っています**。<br>*I'm thinking of cycling to work from next month.*

<ruby>妹<rt>いもうと</rt></ruby>は<ruby>自分<rt>じぶん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>料理<rt>りょうり</rt></ruby>が<ruby>世界<rt>せかい</rt></ruby>で<ruby>一番<rt>いちばん</rt></ruby>おいしい**と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>っている**。<br>*My sister is convinced her own cooking is the best in the world.*

<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>三時<rt>さんじ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>終<rt>お</rt></ruby>わる**と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います**が、<ruby>念<rt>ねん</rt></ruby>のため<ruby>確認<rt>かくにん</rt></ruby>しておきます。<br>*I think the meeting finishes at three, but I'll check to be safe.*

<ruby>正直<rt>しょうじき</rt></ruby>に<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>うと、あの<ruby>計画<rt>けいかく</rt></ruby>はうまくいかない**と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います**。<br>*To be honest, I don't think that plan is going to work.*

---

## ～と思う · Nuance & register

<code><ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う</code> is the plain form and <code><ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います</code> the polite one; everything before `と` is untouched by that choice. This is the single most useful thing to know about the pattern, and the single most common place learners slip.

Beyond grammar, <code>と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います</code> is a **softener**. A bare assertion - その<ruby>方法<rt>ほうほう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>無理<rt>むり</rt></ruby>です - commits you to a fact. Adding <code>と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います</code> reframes it as one person's reading of the situation, which is why Japanese workplace speech is full of it. Overusing it is a real thing too: answering a question about your own department with <code><ruby>多分<rt>たぶん</rt></ruby>そうだと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います</code> can sound as if you have not bothered to find out.

---

## ～と思う · Nuance & register (cont.)

In casual speech you will hear `って` in place of `と` - <ruby>無理<rt>むり</rt></ruby>だって<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>った - and the whole clause often ends in `んだけど` to leave the door open: <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>でもいいと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>うんだけど。 At the other end, formal writing prefers the passive <code>と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>われます</code> or <code>と<ruby>考<rt>かんが</rt></ruby>えられます</code>, which removes the "I" altogether.

One limit worth stating plainly: the plain-form rule is about **indirect** quotation. If you put actual quotation marks round someone's words you are reproducing what came out of their mouth, so anything can appear inside: 「<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>みます」と<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>っていました。 That is a direct quote, and it is not an exception to the rule - it is a different operation.

---

## ～と思う · ～と思う vs ～と思っている

> **Rule of thumb** - <code><ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う</code> is a thought formed **now**, at the moment of speaking. <code><ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>っている</code> is a view somebody **holds** - and it is the only option for a flat statement about a third person.

その<ruby>色<rt>いろ</rt></ruby>のほうが<ruby>似合<rt>にあ</rt></ruby>う**と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う**。<br>*I think that colour suits you better.*

<ruby>父<rt>ちち</rt></ruby>は<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>をまだ<ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>どもだ**と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>っている**。<br>*My father still thinks of me as a child.*

---

## ～と思う · ～と思う vs ～と思っている (cont.)

You cannot see into someone else's head, so a bare ❌<code><ruby>父<rt>ちち</rt></ruby>は…と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う</code> claims access you do not have. The `ている` turns it into an observation about a state you can infer from outside. About yourself both work: <code><ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>もそう<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>っています</code> just adds that you have thought so for a while.

---

## ～と思う · ～と思う vs ～でしょう

> **Rule of thumb** - <code>と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う</code> labels the claim as **mine**. `でしょう` estimates how **likely** the claim is. One is about the speaker, the other about the world.

<ruby>来年<rt>らいねん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>野菜<rt>やさい</rt></ruby>の<ruby>値段<rt>ねだん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がる**と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います**。<br>*I think vegetable prices will go up next year.*

<ruby>来年<rt>らいねん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>野菜<rt>やさい</rt></ruby>の<ruby>値段<rt>ねだん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がる**でしょう**。<br>*Vegetable prices will probably go up next year.*

---

## ～と思う · ～と思う vs ～でしょう (cont.)

The second is what a news presenter says; the first is what you say at dinner. Because <code>と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います</code> keeps the responsibility on you, it is usually the safer choice when you might be wrong, and the wrong choice when you are supposed to be the authority.

---

## ～と思う · ～ないと思う vs ～と思わない

> **Rule of thumb** - English negates "think"; Japanese negates the **thought**. "I don't think it will rain" is <code><ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>らないと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う</code>, not <code><ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>ると<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>わない</code>.

<ruby>彼女<rt>かのじょ</rt></ruby>はその<ruby>話<rt>はなし</rt></ruby>を<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>らない**と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います**。<br>*I don't think she knows about it.*

<code>と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>わない</code> is not ungrammatical - it is simply much stronger. It rejects the proposition rather than doubting it, so it lands as disagreement:

<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>はそうは**<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>いません**。<br>*I don't see it that way.*

---

## ～と思う · ～ないと思う vs ～と思わない (cont.)

Note the `は` on `そう`, which is typical: negating <code><ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う</code> almost always comes with contrastive `は`, and that is part of why it feels like pushing back.

---

## ～と思う · Common mistakes

- ❌ <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が**<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>りますと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います**。 → ✅ <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が**<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>ると<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います**。<br>*Nothing in ます-form may sit in front of `と`. Politeness belongs to the last verb.*

- ❌ この<ruby>辞書<rt>じしょ</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>便利<rt>べんり</rt></ruby>と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う**。 → ✅ この<ruby>辞書<rt>じしょ</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>便利<rt>べんり</rt></ruby>だと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う**。<br>*な-adjectives and nouns keep `だ` before `と`. Only い-adjectives and verbs attach bare.*

- ❌ <ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>はその<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>がつまらないと**<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います**。 → ✅ <ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>はその<ruby>映画<rt>えいが</rt></ruby>がつまらないと**<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>っています**。<br>*A plain statement about what someone else thinks needs `ている` - or a hedge such as <code><ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>っているようです</code>.*

- ❌ <ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>が**あると<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>いません**。 → ✅ <ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>が**ないと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います**。<br>*Put the negative inside the quoted thought. The outer negative is reserved for disagreeing.*

---

## ～と思う · Practice 1

**1.** <ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんは<ruby>来週<rt>らいしゅう</rt></ruby><ruby>出張<rt>しゅっちょう</rt></ruby>____<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います。

{reveal}
<ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんは<ruby>来週<rt>らいしゅう</rt></ruby><ruby>出張<rt>しゅっちょう</rt></ruby>**だと**<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います。

{reveal}
<code><ruby>出張<rt>しゅっちょう</rt></ruby></code> is a noun, and a noun predicate keeps its `だ` in front of the quotative `と`. Dropping it is only correct before `でしょう`.

---

## ～と思う · Practice 2

**2.** Choose: <ruby>姉<rt>あね</rt></ruby>は<ruby>自分<rt>じぶん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>正<rt>ただ</rt></ruby>しい（と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います・と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>っています）。

{reveal}
<ruby>姉<rt>あね</rt></ruby>は<ruby>自分<rt>じぶん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>正<rt>ただ</rt></ruby>しい**と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>っています**。

{reveal}
The subject is a third person, so a bare <code>と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います</code> would claim direct knowledge of her mind. `ている` presents the belief as something you observe her holding.

---

## ～と思う · Practice 3

**3.** Translate into Japanese: "I don't think he will come today."

{reveal}
<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby>**<ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>ないと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います**。

{reveal}
The negative goes inside the quoted thought, not on <code><ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う</code>. <code><ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>ると<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>いません</code> would read as flatly rejecting the idea rather than doubting it.

---

## ～と思う · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: あの<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>は<ruby>親切<rt>しんせつ</rt></ruby>ですと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います。

{reveal}
✅ あの<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>親切<rt>しんせつ</rt></ruby>だと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います**。

{reveal}
Two things go wrong at once: `です` cannot appear before `と`, and the な-adjective still needs its plain copula `だ`. The polite ending survives on <code><ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います</code>.

---

## ～と思う · Practice 5

**5.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) この<ruby>案<rt>あん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>失敗<rt>しっぱい</rt></ruby>すると<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います。 (b) この<ruby>案<rt>あん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>失敗<rt>しっぱい</rt></ruby>するでしょう。

{reveal}
(a) marks the prediction as your own reading and keeps the responsibility with you - appropriate in a meeting where you are offering an opinion someone may argue with.

{reveal}
(b) states it as a likely outcome, the way a forecast or an analysis does. It sounds more detached and more authoritative, which is fine from an expert and presumptuous from a newcomer.

---

# って

**Meaning** · the spoken shortcut - "they said…", "you know…", "the thing called…"

`って` is what `と` (and often `という`, and sometimes `は`) becomes in relaxed speech. It quotes, it reports hearsay, it introduces a name, and it puts a topic on the table with a little more energy than `は` does. One syllable, several jobs - but they all come from the same place: `って` **presents a chunk of language** and asks the listener to take it as a unit.

---

## って · Formation

Like `と`, `って` follows the **plain form**. Nouns and な-adjectives keep `だ` when `って` is quoting; they drop it when `って` is marking a topic.

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Verb - quoting | plain form + って（+ <ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>う／<ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>く／<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う） | <ruby>辞<rt>や</rt></ruby>める → <ruby>辞<rt>や</rt></ruby>めるって<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>ってた |
| Noun / な-adjective - quoting | + だ + って | <ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby> → <ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>だって<ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>いた |
| Sentence-final - hearsay | plain form + って（falling tone） | <ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>ない → <ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>ないって |
| Direct quote | 「…」+ って | 「まだだ」 → 「まだだ」って<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>われた |
| Naming - replaces `という` | Noun + って + Noun | <ruby>林<rt>はやし</rt></ruby> → <ruby>林<rt>はやし</rt></ruby>さんって<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby> |
| Topic - replaces `は` / `というのは` | Noun + って（no だ） | <ruby>敬語<rt>けいご</rt></ruby> → <ruby>敬語<rt>けいご</rt></ruby>って<ruby>難<rt>むずか</rt></ruby>しい |

---

## って · Formation (cont.)

> **Rule of thumb** - `って` inherits the `と` rule exactly: the clause in front of it is **plain**, however polite you are being. ❌<code><ruby>晴<rt>は</rt></ruby>れますって</code> → ✅<code><ruby>晴<rt>は</rt></ruby>れるって</code>. The one exception is a direct quote in 「」, where you are copying someone's actual words.

---

## って · Examples

<ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さん、<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby><ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>ない**って**。<br>*Tanaka says he's not coming tomorrow.*

<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>、<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>だ**って**。<br>*Apparently the meeting's off.*

<ruby>漢字<rt>かんじ</rt></ruby>**って**<ruby>覚<rt>おぼ</rt></ruby>えるのが<ruby>大変<rt>たいへん</rt></ruby>だね。<br>*Kanji really are a slog to memorise, aren't they.*

さっき<ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>宿題<rt>しゅくだい</rt></ruby>はない**って**<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>ってたよ。<br>*The teacher said a moment ago that there's no homework today.*

---

## って · Examples (cont.)

<ruby>林<rt>はやし</rt></ruby>さん**って**<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>から<ruby>電話<rt>でんわ</rt></ruby>がありましたよ。<br>*There was a phone call from someone called Hayashi.*

「もう<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>りたい」**って**<ruby>顔<rt>かお</rt></ruby>をしているよ。<br>*You've got an "I want to go home already" look on your face.*

<ruby>妹<rt>いもうと</rt></ruby>に<ruby>貸<rt>か</rt></ruby>した<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>、まだ<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>んでない**って**<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>うんだけど、もう<ruby>一<rt>いっ</rt></ruby>か<ruby>月<rt>げつ</rt></ruby><ruby>経<rt>た</rt></ruby>つよ。<br>*My sister says she still hasn't read the book I lent her - and it's been a month.*

<ruby>来年<rt>らいねん</rt></ruby><ruby>留学<rt>りゅうがく</rt></ruby>する**って**<ruby>本当<rt>ほんとう</rt></ruby>？いつ<ruby>決<rt>き</rt></ruby>めたの？<br>*Is it true you're studying abroad next year? When did you decide?*

---

## って · Nuance & register

`って` is **spoken casual and nothing else**. It belongs in conversation with friends, family and people you are on plain-form terms with. It does not belong in an email to a client, a report, an essay, or a sentence you are otherwise ending in `ます`. The neutral replacements are `と` for quoting and `そうです`／ `とのことです` for hearsay.

Intonation does a lot of work. Falling `って` at the end of a sentence is hearsay - <ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>になるって。 Rising `って`? is a request for confirmation, close to "wait, did you say…?" - <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby><ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>みだって？ Both are the same particle.

---

## って · Nuance & register (cont.)

Two extensions you will hear constantly and will not find in a textbook: `っていうか` at the head of a sentence, which retracts what you just said and restarts ("or rather…"), and `ってば`, which repeats something impatiently - だから<ruby>違<rt>ちが</rt></ruby>うってば。 The second is distinctly childish or intimate; it is not a neutral emphasis marker.

There is a semi-polite hearsay form, `～んですって`, which keeps a `です` on the end: となりの<ruby>店<rt>みせ</rt></ruby>、<ruby>閉<rt>し</rt></ruby>めるんですって。 It is polite in form but chatty in feel, and in modern Tokyo speech it leans female. `～だってです` is not a form at all.

---

## って · って vs と

> **Rule of thumb** - same grammar, different register: `って` is `と` in a T-shirt. But `って` also covers jobs `と` cannot do, namely naming and topic-marking.

<ruby>課長<rt>かちょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>出席<rt>しゅっせき</rt></ruby>できない**と**<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>っていました。<br>*The section chief said he can't attend.*

<ruby>課長<rt>かちょう</rt></ruby>、<ruby>出席<rt>しゅっせき</rt></ruby>できない**って**。<br>*The boss says he can't make it.*

---

## って · って vs と (cont.)

Both report the same fact. The first is what you write in a message to the team; the second is what you say over your shoulder to the colleague next to you. Where the two part company is self-introduction and any fixed formula: <ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>と<ruby>申<rt>もう</rt></ruby>します is the set phrase, and `って` there is simply wrong.

---

## って · topic って vs は

> **Rule of thumb** - `は` sets a topic quietly. `って` sets a topic and signals that you are about to say something **about the category itself**, usually with a reaction attached.

<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>夏<rt>なつ</rt></ruby>**は**<ruby>暑<rt>あつ</rt></ruby>いです。<br>*Summers in Japan are hot.*

<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>夏<rt>なつ</rt></ruby>**って**<ruby>暑<rt>あつ</rt></ruby>いね。<br>*Japanese summers are hot, aren't they.*

---

## って · topic って vs は (cont.)

The `って` version reads as a comment brought up fresh, and it pairs naturally with `ね`, `よ` and evaluative adjectives. It is close to <code><ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>夏<rt>なつ</rt></ruby>というのは</code>, which is exactly what it is a contraction of - and that is why it can also mean "what is…?": 「バイト」**って**<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>？

---

## って · hearsay って vs ～そうだ

> **Rule of thumb** - identical content, opposite registers. `って` is what you say; `そうです` is what you write.

<ruby>山田<rt>やまだ</rt></ruby>さん、<ruby>来月<rt>らいげつ</rt></ruby><ruby>引<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>っ<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>す**って**。<br>*Yamada's moving house next month, apparently.*

<ruby>山田<rt>やまだ</rt></ruby>さんは<ruby>来月<rt>らいげつ</rt></ruby><ruby>引<rt>ひ</rt></ruby>っ<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>す**そうです**。<br>*I hear that Yamada is moving house next month.*

---

## って · hearsay って vs ～そうだ (cont.)

One practical difference: `って` easily carries a named source in front of it - <ruby>母<rt>はは</rt></ruby>が<ruby>寒<rt>さむ</rt></ruby>くなるって<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>ってた - while `そうだ` usually leaves the source vague or marks it with `によると`. If you want to say who told you, `って` is the more natural spoken frame.

---

## って · Common mistakes

- ❌ <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>**って<ruby>申<rt>もう</rt></ruby>します**。 → ✅ <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>**と<ruby>申<rt>もう</rt></ruby>します**。<br>*Self-introduction is a fixed humble formula. `って` cannot be dropped into a phrase that is formal by definition.*

- ❌ <ruby>天気予報<rt>てんきよほう</rt></ruby>で<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>晴<rt>は</rt></ruby>れますって**<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>ってた。 → ✅ …**<ruby>晴<rt>は</rt></ruby>れるって**<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>ってた。<br>*An indirect quote takes the plain form, exactly as with `と`. `ます` only survives inside 「」.*

- ❌ <ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>、<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>**だってです**。 → ✅ <ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>、<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>**だそうです**。<br>*You cannot make `って` polite by bolting `です` on. Switch to `そうです` or `とのことです`.*

- ❌ (in a written report) <ruby>調査<rt>ちょうさ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>結果<rt>けっか</rt></ruby>、<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>はなかった**って**。 → ✅ …<ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>はなかった**とのことです**。<br>*`って` is a spoken form. In writing it reads as though the report were a text message.*

---

## って · Practice 1

**1.** <ruby>友達<rt>ともだち</rt></ruby>に：「<ruby>山田<rt>やまだ</rt></ruby>さん、<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby><ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>られない____。」

{reveal}
<ruby>山田<rt>やまだ</rt></ruby>さん、<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby><ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>られない**って**。

{reveal}
Sentence-final `って` after a plain form reports what you were told, with the source left implicit. Said with a falling tone it means "apparently", not "did you say?".

---

## って · Practice 2

**2.** Choose the natural option for an email to a client: <ruby>納期<rt>のうき</rt></ruby>は<ruby>来週<rt>らいしゅう</rt></ruby>（だって・だそうです）。

{reveal}
<ruby>納期<rt>のうき</rt></ruby>は<ruby>来週<rt>らいしゅう</rt></ruby>**だそうです**。

{reveal}
`って` is casual spoken Japanese and never appears in business writing. The hearsay meaning is unchanged; only the register is fixed.

---

## って · Practice 3

**3.** Translate into Japanese, casually: "Someone called Kimura came looking for you."

{reveal}
<ruby>木村<rt>きむら</rt></ruby>さん**って<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>**が<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>たよ。

{reveal}
`って` before a noun is the contraction of `という` and is the everyday way of naming someone the listener may not know. <code><ruby>木村<rt>きむら</rt></ruby>さんという<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby></code> is the same thing in a neutral register.

---

## って · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>仕事<rt>しごと</rt></ruby>を<ruby>探<rt>さが</rt></ruby>していますって<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>ってた。

{reveal}
✅ <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>仕事<rt>しごと</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>探<rt>さが</rt></ruby>しているって**<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>ってた。

{reveal}
The quoted clause must be plain. `って` is only a casual `と`, so it obeys the same restriction: nothing in ます-form immediately in front of it.

---

## って · Practice 5

**5.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) <ruby>一人暮<rt>ひとりぐ</rt></ruby>らしはお<ruby>金<rt>かね</rt></ruby>がかかります。 (b) <ruby>一人暮<rt>ひとりぐ</rt></ruby>らし**って**お<ruby>金<rt>かね</rt></ruby>がかかるよね。

{reveal}
(a) is a neutral, polite statement of fact - the kind of line that could open a paragraph in an article about living costs.

{reveal}
(b) raises "living alone" as a topic the two of you both know something about, and adds a shared reaction with `よね`. `って` marks the category as newly put on the table and invites agreement; it is conversation, not exposition.

---

# かどうか

**Meaning** · whether or not - packs a yes/no question inside a bigger sentence

`かどうか` takes a question that could be answered *yes* or *no*, ties it into a single lump, and hands that lump to a verb like <code><ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かる</code>, <code><ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>らない</code> or <code><ruby>調<rt>しら</rt></ruby>べる</code>. It is literally "か（yes?）どう（how?）か" - is it so, or how is it? The English that maps onto it is **whether**, and mapping it onto **if** instead is where nearly all the trouble starts.

---

## かどうか · Formation

`か` attaches to plain forms. Nouns and な-adjectives **lose** their `だ` - the opposite of what happens before the quotative `と`.

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Verb | plain form + かどうか | <ruby>届<rt>とど</rt></ruby>く → <ruby>届<rt>とど</rt></ruby>くかどうか |
| Verb (past) | た-form + かどうか | <ruby>送<rt>おく</rt></ruby>った → <ruby>送<rt>おく</rt></ruby>ったかどうか |
| Verb (negative) | ない-form + かどうか | <ruby>要<rt>い</rt></ruby>らない → <ruby>要<rt>い</rt></ruby>らないかどうか |
| い-adjective | plain form + かどうか | <ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい → <ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しいかどうか |
| な-adjective | drop だ + かどうか | <ruby>安全<rt>あんぜん</rt></ruby>だ → <ruby>安全<rt>あんぜん</rt></ruby>かどうか |
| Noun | drop だ + かどうか | <ruby>本物<rt>ほんもの</rt></ruby>だ → <ruby>本物<rt>ほんもの</rt></ruby>かどうか |
| Both options spelled out | ～か～ないか | <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く → <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くか<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>かないか |

---

## かどうか · Formation (cont.)

Typical main verbs after it: <code><ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かる</code>, <code><ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>らない</code>, <code><ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>く</code>, <code><ruby>調<rt>しら</rt></ruby>べる</code>, <code><ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かめる</code>, <code><ruby>迷<rt>まよ</rt></ruby>う</code>, <code><ruby>覚<rt>おぼ</rt></ruby>えていない</code>, <code><ruby>決<rt>き</rt></ruby>める</code>.

> **Rule of thumb** - nothing polite and no `だ` in front of `か`. ❌<code><ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きますかどうか</code>, ❌<code><ruby>安全<rt>あんぜん</rt></ruby>だかどうか</code> → ✅<code><ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くかどうか</code>, ✅<code><ruby>安全<rt>あんぜん</rt></ruby>かどうか</code>.

> **Note** - the particle that would follow the lump (`を`, `が`) is normally left out: <ruby>届<rt>とど</rt></ruby>いたかどうか<ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かめます. `は` does appear, and adds contrast: <ruby>届<rt>とど</rt></ruby>いたかどうかは、まだ<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かりません。

---

## かどうか · Examples

これでいい**かどうか**、<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>てください。<br>*Please have a look and tell me whether this is all right.*

<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby><ruby>雪<rt>ゆき</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>る**かどうか**<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かりません。<br>*I don't know whether it will snow tomorrow.*

この<ruby>水<rt>みず</rt></ruby>が<ruby>安全<rt>あんぜん</rt></ruby>**かどうか**、<ruby>先<rt>さき</rt></ruby>に<ruby>調<rt>しら</rt></ruby>べたほうがいいよ。<br>*You should check first whether this water is safe.*

<ruby>受<rt>う</rt></ruby>かった**かどうか**は、<ruby>来週<rt>らいしゅう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>金曜日<rt>きんようび</rt></ruby>に<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かります。<br>*Whether I passed or not will be clear next Friday.*

---

## かどうか · Examples (cont.)

パーティーに<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>る**かどうか**、まだ<ruby>迷<rt>まよ</rt></ruby>っているんです。<br>*I still can't make up my mind whether to go to the party.*

<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>本当<rt>ほんとう</rt></ruby>のことを<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>っている**かどうか**、<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>には<ruby>判断<rt>はんだん</rt></ruby>できません。<br>*I'm in no position to judge whether he's telling the truth.*

サイズが<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>う**かどうか**、<ruby>試着<rt>しちゃく</rt></ruby>してから<ruby>決<rt>き</rt></ruby>めようと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います。<br>*I'll try it on before deciding, to see whether the size works.*

<ruby>申<rt>もう</rt></ruby>し<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>みが<ruby>締<rt>し</rt></ruby>め<ruby>切<rt>き</rt></ruby>りに<ruby>間<rt>ま</rt></ruby>に<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>った**かどうか**、<ruby>事務所<rt>じむしょ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>確認<rt>かくにん</rt></ruby>してみます。<br>*I'll check with the office whether my application made the deadline.*

---

## かどうか · Nuance & register

`かどうか` is register-neutral. It appears unchanged in a chat with friends, in a lecture and in a contract; as always, the politeness of the sentence lives on the final verb. It is also one of the few N4 patterns with no casual contraction of its own - although in relaxed speech people often drop `どうか` entirely and leave a bare `か`: <ruby>間<rt>ま</rt></ruby>に<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>うか<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かんない。 That is shorter, not ruder.

The one thing `かどうか` cannot do is finish a sentence. It is a lump that some other verb has to pick up, so <code><ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>るかどうか。</code> on its own is a fragment. If you want to end there, you need the wondering forms instead - <code><ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>るかな</code>, <code><ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>るでしょうか</code>.

---

## かどうか · Nuance & register (cont.)

Two fixed expressions are worth having ready. <code>かどうかは<ruby>別<rt>べつ</rt></ruby>として</code> ("setting aside whether…") concedes a point before moving on, and <code>かどうか<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かりませんが</code> is the standard hedge for offering something you are not sure will help: お<ruby>役<rt>やく</rt></ruby>に<ruby>立<rt>た</rt></ruby>つかどうか<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かりませんが、こちらの<ruby>資料<rt>しりょう</rt></ruby>をどうぞ。

---

## かどうか · かどうか vs か

> **Rule of thumb** - if the embedded question contains a **question word** （<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>, どこ, だれ, いつ, どう, どちら）, use bare `か`. `かどうか` is only for questions whose answer is *yes* or *no*.

<ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby><ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>を<ruby>注文<rt>ちゅうもん</rt></ruby>した**か**<ruby>覚<rt>おぼ</rt></ruby>えていません。<br>*I don't remember what I ordered yesterday.*

<ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby><ruby>注文<rt>ちゅうもん</rt></ruby>した**かどうか**<ruby>覚<rt>おぼ</rt></ruby>えていません。<br>*I don't remember whether I ordered yesterday.*

---

## かどうか · かどうか vs か (cont.)

The first asks about the *contents* of the order, the second about whether the ordering happened at all. Sticking `どうか` onto the first - ❌<code><ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>を<ruby>注文<rt>ちゅうもん</rt></ruby>したかどうか</code> - is ungrammatical, because <ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby> has already supplied the question and `どうか` has nothing left to ask.

Bare `か` is also available for yes/no questions, especially in speech: <ruby>空<rt>あ</rt></ruby>いているか<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>てきます。 `かどうか` simply spells the alternative out and is the clearer choice in writing.

---

## かどうか · かどうか vs ～たら／～ば

> **Rule of thumb** - English "if" is two unrelated words. "If" you could replace with **whether** → `かどうか`. "If" meaning **on condition that** → `たら`／`ば`／`と`.

<ruby>木村<rt>きむら</rt></ruby>さんが<ruby>参加<rt>さんか</rt></ruby>する**かどうか**、<ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>いてみます。<br>*I'll ask whether Kimura is taking part.*

<ruby>木村<rt>きむら</rt></ruby>さんが<ruby>参加<rt>さんか</rt></ruby>し**たら**、<ruby>席<rt>せき</rt></ruby>を<ruby>一<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>つ<ruby>増<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>やします。<br>*If Kimura takes part, I'll add one more seat.*

---

## かどうか · かどうか vs ～たら／～ば (cont.)

These are not stylistic variants - they say different things. The first is about the speaker's ignorance; the second is about a consequence. "I don't know if he's coming" is ❌<code><ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>たら<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かりません</code> and ✅<code><ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>るかどうか<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かりません</code>. This is the most common single error with the pattern, and it comes straight out of English.

---

## かどうか · かどうか vs ～か～ないか

> **Rule of thumb** - same meaning, more deliberate delivery. And when the two options are not *yes* and *no* but two **different things**, only the spelled-out version works.

<ruby>出席<rt>しゅっせき</rt></ruby>する**かどうか**、<ruby>金曜日<rt>きんようび</rt></ruby>までにお<ruby>返事<rt>へんじ</rt></ruby>ください。<br>*Please reply by Friday as to whether you'll attend.*

<ruby>電車<rt>でんしゃ</rt></ruby>で<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く**かバスで<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>くか**、まだ<ruby>決<rt>き</rt></ruby>めていません。<br>*I haven't decided yet whether to go by train or by bus.*

The second could not be rewritten with `かどうか`: there is no *no* to negate, just two alternatives. Keep `かどうか` for the yes/no case and lay both options out when they are genuinely two options.

---

## かどうか · Common mistakes

- ❌ この<ruby>部屋<rt>へや</rt></ruby>が**<ruby>静<rt>しず</rt></ruby>かだかどうか**<ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かめます。 → ✅ この<ruby>部屋<rt>へや</rt></ruby>が**<ruby>静<rt>しず</rt></ruby>かかどうか**<ruby>確<rt>たし</rt></ruby>かめます。<br>*Nouns and な-adjectives drop `だ` before `か`. It is `だ` before `と`, no `だ` before `か` - the two quotative-ish particles behave in opposite ways.*

- ❌ <ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんが**<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>ますかどうか**<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>りません。 → ✅ <ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんが**<ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>るかどうか**<ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>りません。<br>*The embedded clause is plain. `ます` belongs to the end of the sentence, not to the middle of it.*

- ❌ <ruby>荷物<rt>にもつ</rt></ruby>が**<ruby>届<rt>とど</rt></ruby>いたら**<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かりません。 → ✅ <ruby>荷物<rt>にもつ</rt></ruby>が**<ruby>届<rt>とど</rt></ruby>いたかどうか**<ruby>分<rt>わ</rt></ruby>かりません。<br>*"I don't know if the parcel arrived" is *whether*, not a condition. `たら` here would mean "once it arrives, I won't understand", which is nonsense.*

---

## かどうか · Common mistakes (cont.)
