Compare <ruby>赤<rt>あか</rt></ruby>ちゃんは<ruby>夜<rt>よる</rt></ruby>になるとだっこされたがる, "babies want to be held once evening comes" - a pattern of behaviour rather than a report on this baby right now. The generic use is where you will most often meet the bare form, frequently rounded off with `ものだ`.

---

## ～たがる · ～たがる vs ～たいそうです・～たいと言っています

> **Rule of thumb** - `たがる` says you **saw** it. The reporting frames say you **heard** it, and they are the polite route upward.

<ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんは<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>たがっていません。<br>*Tanaka doesn't want to sit in on the meeting.*

That sentence claims to read Tanaka from his conduct, which is fine among peers and rude about a superior. The alternatives shift the source of the information: <ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>たくないそうです ("I hear he doesn't"), <ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>たくないと<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>っています ("he says he doesn't"), <ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>たくないようです ("he seems not to"). All three are softer, and the last two are what you use in a workplace when the person outranks you.

---

## ～たがる · Common mistakes

- ❌ <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く**たがる** → ✅ <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>**きたがる**<br>*`たがる` builds on the ます-stem, exactly like `たい` does.*

- ❌ <ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>どもがジュース**が**<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>みたがっています。 → ✅ <ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>どもがジュース**を**<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>みたがっています。<br>*The `が` option belongs to `たい`. Once the word is a verb, the object must be marked with `を`.*

- ❌ <ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>は<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きたがっ**たです**。 → ✅ <ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>は<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きたがっ**ていました**。<br>*Learners carry `たい`'s adjective endings across. `たがる` is a う-verb: the past polite is <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きたがりました, and for a past state, <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きたがっていました.*

- ❌ <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>辞書<rt>じしょ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>いたがっています。 → ✅ <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>辞書<rt>じしょ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>いたいとおっしゃっていました。<br>*Grammatical, but it inspects a teacher's motives out loud. Report what they said instead.*

---

## ～たがる · Practice 1

**1.** <ruby>妹<rt>いもうと</rt></ruby>は<ruby>外国<rt>がいこく</rt></ruby>で<ruby>働<rt>はたら</rt></ruby>____います。

{reveal}
<ruby>働<rt>はたら</rt></ruby>**きたがって**います

{reveal}
The stem <ruby>働<rt>はたら</rt></ruby>き takes `たがる`, and the て-form plus います gives the current-desire shape. Your sister is a third person, so plain <ruby>働<rt>はたら</rt></ruby>きたいです would be overstepping.

---

## ～たがる · Practice 2

**2.** （<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>・<ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>）は<ruby>海<rt>うみ</rt></ruby>へ<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きたがっています。

{reveal}
**<ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>**は<ruby>海<rt>うみ</rt></ruby>へ<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きたがっています。

{reveal}
`たがる` describes a desire inferred from someone's behaviour, which rules out yourself: you do not need evidence of your own wishes. For the first person the sentence would be <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>海<rt>うみ</rt></ruby>へ<ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きたいです.

---

## ～たがる · Practice 3

**3.** Translate into Japanese: "My grandmother doesn't want to use a smartphone."

{reveal}
<ruby>祖母<rt>そぼ</rt></ruby>はスマホを**<ruby>使<rt>つか</rt></ruby>いたがりません**。

{reveal}
The negative of a う-verb, and the form that carries the "won't, resists it" flavour English gets from "doesn't want to". <ruby>使<rt>つか</rt></ruby>いたがらない is the plain equivalent.

---

## ～たがる · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: <ruby>友<rt>とも</rt></ruby>だちは<ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しいカメラがほしたがっています。

{reveal}
✅ <ruby>友<rt>とも</rt></ruby>だちは<ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しいカメラ**をほしがって**います。

{reveal}
`たがる` attaches to a verb stem, and ほしい is an adjective, so there is no ほしたがる - the form built from ほしい is ほしがる. The particle also has to move from `が` to `を`.

---

## ～たがる · Practice 5

**5.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>はもっと<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>したがっています。 (b) <ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>はもっと<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>したいと<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>っています。

{reveal}
(a) is your reading of his behaviour: he keeps leaning in, he has not finished, you can tell he wants to keep going. Nobody has necessarily said anything, and the judgement is yours - which is why it would be presumptuous about a superior.

{reveal}
(b) hands the claim back to him. He said it; you are relaying it. This version is safe in any company, and it is what you would write in a message to a manager.

---

# ～がする

**Meaning** · a sensation reaches you - a smell, a sound, a taste, a feeling

`する` is not always "do". With a small set of sensation nouns it means something closer to "there is" or "it comes to me": <ruby>音<rt>おと</rt></ruby>がする, "there's a sound"; においがする, "there's a smell". Nobody is performing anything. The sensation arrives, and the noun naming it is the subject.

---

## ～がする · Formation

Sensation noun + `が` + `する`. There is no conjugating of the noun; only `する` moves.

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Sound | <ruby>音<rt>おと</rt></ruby>・<ruby>声<rt>こえ</rt></ruby> + がする | <ruby>変<rt>へん</rt></ruby>な<ruby>音<rt>おと</rt></ruby>がする |
| Smell | におい・<ruby>香<rt>かお</rt></ruby>り + がする | いいにおいがする |
| Taste | <ruby>味<rt>あじ</rt></ruby> + がする | <ruby>甘<rt>あま</rt></ruby>い<ruby>味<rt>あじ</rt></ruby>がする |
| Feeling, hunch | <ruby>気<rt>き</rt></ruby>・<ruby>感<rt>かん</rt></ruby>じ + がする | <ruby>気<rt>き</rt></ruby>がする |
| Bodily sensation | <ruby>寒気<rt>さむけ</rt></ruby>・<ruby>頭痛<rt>ずつう</rt></ruby>・めまい + がする | めまいがする |
| Sense of a presence | <ruby>気配<rt>けはい</rt></ruby> + がする | <ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>の<ruby>気配<rt>けはい</rt></ruby>がする |

`する` is irregular and carries the whole conjugation:

---

## ～がする · Formation (cont.)

| Verb form | Example |
|---|---|
| Polite | <ruby>音<rt>おと</rt></ruby>がします |
| Negative | <ruby>音<rt>おと</rt></ruby>がしない |
| Past | <ruby>音<rt>おと</rt></ruby>がした |
| て-form | <ruby>音<rt>おと</rt></ruby>がして |
| Ongoing | <ruby>音<rt>おと</rt></ruby>がしている |

> **Rule of thumb** - the sensation is the **subject**, so the particle is `が`. Never ❌においをする. Nothing is being done to the smell; the smell is what is there.

---

## ～がする · Formation (cont.)

> **Note** - the list of nouns that work this way is short and fixed. Sight is not on it: for something visible you use <ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>える, never ❌<ruby>山<rt>やま</rt></ruby>がする. Pain is not on it either - it is <ruby>頭<rt>あたま</rt></ruby>が<ruby>痛<rt>いた</rt></ruby>いです or <ruby>痛<rt>いた</rt></ruby>みがあります, though the noun <ruby>頭痛<rt>ずつう</rt></ruby> does take がする.

---

## ～がする · Examples

だれかの**<ruby>声<rt>こえ</rt></ruby>がする**。<br>*I can hear someone's voice.*

<ruby>台所<rt>だいどころ</rt></ruby>からいい**においがします**。<br>*There's a lovely smell coming from the kitchen.*

このスープは<ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>し<ruby>甘<rt>あま</rt></ruby>い**<ruby>味<rt>あじ</rt></ruby>がします**。<br>*This soup tastes slightly sweet.*

<ruby>外<rt>そと</rt></ruby>で<ruby>変<rt>へん</rt></ruby>な**<ruby>音<rt>おと</rt></ruby>がした**ので、<ruby>窓<rt>まど</rt></ruby>を<ruby>開<rt>あ</rt></ruby>けてみました。<br>*There was an odd noise outside, so I opened the window to look.*

---

## ～がする · Examples (cont.)

<ruby>朝<rt>あさ</rt></ruby>から**<ruby>寒気<rt>さむけ</rt></ruby>がする**ので、<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>会社<rt>かいしゃ</rt></ruby>を<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>みます。<br>*I've had chills since this morning, so I'm taking the day off work.*

どこかでお<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>いしたような**<ruby>気<rt>き</rt></ruby>がします**。<br>*I have a feeling we've met somewhere before.*

この<ruby>部屋<rt>へや</rt></ruby>は<ruby>古<rt>ふる</rt></ruby>い<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>の**においがして**、なんだか<ruby>落<rt>お</rt></ruby>ち<ruby>着<rt>つ</rt></ruby>きます。<br>*This room smells of old books, and something about that is calming.*

さっきから<ruby>上<rt>うえ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>階<rt>かい</rt></ruby>で<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>が<ruby>歩<rt>ある</rt></ruby>いている**<ruby>音<rt>おと</rt></ruby>がして**、なかなか<ruby>眠<rt>ねむ</rt></ruby>れません。<br>*I've been hearing someone walking about upstairs for a while now, and I can't get to sleep.*

---

## ～がする · Nuance & register

The defining feature of `がする` is that the sensation is **unbidden and often unidentified**. <ruby>音<rt>おと</rt></ruby>がする is what you say when something made a noise and you do not yet know what: you noticed, you did not investigate. That is why it pairs so naturally with <ruby>変<rt>へん</rt></ruby>な, <ruby>大<rt>おお</rt></ruby>きな and だれかの - words that admit you have not pinned the source down.

The noun can be modified freely, and this is where most of the expressive work happens: レモンの<ruby>味<rt>あじ</rt></ruby>がする, <ruby>焦<rt>こ</rt></ruby>げたにおいがする, <ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>どもの<ruby>声<rt>こえ</rt></ruby>がする. A `の` phrase in front means "the smell/taste/sound *of* that thing", which is how you say something tastes *like* something else.

---

## ～がする · Nuance & register (cont.)

Tense matters more than usual here. `がした` reports one moment - a bang, a whiff. `がする` in the plain present covers a sensation happening now or as a general property （このお<ruby>菓子<rt>かし</rt></ruby>はバターのにおいがする）. `がしている` is available for something clearly ongoing, but Japanese reaches for the plain present far more readily than English does with "is smelling".

**`気がする` deserves separate attention.** It is one of the most used expressions in the spoken language: どこかで<ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>いたことがあるような<ruby>気<rt>き</rt></ruby>がする, 「<ruby>忘<rt>わす</rt></ruby>れ<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>をしたような<ruby>気<rt>き</rt></ruby>がする」. It reports a hunch you cannot justify, and because it commits you to nothing it is very useful for softening - <ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>し<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>いような<ruby>気<rt>き</rt></ruby>がします is a gentler way to say something is overpriced.

---

## ～がする · Nuance & register (cont.)

The pattern is register-neutral: identical in casual and polite speech, and completely standard in writing. The medical uses - <ruby>寒気<rt>さむけ</rt></ruby>がする, <ruby>吐<rt>は</rt></ruby>き<ruby>気<rt>け</rt></ruby>がする, めまいがする - are the phrases you actually need at a clinic, and they are worth memorising as units.

---

## ～がする · ～がする vs 聞こえる・見える

> **Rule of thumb** - <code><ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>こえる</code> says **you heard** a particular thing. `がする` says **there was** a sound. And there is no visual `がする`: for sight, only <code><ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>える</code>.

<ruby>夜中<rt>よなか</rt></ruby>に<ruby>猫<rt>ねこ</rt></ruby>の**<ruby>声<rt>こえ</rt></ruby>がして**、<ruby>目<rt>め</rt></ruby>が<ruby>覚<rt>さ</rt></ruby>めました。<br>*A cat's cry in the night woke me up.*

---

## ～がする · ～がする vs 聞こえる・見える (cont.)

Compare <ruby>猫<rt>ねこ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>声<rt>こえ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>こえました, "I could hear a cat." Both are correct, and the difference is where the sentence puts you. `聞こえる` is about your ears reaching the sound and implies you made it out; `がする` is about the sound being there at all, and sits comfortably with not knowing what it was. This is also why <ruby>気配<rt>けはい</rt></ruby>がする works while ❌<ruby>気配<rt>けはい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>こえる does not - a presence is not a thing you hear.

---

## ～がする · 気がする vs と思う

> **Rule of thumb** - <code><ruby>気<rt>き</rt></ruby>がする</code> is a hunch with no grounds behind it. <code>と<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>う</code> is an opinion you would defend.

<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>りそうな**<ruby>気<rt>き</rt></ruby>がします**。<br>*I've got a feeling it's going to rain today.*

Say <ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>降<rt>ふ</rt></ruby>ると<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>います instead and you sound as though you checked the forecast. `気がする` explicitly declines to give a reason, which makes it the safer form when you are half-remembering something or disagreeing gently with someone senior.

---

## ～がする · ～がする vs ～をしている

> **Rule of thumb** - `がする` is a sensation coming **to** you. `をしている` describes a property a thing **has** - its colour, its shape, its expression.

この<ruby>石<rt>いし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>変<rt>へん</rt></ruby>わった<ruby>形<rt>かたち</rt></ruby>をしています。<br>*This stone has an unusual shape.*

Same verb, opposite direction, opposite particle. <ruby>色<rt>いろ</rt></ruby>をしている, <ruby>形<rt>かたち</rt></ruby>をしている, <ruby>顔<rt>かお</rt></ruby>をしている are the three you will actually meet: <ruby>青<rt>あお</rt></ruby>い<ruby>目<rt>め</rt></ruby>をした<ruby>猫<rt>ねこ</rt></ruby>, <ruby>悲<rt>かな</rt></ruby>しそうな<ruby>顔<rt>かお</rt></ruby>をしていた. Sensations never take `を`, and appearances never take `が` in this construction.

---

## ～がする · Common mistakes

- ❌ いいにおい**を**します。 → ✅ いいにおい**が**します。<br>*The smell is the subject of the sentence, not an object someone acts on.*

- ❌ この<ruby>花<rt>はな</rt></ruby>はいいにおいが**あります**。 → ✅ この<ruby>花<rt>はな</rt></ruby>はいいにおいが**します**。<br>*English "has a nice smell" pushes learners towards ある. Japanese treats a perceived smell as something that *does* - it `する`.*

- ❌ <ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>から<ruby>頭痛<rt>ずつう</rt></ruby>を**しています**。 → ✅ <ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>から<ruby>頭痛<rt>ずつう</rt></ruby>が**します**。<br>*Same particle error in a medical setting, where being understood matters most.*

---

## ～がする · Common mistakes (cont.)

- ❌ あそこに<ruby>大<rt>おお</rt></ruby>きい<ruby>建物<rt>たてもの</rt></ruby>が**します**。 → ✅ あそこに<ruby>大<rt>おお</rt></ruby>きい<ruby>建物<rt>たてもの</rt></ruby>が**<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>えます**。<br>*`がする` covers hearing, smell, taste and bodily feeling - never sight.*

---

## ～がする · Practice 1

**1.** <ruby>台所<rt>だいどころ</rt></ruby>からカレーのにおい____。

{reveal}
カレーのにおい**がします**

{reveal}
Smell is one of the sensations that take this pattern, and the `の` phrase in front means the smell *of* curry. Polite present is します; in casual speech you would simply say がする.

---

## ～がする · Practice 2

**2.** となりの<ruby>部屋<rt>へや</rt></ruby>から<ruby>音<rt>おと</rt></ruby>が（します・あります）。

{reveal}
となりの<ruby>部屋<rt>へや</rt></ruby>から<ruby>音<rt>おと</rt></ruby>が**します**。

{reveal}
A sound that reaches you is reported with する, not ある. Using ある would be treating the noise as an object sitting in the next room rather than something you are perceiving right now.

---

## ～がする · Practice 3

**3.** Translate into Japanese: "This tea tastes a little bitter."

{reveal}
このお<ruby>茶<rt>ちゃ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>し<ruby>苦<rt>にが</rt></ruby>い**<ruby>味<rt>あじ</rt></ruby>がします**。

{reveal}
The adjective modifies <ruby>味<rt>あじ</rt></ruby>, and the whole sensation is the subject of します. You could also say このお<ruby>茶<rt>ちゃ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>し<ruby>苦<rt>にが</rt></ruby>いです; the <ruby>味<rt>あじ</rt></ruby>がする version foregrounds the taste as something you are registering.

---

## ～がする · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: <ruby>朝<rt>あさ</rt></ruby>からめまいをしていて、<ruby>立<rt>た</rt></ruby>てません。

{reveal}
✅ <ruby>朝<rt>あさ</rt></ruby>からめまい**がして**いて、<ruby>立<rt>た</rt></ruby>てません。

{reveal}
めまい belongs to the bodily-sensation group, and every member of that group takes `が`. The `を` version would suggest you are producing the dizziness on purpose.

---

## ～がする · Practice 5

**5.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) <ruby>下<rt>した</rt></ruby>の<ruby>階<rt>かい</rt></ruby>で<ruby>音<rt>おと</rt></ruby>がします。 (b) <ruby>下<rt>した</rt></ruby>の<ruby>階<rt>かい</rt></ruby>の<ruby>音<rt>おと</rt></ruby>が<ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>こえます。

{reveal}
(a) reports that a noise is occurring downstairs. It leaves the source open - you noticed something, you could not say what, and the sentence is what you would say while looking up from your book.

{reveal}
(b) puts your ears at the centre: the sound from downstairs reaches you and you can make it out. It suits describing how thin the walls are, or answering someone who asked whether you can hear anything. Where (a) is about the event, (b) is about your perception of it.

---

# ～のは○○だ - cleft sentences

**Meaning** · singles out one part of a sentence and puts it in the spotlight - "the one who did it was…", "it was last year that…"

Take a sentence, nominalise all of it except the piece you care about, and put that piece after `は`…`だ`. <ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>が<ruby>窓<rt>まど</rt></ruby>を<ruby>割<rt>わ</rt></ruby>った becomes <ruby>窓<rt>まど</rt></ruby>を<ruby>割<rt>わ</rt></ruby>った**のは<ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>です** - "the one who broke the window was my brother." Everything before `のは` is treated as already agreed; everything after it is the answer.

---

## ～のは○○だ - cleft sentences · Formation

The clause takes the plain form and then `の`, exactly as with the N5 nominaliser. The focused element follows `は`, with `だ` or `です` closing the sentence.

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Verb (plain) | dictionary form + のは…だ | <ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>る → <ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>るのは<ruby>母<rt>はは</rt></ruby>です |
| Verb (past) | た-form + のは…だ | <ruby>落<rt>お</rt></ruby>とした → <ruby>落<rt>お</rt></ruby>としたのは<ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>です |
| Verb (negative) | ない-form + のは…だ | <ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>なかった → <ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>なかったのは<ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんです |
| い-adjective | plain form + のは…だ | <ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>い → <ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>いのはこちらです |
| な-adjective | ～**な** + のは…だ | <ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きだ → <ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>き**な**のは<ruby>秋<rt>あき</rt></ruby>です |
| Focus = a reason | …のは…**からです** | <ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>んだのは<ruby>熱<rt>ねつ</rt></ruby>があったからです |

---

## ～のは○○だ - cleft sentences · Formation (cont.)

> **Rule of thumb** - the subject inside the `の`-clause takes `が`, never `は`. The sentence already has its `は`, and it belongs to the `のは` frame: <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>**が**<ruby>買<rt>か</rt></ruby>ったのはこの<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>です.

When the focus is a time, a place or a person, the particle that element would have carried is normally dropped: <ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>ったのは<ruby>駅<rt>えき</rt></ruby>です. Keeping it - <ruby>駅<rt>えき</rt></ruby>ででした - is possible in careful writing but sounds heavy, and learners are safer without it. A reason is the exception: it keeps `から` and adds です, as in the last row above.

---

## ～のは○○だ - cleft sentences · Formation (cont.)

> **Note** - the `の` here is a light noun meaning "the one / the thing / the time". You can often replace it with the specific noun for extra clarity: <ruby>割<rt>わ</rt></ruby>った**<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>**は<ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>です, <ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>に<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>た**とき**は<ruby>去年<rt>きょねん</rt></ruby>でした. `の` is the general-purpose version, and it is what you reach for when no particular noun suggests itself.

---

## ～のは○○だ - cleft sentences · Examples

この<ruby>絵<rt>え</rt></ruby>を**かいたのは<ruby>妹<rt>いもうと</rt></ruby>です**。<br>*My little sister is the one who drew this picture.*

<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>が**<ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きなのは<ruby>秋<rt>あき</rt></ruby>です**。<br>*The season I like is autumn.*

<ruby>日本<rt>にほん</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>たのは<ruby>去年<rt>きょねん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>春<rt>はる</rt></ruby>です**。<br>*It was last spring that I came to Japan.*

**<ruby>悪<rt>わる</rt></ruby>いのは<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>です**。<ruby>本当<rt>ほんとう</rt></ruby>にすみませんでした。<br>*I'm the one at fault. I really am sorry.*

---

## ～のは○○だ - cleft sentences · Examples (cont.)

<ruby>最初<rt>さいしょ</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>気<rt>き</rt></ruby>がついたのは<ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんでした**。<br>*Tanaka was the one who noticed first.*

<ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby>**<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>んだのは<ruby>熱<rt>ねつ</rt></ruby>があったからです**。<br>*The reason I was off yesterday is that I had a temperature.*

<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>が<ruby>毎朝<rt>まいあさ</rt></ruby>**<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>むのはコーヒーではなく<ruby>紅茶<rt>こうちゃ</rt></ruby>です**。<br>*What I drink every morning isn't coffee but tea.*

<ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby>で**<ruby>反対<rt>はんたい</rt></ruby>したのは<ruby>山田<rt>やまだ</rt></ruby>さんだけ**で、ほかの<ruby>人<rt>ひと</rt></ruby>はみんな<ruby>賛成<rt>さんせい</rt></ruby>しました。<br>*The only person who objected at the meeting was Yamada; everyone else was in favour.*

---

## ～のは○○だ - cleft sentences · Nuance & register

A cleft splits a sentence into two halves that do different jobs. The `の`-clause is the part you and your listener are already taking for granted - somebody broke the window, I came to Japan at some point. The part after `は` is the news, and because the frame exists only to deliver it, the emphasis is much stronger than in an ordinary sentence.

That makes clefts the natural answer to a question word. Ask だれが<ruby>割<rt>わ</rt></ruby>ったんですか and <ruby>割<rt>わ</rt></ruby>ったのは<ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>です answers it exactly; ask いつ<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>ましたか and <ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>たのは<ruby>先週<rt>せんしゅう</rt></ruby>です does the same. It is equally the form for **correcting** someone, because the frame lets you accept everything except the one piece you are disputing: <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>が<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>ったのはそういう<ruby>意味<rt>いみ</rt></ruby>ではありません。

---

## ～のは○○だ - cleft sentences · Nuance & register (cont.)

The pattern is register-neutral. In polite speech the ending is です／でした; in casual speech it becomes `だ`, or vanishes altogether - <ruby>落<rt>お</rt></ruby>としたの、<ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>? is a perfectly ordinary question between friends. It is if anything even commoner in writing, where <ruby>大切<rt>たいせつ</rt></ruby>なのは… and <ruby>問題<rt>もんだい</rt></ruby>なのは… open paragraphs constantly.

One shape worth learning whole: <code><ruby>大切<rt>たいせつ</rt></ruby>なのは…ことです</code>. When the focus itself is an action rather than a thing, it has to be nominalised too, and there the nominaliser must be `こと`, not `の` - see the next section.

---

## ～のは○○だ - cleft sentences · ～のは○○だ vs plain `が` focus

> **Rule of thumb** - `が` presents its noun as the news. The cleft does that *and* states out loud what everyone is presupposing, which makes it more emphatic and more exclusive.

<ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby><ruby>遅<rt>おく</rt></ruby>れたのは**<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>です**。<br>*The one who was late yesterday was me.*

Compare <ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby><ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>が<ruby>遅<rt>おく</rt></ruby>れました, which simply reports the event with the subject highlighted. The cleft takes for granted that somebody was late - it is the sentence you use when that is already on the table - and it carries a clear implication that nobody else was. That exclusivity is why clefts are so useful for owning up, for correcting, and for singling one item out of a list.

---

## ～のは○○だ - cleft sentences · `の` vs `こと` as the nominaliser

> **Rule of thumb** - `の` when the focus is a **person, thing, time or place**. `こと` when what you are naming is itself an **action or a proposition**, and always when the nominalised clause sits before `だ`／`です` as the predicate.

For a cleft that identifies an entity, only `の` works: <ruby>落<rt>お</rt></ruby>としたのは<ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>です, never ❌<ruby>落<rt>お</rt></ruby>としたことは<ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>です. A person is not an event, so `こと` has nothing to name.

Turn the sentence round, though, and the requirement flips:

<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>の<ruby>趣味<rt>しゅみ</rt></ruby>は**<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>を<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>むことです**。<br>*My hobby is reading.*

---

## ～のは○○だ - cleft sentences · `の` vs `こと` as the nominaliser (cont.)

Here the nominalised clause is the predicate, and ❌<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>むのです is not available - that string already means something else entirely, the explanatory `んです`. The same rule governs <ruby>大切<rt>たいせつ</rt></ruby>なのは<ruby>毎日<rt>まいにち</rt></ruby><ruby>続<rt>つづ</rt></ruby>けることです.

Two more places where the choice is fixed, both worth memorising. Before a verb of direct perception - <ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>る, <ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>く, <ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>こえる, <ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>える - only `の` is possible, because you witness an event rather than a fact: <ruby>子<rt>こ</rt></ruby>どもが<ruby>泣<rt>な</rt></ruby>いているのを<ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>きました. And a set of idioms takes `こと` and nothing else: ことができる, たことがある.

---

## ～のは○○だ - cleft sentences · ～のは○○だ vs ～んです

> **Rule of thumb** - both contain `の`, and they do opposite things. `んです` explains the **whole** situation. `のは…だ` isolates **one element** of it.

<ruby>来週<rt>らいしゅう</rt></ruby><ruby>出張<rt>しゅっちょう</rt></ruby>する**のは<ruby>大阪<rt>おおさか</rt></ruby>です**。<br>*The place I'm travelling to next week is Osaka.*

Set that beside <ruby>来週<rt>らいしゅう</rt></ruby><ruby>大阪<rt>おおさか</rt></ruby>に<ruby>出張<rt>しゅっちょう</rt></ruby>するんです, "the thing is, I'm off to Osaka next week" - an explanation offered as background, with no single element picked out. If you can point at one word and say "that is the answer", you want the cleft; if the whole sentence is the answer, you want `んです`.

---

## ～のは○○だ - cleft sentences · Common mistakes

- ❌ <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>**は**<ruby>一番<rt>いちばん</rt></ruby><ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きなのは<ruby>夏<rt>なつ</rt></ruby>です。 → ✅ <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>**が**<ruby>一番<rt>いちばん</rt></ruby><ruby>好<rt>す</rt></ruby>きなのは<ruby>夏<rt>なつ</rt></ruby>です。<br>*The subject sits inside the nominalised clause, and a clause like that takes `が`. Two `は` in one sentence leaves the first one homeless.*

- ❌ <ruby>静<rt>しず</rt></ruby>か**だ**のは<ruby>朝<rt>あさ</rt></ruby>だけです。 → ✅ <ruby>静<rt>しず</rt></ruby>か**な**のは<ruby>朝<rt>あさ</rt></ruby>だけです。<br>*な-adjectives take `な` before a nominalising `の`, the same shape they use before `ので` and `のに`.*

- ❌ <ruby>大切<rt>たいせつ</rt></ruby>なのは<ruby>練習<rt>れんしゅう</rt></ruby>する**のです**。 → ✅ <ruby>大切<rt>たいせつ</rt></ruby>なのは<ruby>練習<rt>れんしゅう</rt></ruby>する**ことです**。<br>*A nominalised clause standing before `です` must use `こと`. With `の` the sentence turns into an explanatory `んです` and stops meaning what you wanted.*

---

## ～のは○○だ - cleft sentences · Common mistakes (cont.)

- ❌ <ruby>皿<rt>さら</rt></ruby>を<ruby>割<rt>わ</rt></ruby>った**ことは**<ruby>猫<rt>ねこ</rt></ruby>です。 → ✅ <ruby>皿<rt>さら</rt></ruby>を<ruby>割<rt>わ</rt></ruby>った**のは**<ruby>猫<rt>ねこ</rt></ruby>です。<br>*When the focus is a creature, a thing or a time, the nominaliser is `の`. `こと` would be naming an event, which cannot equal a cat.*

---

## ～のは○○だ - cleft sentences · Practice 1

**1.** この<ruby>料理<rt>りょうり</rt></ruby>を<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>った____<ruby>父<rt>ちち</rt></ruby>です。

{reveal}
<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>った**のは**<ruby>父<rt>ちち</rt></ruby>です

{reveal}
The cook is a person, so the light noun `の` is the one you want, followed by `は` to mark everything before it as shared background. The past form <ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>った goes straight in front of `の`.

---

## ～のは○○だ - cleft sentences · Practice 2

**2.** <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>の<ruby>夢<rt>ゆめ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>世界<rt>せかい</rt></ruby>を<ruby>旅行<rt>りょこう</rt></ruby>する（の・こと）です。

{reveal}
<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>の<ruby>夢<rt>ゆめ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>世界<rt>せかい</rt></ruby>を<ruby>旅行<rt>りょこう</rt></ruby>する**こと**です。

{reveal}
A nominalised clause immediately in front of `です` has to use `こと`. Writing するのです would produce the explanatory `んです` pattern, which says something completely different.

---

## ～のは○○だ - cleft sentences · Practice 3

**3.** Translate into Japanese: "It was in Osaka that we first met."

{reveal}
<ruby>初<rt>はじ</rt></ruby>めて<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>った**のは<ruby>大阪<rt>おおさか</rt></ruby>でした**。

{reveal}
The meeting is presupposed and the place is the news, which is exactly what a cleft is for. Note that the `で` you would use in <ruby>大阪<rt>おおさか</rt></ruby>で<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>いました is dropped once the place moves into the focus slot.

---

## ～のは○○だ - cleft sentences · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: <ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby><ruby>学校<rt>がっこう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>んだのは<ruby>頭<rt>あたま</rt></ruby>が<ruby>痛<rt>いた</rt></ruby>かったです。

{reveal}
✅ <ruby>昨日<rt>きのう</rt></ruby><ruby>学校<rt>がっこう</rt></ruby>を<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>んだのは<ruby>頭<rt>あたま</rt></ruby>が<ruby>痛<rt>いた</rt></ruby>かった**からです**。

{reveal}
When the element in focus is a reason rather than a thing, the clause has to be closed with `から` before `です`. Without it the sentence claims that the act of staying home *was* a headache.

---

## ～のは○○だ - cleft sentences · Practice 5

**5.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) <ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>が<ruby>皿<rt>さら</rt></ruby>を<ruby>落<rt>お</rt></ruby>としました。 (b) <ruby>皿<rt>さら</rt></ruby>を<ruby>落<rt>お</rt></ruby>としたのは<ruby>弟<rt>おとうと</rt></ruby>です。

{reveal}
(a) reports the event as a whole, with the subject marked as the new piece of information. It works as an answer to "what happened?" and does not assume the listener knows anything yet.

{reveal}
(b) assumes the broken plate is already common knowledge and supplies the missing name. It answers "who did it?", it excludes everyone else, and depending on the situation it can sound like an accusation or like clearing someone's name. Use it when the event is settled and only the identity is in question.

---

# N4 - Polite, humble, and honorific speech

- お○○になる
- お○○ください
- いらっしゃる
- なさる
- 敬語の動詞
- お○○する
- いたす
- ございます

---

# N4 - Polite, humble, and honorific speech (cont.)

- でございます

---

# お○○になる

**Meaning** · the general-purpose honorific frame - describes *someone else's* action while raising them

Japanese politeness runs on three separate systems. <ruby>丁寧<rt>ていねい</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby> - です／ます - makes your *speech* polite to whoever is listening. <ruby>尊敬<rt>そんけい</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby> raises the **person you are talking about**. <ruby>謙譲<rt>けんじょう</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby> lowers **you**. `お○○になる` is the workhorse of the second group: take almost any verb, and it becomes a respectful description of what your customer, your teacher or your boss did.

---

## お○○になる · Formation

Take the ます-stem, put `お` in front and `になる` behind. `になる` then conjugates as an ordinary う-verb (<ruby>五段<rt>ごだん</rt></ruby>, Group 1).

---

## お○○になる · Formation (cont.)

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Verb (う-verb) | お + ます-stem + になる | <ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>きます → お<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>きになる |
| Verb (る-verb) | お + ます-stem + になる | <ruby>調<rt>しら</rt></ruby>べます → お<ruby>調<rt>しら</rt></ruby>べになる |
| する-verb, Chinese-derived root | ご + noun + になる | <ruby>利用<rt>りよう</rt></ruby>する → ご<ruby>利用<rt>りよう</rt></ruby>になる |
| する-verb, native root | お + noun + になる | <ruby>問<rt>と</rt></ruby>い<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>わせする → お<ruby>問<rt>と</rt></ruby>い<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>わせになる |
| Polite / past | お + stem + になります／になりました | お<ruby>使<rt>つか</rt></ruby>いになりました |
| Verb with its own honorific | frame **not** used | <ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べる → <ruby>召<rt>め</rt></ruby>し<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がる |
| One-mora ます-stem | frame **not** used | <ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>る → ご<ruby>覧<rt>らん</rt></ruby>になる、<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>る → お<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>みになる |

---

## お○○になる · Formation (cont.)

> **Rule of thumb** - if the ます-stem is only one mora long （<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>、<ruby>着<rt>き</rt></ruby>、<ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>、<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>、し）, the frame will not carry it. Those verbs all have a dedicated honorific word instead: ご<ruby>覧<rt>らん</rt></ruby>になる、お<ruby>召<rt>め</rt></ruby>しになる、お<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>みになる、いらっしゃる、なさる.

---

## お○○になる · Examples

<ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>何時<rt>なんじ</rt></ruby>に**お<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>りになります**か。<br>*What time will you be leaving, sensei?*

この<ruby>本<rt>ほん</rt></ruby>をもう**お<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>みになりました**か。<br>*Have you read this book already?*

<ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>昼<rt>ひる</rt></ruby>すぎに**お<ruby>出<rt>で</rt></ruby>かけになりました**。<br>*The department head went out in the early afternoon.*

お<ruby>客<rt>きゃく</rt></ruby><ruby>様<rt>さま</rt></ruby>が**お<ruby>選<rt>えら</rt></ruby>びになった**のは、こちらの<ruby>色<rt>いろ</rt></ruby>でよろしいでしょうか。<br>*Is this the colour you chose, madam?*

---

## お○○になる · Examples (cont.)

<ruby>課長<rt>かちょう</rt></ruby>が**お<ruby>決<rt>き</rt></ruby>めになった**<ruby>方法<rt>ほうほう</rt></ruby>で<ruby>進<rt>すす</rt></ruby>めます。<br>*We'll go ahead with the method the section chief settled on.*

エレベーターを**ご<ruby>利用<rt>りよう</rt></ruby>になる**<ruby>方<rt>かた</rt></ruby>は、<ruby>右<rt>みぎ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>通路<rt>つうろ</rt></ruby>へお<ruby>回<rt>まわ</rt></ruby>りください。<br>*Those using the lift, please go round to the right-hand corridor.*

<ruby>皆<rt>みな</rt></ruby><ruby>様<rt>さま</rt></ruby>が**お<ruby>集<rt>あつ</rt></ruby>まりになる**<ruby>時間<rt>じかん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>午後<rt>ごご</rt></ruby><ruby>二時<rt>にじ</rt></ruby>でよろしいでしょうか。<br>*Would two o'clock suit as the time for everyone to gather?*

<ruby>新<rt>あたら</rt></ruby>しい<ruby>計画<rt>けいかく</rt></ruby>について、<ruby>社長<rt>しゃちょう</rt></ruby>はどう**お<ruby>考<rt>かんが</rt></ruby>えになっている**のでしょうか。<br>*I wonder what the president makes of the new plan.*

---

## お○○になる · Nuance & register

This is business and service language. In a shop, a hospital, a hotel, a <ruby>会議<rt>かいぎ</rt></ruby><ruby>室<rt>しつ</rt></ruby> or a classroom it is completely ordinary; among friends it is not. Saying お<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べになりますか to a classmate is not "extra polite", it is strange - it puts a counter between the two of you. Overusing <ruby>敬語<rt>けいご</rt></ruby> socially is a real mistake, not a safe default.

Three things follow from the fact that `お○○になる` is <ruby>尊敬<rt>そんけい</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby>:

- **Never about yourself.** ❌<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>がお<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>りになりました is the<br>*single commonest <ruby>敬語<rt>けいご</rt></ruby> error learners make. You cannot raise your own head. Your own actions take <ruby>謙譲<rt>けんじょう</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby> - お<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>りしました*

- or plain ます.

---

## お○○になる · Nuance & register (cont.)

- **Never doubled.** ❌お<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>みになられる stacks the frame on top of the<br>*`られる` honorific. That is <ruby>二重<rt>にじゅう</rt></ruby><ruby>敬語<rt>けいご</rt></ruby>, and it sounds overcooked rather than extra respectful. One layer is enough.*
- **Not for your own side.** Speaking to a customer about a colleague, even your<br>*own boss, you drop the honorific: <ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>はただいま<ruby>席<rt>せき</rt></ruby>をはずしております - never お<ruby>席<rt>せき</rt></ruby>をはずしになっています.*

On the politeness ladder, `お○○になる` sits above `れる／られる` and below the set honorific verbs. Treat that as a tendency rather than a measurement: in most offices お<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>きになる and <ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>かれる are simply two acceptable choices, and which one a person reaches for depends on the workplace and on how far above them the other person stands.

---

## お○○になる · お○○になる vs ～れる／～られる

> **Rule of thumb** - both are honorific. `られる` is the light, everyday office form; `お○○になる` is heavier, more deferential, and unambiguous.

<ruby>社長<rt>しゃちょう</rt></ruby>はもう**<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>られました**。<br>*The president has already left for the day.*

<ruby>社長<rt>しゃちょう</rt></ruby>はもう**お<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>りになりました**。<br>*The president has already left for the day.*

---

## お○○になる · お○○になる vs ～れる／～られる (cont.)

The second is the more respectful of the two, and it is what you would say to an outside visitor; the first is what one colleague says to another. The practical advantage of `お○○になる` is that it cannot be misread. <code><ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>られる</code> is also the passive and the potential, so <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>に<ruby>来<rt>こ</rt></ruby>られました can be read two ways, while <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>がお<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>しになりました cannot.

---

## お○○になる · お○○になる vs お○○する

> **Rule of thumb** - same stem, opposite direction. `になる` raises the other person; `する` lowers you.

<ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>荷物<rt>にもつ</rt></ruby>を**お<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>ちになります**。<br>*The teacher is going to carry the bags himself.*

<ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>の<ruby>荷物<rt>にもつ</rt></ruby>を**お<ruby>持<rt>も</rt></ruby>ちします**。<br>*I'll carry your bags for you, sensei.*

One says the teacher does the carrying; the other offers to do it for him. Swapping them reverses who is being honoured, which is why the pair is worth drilling until it is automatic.

---

## お○○になる · お○○になる vs the set honorific verbs

> **Rule of thumb** - if a verb owns a dedicated honorific word, the frame is closed to it. Learn that short list; use the frame for everything else.

<ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>はもうお<ruby>昼<rt>ひる</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>召<rt>め</rt></ruby>し<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がりました**か。<br>*Has sensei had lunch yet?*

<ruby>資料<rt>しりょう</rt></ruby>はもう**ご<ruby>覧<rt>らん</rt></ruby>になりました**か。<br>*Have you had a look at the documents yet?*

---

## お○○になる · お○○になる vs the set honorific verbs (cont.)

<code><ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べる</code>, <code><ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>る</code>, <code><ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>う</code>, `する`, <code><ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く</code>, <code><ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>る</code>, `いる` and <code><ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>る</code> all belong to that closed set. Note that <code>ご<ruby>覧<rt>らん</rt></ruby>になる</code> ends in `になる` but is not built from a ます-stem - <code>ご<ruby>覧<rt>らん</rt></ruby></code> is a noun, and the word has to be memorised whole.

---

## お○○になる · Common mistakes

- ❌ <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>が<ruby>資料<rt>しりょう</rt></ruby>を**お<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>りになりました**。 → ✅ <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>が<ruby>資料<rt>しりょう</rt></ruby>を**お<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>りしました**。<br>*Honorific language points away from the speaker. Describing your own work with `お○○になる` is the error a Japanese listener notices fastest.*

- ❌ <ruby>地図<rt>ちず</rt></ruby>を**お<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>になりました**か。 → ✅ <ruby>地図<rt>ちず</rt></ruby>を**ご<ruby>覧<rt>らん</rt></ruby>になりました**か。<br>*<code><ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>る</code> has a one-mora stem and its own honorific verb. The frame does not build on it.*

- ❌ <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>が**お<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>しになられました**。 → ✅ <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>が**お<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>しになりました**。<br>*Two honorific layers on one verb is <ruby>二重<rt>にじゅう</rt></ruby><ruby>敬語<rt>けいご</rt></ruby>. Pick one.*

---

## お○○になる · Common mistakes (cont.)

- ❌ <ruby>課長<rt>かちょう</rt></ruby>が**お<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>になりました**。 → ✅ <ruby>課長<rt>かちょう</rt></ruby>が**ご<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>になりました**。<br>*A Chinese-derived する-verb root takes `ご`: ご<ruby>利用<rt>りよう</rt></ruby>、 ご<ruby>出発<rt>しゅっぱつ</rt></ruby>、ご<ruby>記入<rt>きにゅう</rt></ruby>.*

- ❌ ねえ、この<ruby>漫画<rt>まんが</rt></ruby>**お<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>みになった**? → ✅ ねえ、この<ruby>漫画<rt>まんが</rt></ruby><ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>んだ?<br>*Grammatical, wrong for the situation. Full <ruby>敬語<rt>けいご</rt></ruby> aimed at a friend reads as sarcasm or as sudden distance.*

---

## お○○になる · Practice 1

**1.** <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>毎朝<rt>まいあさ</rt></ruby><ruby>新聞<rt>しんぶん</rt></ruby>を____<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>____になります。

{reveal}
<ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>毎朝<rt>まいあさ</rt></ruby><ruby>新聞<rt>しんぶん</rt></ruby>を**お<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>みになります**。

{reveal}
The frame is `お` + ます-stem + `になる`. The stem of <code><ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>みます</code> is <code><ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>み</code>, so `お` goes in front of it and `になります` behind.

---

## お○○になる · Practice 2

**2.** Choose: <ruby>係<rt>かかり</rt></ruby>の<ruby>者<rt>もの</rt></ruby>が（ご<ruby>案内<rt>あんない</rt></ruby>になります・ご<ruby>案内<rt>あんない</rt></ruby>します）。

{reveal}
<ruby>係<rt>かかり</rt></ruby>の<ruby>者<rt>もの</rt></ruby>が**ご<ruby>案内<rt>あんない</rt></ruby>します**。

{reveal}
<code><ruby>係<rt>かかり</rt></ruby>の<ruby>者<rt>もの</rt></ruby></code> is a member of your own side, so the sentence has to lower rather than raise. `ご○○になる` would honour your own staff in front of a customer, which is exactly backwards.

---

## お○○になる · Practice 3

**3.** Translate into Japanese: "What time will the president be arriving?"

{reveal}
<ruby>社長<rt>しゃちょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>何時<rt>なんじ</rt></ruby>に**お<ruby>着<rt>つ</rt></ruby>きになります**か。

{reveal}
<code><ruby>着<rt>つ</rt></ruby>きます</code> gives the stem <code><ruby>着<rt>つ</rt></ruby>き</code>, hence お<ruby>着<rt>つ</rt></ruby>きになります. ご<ruby>到着<rt>とうちゃく</rt></ruby>になりますか works too, since <ruby>到着<rt>とうちゃく</rt></ruby> is a Chinese-derived root and takes `ご`.

---

## お○○になる · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>、<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>十時<rt>じゅうじ</rt></ruby>にお<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>しになります。

{reveal}
✅ <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>、<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>十時<rt>じゅうじ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>参<rt>まい</rt></ruby>ります。

{reveal}
Two faults in one clause. The verb describes you, so it needs <ruby>謙譲<rt>けんじょう</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby>, not <ruby>尊敬<rt>そんけい</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby>. And <code><ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>る</code> is outside the frame anyway: the honorific for someone else coming is お<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>しになる or いらっしゃる, while the humble word for your own coming is <ruby>参<rt>まい</rt></ruby>る.

---

## お○○になる · Practice 5

**5.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) <ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby><ruby>様<rt>さま</rt></ruby>はいつ<ruby>出発<rt>しゅっぱつ</rt></ruby>されますか。 (b) <ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby><ruby>様<rt>さま</rt></ruby>はいつご<ruby>出発<rt>しゅっぱつ</rt></ruby>になりますか。

{reveal}
Both are honorific and both are correct. (a) uses the `される` form, which is light and quick - the register of a colleague, or of a routine business email.

{reveal}
(b) is the heavier frame, and it is what a hotel clerk or a receptionist would say to a guest. It sounds more careful and more deliberate. The gap is one of degree, not of grammar: choosing (a) with a customer would not offend anyone, it would only sound a little brisk.

---

# お○○ください

**Meaning** · "please do ○○" - an honorific request, the form used to customers, guests and audiences

`お○○ください` asks the listener to do something while raising them. It is the <ruby>尊敬<rt>そんけい</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby> counterpart of `～てください`: same job, but the listener is honoured rather than simply addressed politely. Every announcement you hear on a Japanese train, in a lift and in a shop is built out of this frame.

---

## お○○ください · Formation

`ください` is the imperative of `くださる`, the honorific of `くれる`. Put it after `お` + the ます-stem.

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Verb (う-verb) | お + ます-stem + ください | <ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ちます → お<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ちください |
| Verb (る-verb) | お + ます-stem + ください | <ruby>調<rt>しら</rt></ruby>べます → お<ruby>調<rt>しら</rt></ruby>べください |
| する-verb, Chinese-derived root | ご + noun + ください | <ruby>確認<rt>かくにん</rt></ruby>する → ご<ruby>確認<rt>かくにん</rt></ruby>ください |
| する-verb, native root | お + noun + ください | <ruby>申<rt>もう</rt></ruby>し<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>みする → お<ruby>申<rt>もう</rt></ruby>し<ruby>込<rt>こ</rt></ruby>みください |
| Set honorific verb | fixed form | <ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>る → ご<ruby>覧<rt>らん</rt></ruby>ください |
| Extra-polite service form | + ませ | お<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ちくださいませ |
| Negative ("please don't") | frame **not** used | ご<ruby>遠慮<rt>えんりょ</rt></ruby>ください／～ないでください |

---

## お○○ください · Formation (cont.)

> **Note** - one-mora stems are shut out here for the same reason as in `お○○になる`: ❌お<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>ください、❌お<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>ください do not exist. Use ご<ruby>覧<rt>らん</rt></ruby>ください and お<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>しください.

---

## お○○ください · Examples

こちらで**お<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ちください**。<br>*Please wait here.*

どうぞ**おかけください**。<br>*Please have a seat.*

この<ruby>線<rt>せん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>内側<rt>うちがわ</rt></ruby>まで**お<ruby>下<rt>さ</rt></ruby>がりください**。<br>*Please step back behind this line.*

<ruby>温<rt>あたた</rt></ruby>かいうちに**お<ruby>召<rt>め</rt></ruby>し<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がりください**。<br>*Please eat it while it's still warm.*

---

## お○○ください · Examples (cont.)

<ruby>足元<rt>あしもと</rt></ruby>に**ご<ruby>注意<rt>ちゅうい</rt></ruby>ください**。<br>*Please mind your step.*

<ruby>順番<rt>じゅんばん</rt></ruby>にご<ruby>案内<rt>あんない</rt></ruby>しますので、こちらに**お<ruby>並<rt>なら</rt></ruby>びください**。<br>*We'll show you through in turn, so please queue here.*

ご<ruby>不明<rt>ふめい</rt></ruby>な<ruby>点<rt>てん</rt></ruby>がございましたら、いつでも**お<ruby>問<rt>と</rt></ruby>い<ruby>合<rt>あ</rt></ruby>わせください**。<br>*If anything is unclear, please get in touch at any time.*

<ruby>会場<rt>かいじょう</rt></ruby>にお<ruby>入<rt>はい</rt></ruby>りの<ruby>際<rt>さい</rt></ruby>は、<ruby>受付<rt>うけつけ</rt></ruby>でこちらの<ruby>用紙<rt>ようし</rt></ruby>を**お<ruby>出<rt>だ</rt></ruby>しください**。<br>*When you enter the hall, please hand this form in at reception.*

---

## お○○ください · Nuance & register

This frame is service and announcement language, and it carries a faint flavour of *instruction*. A station guard, a shop assistant, a nurse calling a patient and a website's help page all use it. Between friends it is bizarre - you do not tell a classmate ❌ちょっとお<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ちください unless you are joking.

The instructional flavour matters when you want a personal favour. `ください` is still an imperative underneath, so a bare お<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>きください to your boss can land like a directive from below. For asking a superior for something, shift to a question form:

---

## お○○ください · Nuance & register (cont.)

- お<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>きいただけますか - "could you write it?"
- お<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>きいただけませんでしょうか - the softest, and standard in email.
- <ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>いていただけると<ruby>助<rt>たす</rt></ruby>かります - "it would help me if you would."

`ませ` on the end（お<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ちくださいませ、いらっしゃいませ）belongs to shop and hotel speech specifically. It is warm and formal at once, and it is heard far more from staff than from anyone else.

---

## お○○ください · Nuance & register (cont.)

Two words about お<ruby>召<rt>め</rt></ruby>し<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がりください and お<ruby>求<rt>もと</rt></ruby>めください. Strictly, <ruby>召<rt>め</rt></ruby>し<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がる is already honorific, so adding `お` makes a double layer; usage guides nonetheless list these as established by custom, and you will hear them constantly. Treat them as fixed phrases rather than as models for building new ones.

One more tendency worth knowing: many speakers avoid お<ruby>座<rt>すわ</rt></ruby>りください in favour of おかけください, because お<ruby>座<rt>すわ</rt></ruby>り on its own is what you say to a dog. Plenty of hospitals and offices say お<ruby>座<rt>すわ</rt></ruby>りください anyway, so it is a preference rather than a rule - but おかけください is never the wrong choice.

---

## お○○ください · お○○ください vs ～てください

> **Rule of thumb** - `～てください` is polite; `お○○ください` is polite **and** honorific. The first addresses the listener courteously, the second raises them.

ここに<ruby>名前<rt>なまえ</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>いてください**。<br>*Please write your name here.*

こちらにお<ruby>名前<rt>なまえ</rt></ruby>を**お<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>きください**。<br>*Please write your name here.*

---

## お○○ください · お○○ください vs ～てください (cont.)

The first is what a teacher says to a class, or a friend to a friend. The second is what a bank clerk says to a customer - notice how `ここ` becomes `こちら` and <ruby>名前<rt>なまえ</rt></ruby> takes its prefix. <ruby>敬語<rt>けいご</rt></ruby> rarely arrives alone; the whole sentence shifts register together.

---

## お○○ください · お○○ください vs お○○いただけますか

> **Rule of thumb** - `ください` tells; `いただけますか` asks. When the favour is for *your* benefit, ask.

<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>までに**ご<ruby>返事<rt>へんじ</rt></ruby>ください**。<br>*Please reply by tomorrow.*

<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>までに**ご<ruby>返事<rt>へんじ</rt></ruby>いただけますでしょうか**。<br>*Might I ask you to reply by tomorrow?*

---

## お○○ください · お○○ください vs お○○いただけますか (cont.)

Both are polite. The first states what needs to happen and suits a notice or a form; the second leaves the decision with the listener and suits a request to a client or a superior. `いただく` is <ruby>謙譲<rt>けんじょう</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby>, so the second sentence lowers you at the same time as it raises them - which is why it feels so much softer.

---

## お○○ください · お○○ください vs ご遠慮ください

> **Rule of thumb** - the frame has no negative. To ask someone *not* to do something, use a different verb: ご<ruby>遠慮<rt>えんりょ</rt></ruby>ください or お<ruby>控<rt>ひか</rt></ruby>えください.

<ruby>車内<rt>しゃない</rt></ruby>でのお<ruby>電話<rt>でんわ</rt></ruby>は**ご<ruby>遠慮<rt>えんりょ</rt></ruby>ください**。<br>*Please refrain from making phone calls on board.*

<ruby>写真<rt>しゃしん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>撮影<rt>さつえい</rt></ruby>は**お<ruby>控<rt>ひか</rt></ruby>えください**。<br>*Please refrain from taking photographs.*

---

## お○○ください · お○○ください vs ご遠慮ください (cont.)

There is no ❌お<ruby>話<rt>はな</rt></ruby>しにならないでください in ordinary use. Japanese public notices prefer to name a polite verb of refraining rather than to negate the request - it reads as an appeal to the listener's discretion instead of a ban.

---

## お○○ください · Common mistakes

- ❌ <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby><ruby>会社<rt>かいしゃ</rt></ruby>に**お<ruby>来<rt>き</rt></ruby>ください**。 → ✅ <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby><ruby>会社<rt>かいしゃ</rt></ruby>に**お<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>しください**。<br>*<code><ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>る</code> has no place in the frame. Use お<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>しください, おいでください or いらしてください.*

- ❌ こちらのボタンを**ご<ruby>確認<rt>かくにん</rt></ruby>してください**。 → ✅ こちらのボタンを**ご<ruby>確認<rt>かくにん</rt></ruby>ください**。<br>*`ご○○する` is the *humble* frame, so <code>ご<ruby>確認<rt>かくにん</rt></ruby>してください</code> tells the listener to humble themselves. Drop the `して`.*

- ❌ メニューを**お<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>ください**。 → ✅ メニューを**ご<ruby>覧<rt>らん</rt></ruby>ください**。<br>*One-mora stem, dedicated honorific verb. The same goes for お<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べください → お<ruby>召<rt>め</rt></ruby>し<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がりください.*

---

## お○○ください · Common mistakes (cont.)

- ❌ <ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>、この<ruby>書類<rt>しょるい</rt></ruby>に**おサインください**。 → ✅ <ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>、この<ruby>書類<rt>しょるい</rt></ruby>に**ご<ruby>署名<rt>しょめい</rt></ruby>いただけますでしょうか**。<br>*Two problems: loanwords do not take the prefix, and a direct `ください` to your own boss for your own paperwork is too flat. Ask with `いただけますか`.*

---

## お○○ください · Practice 1

**1.** <ruby>危<rt>あぶ</rt></ruby>ないですので、<ruby>白線<rt>はくせん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>内側<rt>うちがわ</rt></ruby>まで____<ruby>下<rt>さ</rt></ruby>がり____。

{reveal}
<ruby>危<rt>あぶ</rt></ruby>ないですので、<ruby>白線<rt>はくせん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>内側<rt>うちがわ</rt></ruby>まで**お<ruby>下<rt>さ</rt></ruby>がりください**。

{reveal}
`お` + ます-stem + `ください`. <code><ruby>下<rt>さ</rt></ruby>がります</code> gives the stem <code><ruby>下<rt>さ</rt></ruby>がり</code>. This is the standard platform announcement, and it is honorific because it is addressed to passengers.

---

## お○○ください · Practice 2

**2.** Choose: <ruby>資料<rt>しりょう</rt></ruby>を（ご<ruby>覧<rt>らん</rt></ruby>ください・<ruby>拝見<rt>はいけん</rt></ruby>ください）。

{reveal}
<ruby>資料<rt>しりょう</rt></ruby>を**ご<ruby>覧<rt>らん</rt></ruby>ください**。

{reveal}
<code><ruby>拝見<rt>はいけん</rt></ruby>する</code> is <ruby>謙譲<rt>けんじょう</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby> - it lowers the person doing the looking. Telling the listener to <ruby>拝見<rt>はいけん</rt></ruby> orders them to be humble towards you, which is the opposite of what a request should do.

---

## お○○ください · Practice 3

**3.** Translate into Japanese: "Please use the lift on the left."

{reveal}
<ruby>左<rt>ひだり</rt></ruby>のエレベーターを**ご<ruby>利用<rt>りよう</rt></ruby>ください**。

{reveal}
<ruby>利用<rt>りよう</rt></ruby> is a Chinese-derived する-verb root, so it takes `ご` and the `する` disappears entirely: ご<ruby>利用<rt>りよう</rt></ruby>ください, not ❌ご<ruby>利用<rt>りよう</rt></ruby>してください.

---

## お○○ください · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: <ruby>館内<rt>かんない</rt></ruby>ではおタバコをお<ruby>吸<rt>す</rt></ruby>いにならないでください。

{reveal}
✅ <ruby>館内<rt>かんない</rt></ruby>での<ruby>喫煙<rt>きつえん</rt></ruby>は**ご<ruby>遠慮<rt>えんりょ</rt></ruby>ください**。

{reveal}
Two faults. Loanwords do not take the polite prefix, and the honorific frame has no natural negative - Japanese notices name a verb of refraining instead. <ruby>館内<rt>かんない</rt></ruby>ではタバコをお<ruby>吸<rt>す</rt></ruby>いにならないでください is understandable but sounds clumsy next to the fixed phrase.

---

## お○○ください · Practice 5

**5.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) <ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>々お<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ちください。 (b) <ruby>少<rt>すこ</rt></ruby>々お<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>ちいただけますか。

{reveal}
(a) is the standard service line - a receptionist, a phone operator, a waiter. It is honorific and perfectly courteous, but it *tells* the listener what will happen, which is fine when the waiting is part of the process.

{reveal}
(b) turns the same content into a question, so the listener is free to say no. It is what you use when the delay is your fault, or when you are asking a favour of someone senior. Between colleagues (a) would sound oddly official; from a shop assistant (b) can sound over-apologetic. Match the form to who owns the delay.

---

# いらっしゃる

**Meaning** · the honorific verb covering いる, <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く and <ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>る all at once

`いらっしゃる` is <ruby>尊敬<rt>そんけい</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby>: it raises the person it describes, so it is used about your teacher, your client, your guest - never about yourself. Three ordinary verbs collapse into it, and Japanese speakers do not find that ambiguous, because the situation always says which one is meant.

---

## いらっしゃる · Formation

| Plain verb | Honorific | Example |
|---|---|---|
| いる | いらっしゃる | <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>部屋<rt>へや</rt></ruby>にいらっしゃいます |
| <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く | いらっしゃる | どちらへいらっしゃいますか |
| <ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>る | いらっしゃる | よくいらっしゃいました |
| ～ている | ～ていらっしゃる | <ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>っていらっしゃいます |
| Noun + です (about a person) | ～でいらっしゃる | <ruby>社長<rt>しゃちょう</rt></ruby>でいらっしゃいます |

It is a う-verb, but its ます-form is irregular - the `り` you expect becomes `い`. Four verbs share this quirk, and they are all <ruby>敬語<rt>けいご</rt></ruby>:

---

## いらっしゃる · Formation (cont.)

| Dictionary | ます-form | Never |
|---|---|---|
| いらっしゃる | いらっしゃいます | ❌いらっしゃります |
| おっしゃる | おっしゃいます | ❌おっしゃります |
| なさる | なさいます | ❌なさります |
| くださる | くださいます | ❌くださります |

---

## いらっしゃる · Formation (cont.)

| Other forms | Shape |
|---|---|
| Negative polite | いらっしゃいません |
| Plain negative | いらっしゃらない |
| て-form | いらっしゃって（contracted: いらして） |
| Request | いらしてください／お<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>しください |
| Greeting form | いらっしゃい／いらっしゃいませ |

---

## いらっしゃる · Examples

<ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>教室<rt>きょうしつ</rt></ruby>に**いらっしゃいます**か。<br>*Is the teacher in the classroom?*

どちらへ**いらっしゃいます**か。<br>*Where are you off to?*

<ruby>遠<rt>とお</rt></ruby>いところ、よく**いらっしゃいました**。<br>*Thank you for coming all this way.*

<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>の<ruby>会<rt>かい</rt></ruby>には<ruby>何名<rt>なんめい</rt></ruby>ほど**いらっしゃいます**か。<br>*Roughly how many people will be coming to tomorrow's gathering?*

---

## いらっしゃる · Examples (cont.)

<ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>、<ruby>会議室<rt>かいぎしつ</rt></ruby>には**いらっしゃいません**。<br>*The department head isn't in the meeting room at the moment.*

<ruby>山田<rt>やまだ</rt></ruby><ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>来週<rt>らいしゅう</rt></ruby><ruby>大阪<rt>おおさか</rt></ruby>から**いらっしゃる**そうです。<br>*I hear Professor Yamada is coming up from Osaka next week.*

お<ruby>客<rt>きゃく</rt></ruby><ruby>様<rt>さま</rt></ruby>が<ruby>先<rt>さき</rt></ruby>ほどから<ruby>受付<rt>うけつけ</rt></ruby>で**<ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>っていらっしゃいます**。<br>*The customer has been waiting at reception for a little while now.*

<ruby>失礼<rt>しつれい</rt></ruby>ですが、<ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby><ruby>様<rt>さま</rt></ruby>で**いらっしゃいます**か。<br>*Excuse me - would you be Mr Tanaka?*

---

## いらっしゃる · Nuance & register

`いらっしゃる` is the first <ruby>敬語<rt>けいご</rt></ruby> verb most learners can actually use, because it turns up everywhere: shop doorways, phone calls, introductions, reception desks. It belongs to business, service and formal social speech. Saying it about a friend - ❌ゆうべ<ruby>友<rt>とも</rt></ruby>だちが<ruby>家<rt>いえ</rt></ruby>にいらっしゃった - is not extra-polite, it is odd, because you are honouring someone who is on your own level.

Some texture:

---

## いらっしゃる · Nuance & register (cont.)

- **いらっしゃいませ** is not an invitation to come. It is a shop and restaurant<br>*greeting, roughly "welcome", and it expects no reply at all.*
- **いらっしゃい** on its own is warm and informal - a host to a guest, an adult to<br>*a child, a market stall to passers-by.*
- **いらして／いらしてください** is the contracted て-form. It is softer and a<br>*little lighter than いらっしゃって, and it leans towards polite conversational speech rather than announcements.*
- **お<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>しになる, おいでになる, お<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>えになる** are alternatives for<br>*the "come" sense, each a shade more formal than plain いらっしゃる.*

---

## いらっしゃる · Nuance & register (cont.)

The trap that catches every English speaker is the **in-group rule**. Japanese politeness is not about rank in the abstract; it is about which side of a line the person stands on. Inside your company, <ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby> outranks you and takes <ruby>尊敬<rt>そんけい</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby>. The moment you speak to somebody *outside* the company - a client, a supplier, a caller - your whole company becomes your in-group, and your boss is lowered along with you:

- To a colleague: <ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>はもうお<ruby>帰<rt>かえ</rt></ruby>りになりました。
- To a client: <ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>は<ruby>本日<rt>ほんじつ</rt></ruby><ruby>外出<rt>がいしゅつ</rt></ruby>しております。

---

## いらっしゃる · Nuance & register (cont.)

No title, no `さん`, and `おります` rather than `いらっしゃいます`. It feels disloyal to an English speaker; in Japanese it is exactly the loyal thing to do, because lowering your own side is how you raise the customer.

---

## いらっしゃる · いらっしゃる vs おる

> **Rule of thumb** - `いらっしゃる` for people you are raising; `おる` for yourself and for anyone on your own side of the line.

<ruby>社長<rt>しゃちょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>三階<rt>さんがい</rt></ruby>に**いらっしゃいます**。<br>*The president is on the third floor.*

<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>どもは<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>も<ruby>店<rt>みせ</rt></ruby>に**おります**。<br>*We'll be at the shop tomorrow as well.*

---

## いらっしゃる · いらっしゃる vs おる (cont.)

The same phone call can need both, one clause apart. An outside caller asking <ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>さんはいらっしゃいますか is right - from where they stand, <ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby> is an outsider and deserves the honorific. Your reply, <ruby>田中<rt>たなか</rt></ruby>はただいま<ruby>席<rt>せき</rt></ruby>をはずしております, is also right, because from where *you* stand he is family.

---

## いらっしゃる · いらっしゃる vs 参る・伺う

> **Rule of thumb** - `いらっしゃる` is them going or coming; <code><ruby>参<rt>まい</rt></ruby>る</code> and <code><ruby>伺<rt>うかが</rt></ruby>う</code> are you going or coming.

<ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>三時<rt>さんじ</rt></ruby>に**いらっしゃいます**。<br>*Sensei will be arriving at three.*

<ruby>三時<rt>さんじ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>研究室<rt>けんきゅうしつ</rt></ruby>へ**<ruby>伺<rt>うかが</rt></ruby>います**。<br>*I'll come to your office at three.*

<code><ruby>伺<rt>うかが</rt></ruby>う</code> is used when the place you are going belongs to somebody you respect; <code><ruby>参<rt>まい</rt></ruby>る</code> is the plainer humble word and works even when nobody in particular is being honoured - <ruby>電車<rt>でんしゃ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>参<rt>まい</rt></ruby>ります on a platform announcement is about a train, not a person.

---

## いらっしゃる · いらっしゃる vs おいでになる・お見えになる

> **Rule of thumb** - all three are honorific. `いらっしゃる` is the default; `おいでになる` is more formal; <code>お<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>えになる</code> only ever means "come".

<ruby>会長<rt>かいちょう</rt></ruby>が<ruby>会場<rt>かいじょう</rt></ruby>に**おいでになりました**。<br>*The chairman has arrived at the venue.*

お<ruby>約束<rt>やくそく</rt></ruby>の<ruby>方<rt>かた</rt></ruby>が**お<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>えになりました**。<br>*Your appointment has arrived.*

---

## いらっしゃる · いらっしゃる vs おいでになる・お見えになる (cont.)

Because `いらっしゃる` covers three meanings, the alternatives are sometimes chosen simply for clarity: お<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>えになりました can only be an arrival, so nobody has to work out whether the person came, went or is present.

---

## いらっしゃる · Common mistakes

- ❌ <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>**いらっしゃります**。 → ✅ <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>**いらっしゃいます**。<br>*The `り` becomes `い` in the ます-form. The same applies to おっしゃいます, なさいます and くださいます.*

- ❌ <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>、<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>が<ruby>会社<rt>かいしゃ</rt></ruby>に**いらっしゃいます**。 → ✅ <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>、<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>が<ruby>会社<rt>かいしゃ</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>参<rt>まい</rt></ruby>ります**。<br>*<ruby>尊敬<rt>そんけい</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby> about yourself is the classic error. You cannot raise your own head - use the humble verb.*

- ❌ （to a client）<ruby>弊社<rt>へいしゃ</rt></ruby>の<ruby>社長<rt>しゃちょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>今<rt>いま</rt></ruby>**いらっしゃいません**。 → ✅ <ruby>社長<rt>しゃちょう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>佐藤<rt>さとう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>本日<rt>ほんじつ</rt></ruby>**おりません**。<br>*The in-group rule. Talking to an outsider, your own president is lowered like everyone else on your side - and loses the `さん`.*

---

## いらっしゃる · Common mistakes (cont.)

- ❌ こちらの<ruby>資料<rt>しりょう</rt></ruby>は**いらっしゃいます**か。 → ✅ こちらの<ruby>資料<rt>しりょう</rt></ruby>は**ございます**か。<br>*`いらっしゃる` honours a person. Objects take `ある` and its polite form `ございます`; there is nobody there to raise.*

---

## いらっしゃる · Practice 1

**1.** <ruby>校長<rt>こうちょう</rt></ruby><ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>職員室<rt>しょくいんしつ</rt></ruby>に____か。

{reveal}
<ruby>校長<rt>こうちょう</rt></ruby><ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>職員室<rt>しょくいんしつ</rt></ruby>に**いらっしゃいます**か。

{reveal}
`いる` about someone you are honouring becomes `いらっしゃる`, and its polite form is いらっしゃいます - not ❌いらっしゃります.

---

## いらっしゃる · Practice 2

**2.** Choose: （<ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>はいらっしゃいません・<ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>中村<rt>なかむら</rt></ruby>はおりません） - said on the phone to a customer.

{reveal}
**<ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>中村<rt>なかむら</rt></ruby>はおりません**。

{reveal}
Speaking to somebody outside the company, your own department head belongs to your in-group. He is referred to without `さん` and with the humble `おる`. The first version honours your own side in front of a customer, which sounds arrogant rather than respectful.

---

## いらっしゃる · Practice 3

**3.** Translate into Japanese: "Which floor are you going to?"

{reveal}
<ruby>何階<rt>なんがい</rt></ruby>へ**いらっしゃいます**か。

{reveal}
Here `いらっしゃる` carries the <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く sense. Nothing in the form changes; the question word and the `へ` are what tell the listener that going, rather than being, is meant.

---

## いらっしゃる · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>来月<rt>らいげつ</rt></ruby>、<ruby>京都<rt>きょうと</rt></ruby>にいらっしゃる<ruby>予定<rt>よてい</rt></ruby>です。

{reveal}
✅ <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>来月<rt>らいげつ</rt></ruby>、<ruby>京都<rt>きょうと</rt></ruby>に**<ruby>参<rt>まい</rt></ruby>る**<ruby>予定<rt>よてい</rt></ruby>です。

{reveal}
The subject is <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>, so an honorific verb is impossible. Use <ruby>参<rt>まい</rt></ruby>る, or simply <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>きます if the situation does not call for <ruby>謙譲<rt>けんじょう</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby> at all.

---

## いらっしゃる · Practice 5

**5.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) いらっしゃいませ。 (b) いらっしゃい。

{reveal}
(a) is service language. A shop assistant, a waiter or a hotel receptionist says it as you walk in, and it is not really addressed to you as an individual - no reply is expected.

{reveal}
(b) is the same word without the `ませ`, and dropping `ませ` drops the formality. It is what a host says opening the door to a guest, or a parent to a child's friend: friendly and personal. A market trader shouting いらっしゃい, いらっしゃい is using it as a call to passers-by, which is friendlier still.

---

# なさる

**Meaning** · the honorific of する - "to do", said about someone you are raising

`なさる` is <ruby>尊敬<rt>そんけい</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby>. Because `する` combines with hundreds of nouns, `なさる` gives you an honorific for every one of them at a stroke: <ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>なさる、<ruby>運転<rt>うんてん</rt></ruby>なさる、ご<ruby>結婚<rt>けっこん</rt></ruby>なさる. It is also the verb behind the two most useful service questions in Japanese, どうなさいますか and いかがなさいましたか.

---

## なさる · Formation

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| する | なさる | する → なさる |
| Noun + する | Noun + なさる | <ruby>運転<rt>うんてん</rt></ruby>する → <ruby>運転<rt>うんてん</rt></ruby>なさる |
| Noun + する, with prefix | ご／お + Noun + なさる | <ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>する → ご<ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>なさる |
| ～ている | ～なさっている | <ruby>研究<rt>けんきゅう</rt></ruby>している → <ruby>研究<rt>けんきゅう</rt></ruby>なさっている |
| Choosing between options | Noun + に + なさる | コーヒーにする → コーヒーになさる |

Like `いらっしゃる`, it is a う-verb with an irregular ます-form:

---

## なさる · Formation (cont.)

| Form | Shape |
|---|---|
| Polite | なさいます（❌なさります） |
| Past polite | なさいました |
| Negative | なさらない／なさいません |
| て-form | なさって |
| Negative request | ～なさらないでください |
| Softened command | ます-stem + なさい（<ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べなさい） |

---

## なさる · Formation (cont.)

> **Note** - `～なさい` is built from this verb but does **not** honour anyone. It is a gentle order aimed *downward*: a parent to a child, a teacher to a class, a test paper to a candidate. おやすみなさい and ごめんなさい are fossilised leftovers of the same form.

---

## なさる · Examples

どう**なさいました**か。<br>*What seems to be the trouble?*

コーヒーと<ruby>紅茶<rt>こうちゃ</rt></ruby>、どちらに**なさいます**か。<br>*Coffee or tea - which would you like?*

<ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>毎朝<rt>まいあさ</rt></ruby><ruby>散歩<rt>さんぽ</rt></ruby>を**なさいます**。<br>*Sensei goes for a walk every morning.*

どうぞご<ruby>心配<rt>しんぱい</rt></ruby>**なさらないで**ください。<br>*Please don't worry about it.*

---

## なさる · Examples (cont.)

<ruby>社長<rt>しゃちょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>週末<rt>しゅうまつ</rt></ruby>にゴルフを**なさる**そうです。<br>*I gather the president plays golf at weekends.*

<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>の<ruby>集合<rt>しゅうごう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>何時<rt>なんじ</rt></ruby>に**なさいます**か。<br>*What time would you like to meet tomorrow?*

<ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>長年<rt>ながねん</rt></ruby>**<ruby>研究<rt>けんきゅう</rt></ruby>なさっている**テーマについて<ruby>伺<rt>うかが</rt></ruby>いたいと<ruby>思<rt>おも</rt></ruby>っております。<br>*I'd like to ask you about the subject you have been researching for so many years.*

<ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>はこの<ruby>件<rt>けん</rt></ruby>をどのように<ruby>処理<rt>しょり</rt></ruby>**なさる**おつもりでしょうか。<br>*How does the department head intend to handle this matter?*

---

## なさる · Nuance & register

`なさる` is squarely business, service and formal-social language. Shop staff, receptionists, doctors, flight attendants and hotel clerks use it constantly, mostly in the fixed openers どうなさいますか（"what would you like to do?"）, いかがなさいますか（the more formal version）and どうなさいましたか（"what's wrong?"）. To a friend, ❌<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>をなさっているんですか would be comic.

Because it is <ruby>尊敬<rt>そんけい</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby> it obeys the same two hard limits as the rest of the system. It never describes your own action - that is `いたす` - and it never describes your own side when you are speaking to an outsider. On the phone to a customer, ❌<ruby>担当<rt>たんとう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>者<rt>もの</rt></ruby>が<ruby>確認<rt>かくにん</rt></ruby>なさいます honours your own colleague; the sentence you want is <ruby>担当<rt>たんとう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>者<rt>もの</rt></ruby>が<ruby>確認<rt>かくにん</rt></ruby>いたします.

---

## なさる · Nuance & register (cont.)

`される` is the lighter alternative: <ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>はどうされますか is perfectly polite and rather more everyday than <ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>はどうなさいますか. As a tendency, `なさる` is felt as warmer and more attentive, and it is heard more often from service staff and in careful formal speech; `される` is the workhorse of ordinary office Japanese. Neither is wrong in the other's setting.

Do not stack layers. ❌おなさりになる and ❌なさられる are <ruby>二重<rt>にじゅう</rt></ruby><ruby>敬語<rt>けいご</rt></ruby>; `なさる` on its own is already the honorific.

---

## なさる · なさる vs いたす

> **Rule of thumb** - `なさる` for what *they* do; `いたす` for what *you* do. Same verb, opposite directions.

お<ruby>客<rt>きゃく</rt></ruby><ruby>様<rt>さま</rt></ruby>はどちらに**なさいます**か。<br>*Which will you have, madam?*

<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>どもがご<ruby>用意<rt>ようい</rt></ruby>**いたします**。<br>*We'll get it ready for you.*

This pair is the cleanest illustration of the whole three-way system. Both sentences are polite to the customer; the first gets there by lifting her, the second by lowering the speaker. Using `なさる` about yourself does not merely sound odd - it claims a status you have just given to somebody else.

---

## なさる · なさる vs される

> **Rule of thumb** - both are honorific. `される` is lighter and unmarked; `なさる` is more attentive and more distinctly <ruby>敬語<rt>けいご</rt></ruby>.

<ruby>課長<rt>かちょう</rt></ruby>はいつ<ruby>出張<rt>しゅっちょう</rt></ruby>**されます**か。<br>*When are you going on the business trip, <ruby>課長<rt>かちょう</rt></ruby>?*

<ruby>会長<rt>かいちょう</rt></ruby>はいつ<ruby>出張<rt>しゅっちょう</rt></ruby>**なさいます**か。<br>*When will the chairman be going on his trip?*

---

## なさる · なさる vs される (cont.)

There is one practical reason to reach for `なさる`: `される` is also the passive. <ruby>注意<rt>ちゅうい</rt></ruby>されました can mean "you kindly took care" or "I got told off", and <ruby>注意<rt>ちゅうい</rt></ruby>なさいました can only mean the first.

---

## なさる · なさる vs ～なさい

> **Rule of thumb** - `なさる` looks up; `～なさい` looks down. They come from the same root and point in opposite social directions.

<ruby>宿題<rt>しゅくだい</rt></ruby>を<ruby>先<rt>さき</rt></ruby>に**しなさい**。<br>*Do your homework first.*

<ruby>宿題<rt>しゅくだい</rt></ruby>はもう**なさいました**か。<br>*Have you done your homework yet? (said respectfully)*

---

## なさる · なさる vs ～なさい (cont.)

`～なさい` is softer than the bare imperative しろ, which is why parents and teachers like it - but softness is not respect. Aimed upward it is an insult, so ❌<ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>、こちらに<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>きなさい must be <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>、こちらにお<ruby>書<rt>か</rt></ruby>きください.

---

## なさる · Common mistakes

- ❌ <ruby>社長<rt>しゃちょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>何時<rt>なんじ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>出発<rt>しゅっぱつ</rt></ruby>**なさりますか**。 → ✅ <ruby>社長<rt>しゃちょう</rt></ruby>は<ruby>何時<rt>なんじ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>出発<rt>しゅっぱつ</rt></ruby>**なさいますか**。<br>*The `り` turns into `い` before ます. Same irregularity as いらっしゃいます and くださいます.*

- ❌ <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>がご<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>**なさいます**。 → ✅ <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>がご<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>**いたします**。<br>*<ruby>尊敬<rt>そんけい</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby> pointed at yourself. Your own actions take <ruby>謙譲<rt>けんじょう</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby>.*

- ❌ お<ruby>客<rt>きゃく</rt></ruby><ruby>様<rt>さま</rt></ruby>、どう**しましたか**。 → ✅ お<ruby>客<rt>きゃく</rt></ruby><ruby>様<rt>さま</rt></ruby>、どう**なさいましたか**。<br>*Grammatically fine, socially thin. `しましたか` is only <ruby>丁寧<rt>ていねい</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby> - polite speech with no honorific in it - and a customer expects to be raised, not merely addressed politely.*

---

## なさる · Common mistakes (cont.)

- ❌ <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>**なさられました**。 → ✅ <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>**なさいました**。<br>*`なさる` plus `られる` is two honorifics on one verb. One is the ceiling.*

---

## なさる · Practice 1

**1.** お<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>み<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>は<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>に____か。

{reveal}
お<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>み<ruby>物<rt>もの</rt></ruby>は<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>に**なさいます**か。

{reveal}
<code><ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>にする</code> - "go for which one" - becomes <ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>になさる when the chooser is the person you are serving. This is the standard restaurant line.

---

## なさる · Practice 2

**2.** Choose: <ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>が（<ruby>案内<rt>あんない</rt></ruby>なさいます・ご<ruby>案内<rt>あんない</rt></ruby>いたします）。

{reveal}
<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>は<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>が**ご<ruby>案内<rt>あんない</rt></ruby>いたします**。

{reveal}
The subject is <ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>, so the sentence must lower rather than raise. `なさる` would put the honorific on your own action. Note also that <ruby>案内<rt>あんない</rt></ruby> is a Chinese-derived root, so it takes `ご`.

---

## なさる · Practice 3

**3.** Translate into Japanese: "Does the teacher drive?"

{reveal}
<ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>運転<rt>うんてん</rt></ruby>を**なさいます**か。

{reveal}
<ruby>運転<rt>うんてん</rt></ruby>する is a noun + `する`, so the honorific is made simply by swapping `する` for `なさる`. <ruby>運転<rt>うんてん</rt></ruby>されますか is equally correct and a little lighter.

---

## なさる · Practice 4

**4.** Find and fix the error: <ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>、この<ruby>書類<rt>しょるい</rt></ruby>を<ruby>確認<rt>かくにん</rt></ruby>しなさい。

{reveal}
✅ <ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>、この<ruby>書類<rt>しょるい</rt></ruby>をご<ruby>確認<rt>かくにん</rt></ruby>いただけますでしょうか。

{reveal}
`～なさい` is a command directed downward - fine from a teacher to a pupil, unacceptable to your own department head. A request upward needs the honorific frame, and softening it into a question softens it further.

---

## なさる · Practice 5

**5.** Explain the difference in nuance: (a) <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>を<ruby>研究<rt>けんきゅう</rt></ruby>していますか。 (b) <ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>は<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>を<ruby>研究<rt>けんきゅう</rt></ruby>なさっていますか。

{reveal}
Both are polite in form, and neither is rude. (a) uses only <ruby>丁寧<rt>ていねい</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby>: the `ます` makes your speech courteous, but the verb itself says nothing about the teacher's standing. It is what a student might say to a lecturer they know well.

{reveal}
(b) adds <ruby>尊敬<rt>そんけい</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby> on top, so the teacher is lifted by the verb as well as addressed politely. It suits a first meeting, an interview or a formal setting. The difference is not politeness versus rudeness - it is distance and deference.

---

# 敬語の動詞

**Meaning** · the closed set of verbs that have their own honorific and humble replacements

A dozen or so of the commonest Japanese verbs do not use the お○○になる／お○○する frames at all. They have **separate words** instead - one that raises the person you are talking about, and one that lowers you. Learn them as pairs and most of <ruby>敬語<rt>けいご</rt></ruby> is done.

---

## 敬語の動詞 · Formation

These verbs are not built; they are swapped in. The plain verb disappears and a different word takes its place.

| Attaches to | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Verb with a set honorific | plain verb → <ruby>尊敬<rt>そんけい</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby> word | <ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べる → <ruby>召<rt>め</rt></ruby>し<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がる |
| Verb with a set humble | plain verb → <ruby>謙譲<rt>けんじょう</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby> word | <ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>る → <ruby>拝見<rt>はいけん</rt></ruby>する |
| Noun + する (honorific) | ご／お + noun + になる・なさる | <ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>する → ご<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>になる |
| Noun + する (humble) | ご／お + noun + する・いたす | <ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>する → ご<ruby>説明<rt>せつめい</rt></ruby>いたす |
| ～ている (honorific) | ～ていらっしゃる | <ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>っている → <ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>っていらっしゃる |
| ～ている (humble) | ～ておる | <ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>っている → <ruby>待<rt>ま</rt></ruby>っております |

---

## 敬語の動詞 · Formation (cont.)

The set itself, laid out as the mirror it is. The middle column is for the other person; the right-hand column is for you and for anyone on your side.

---

## 敬語の動詞 · Formation (cont.)

| Plain verb | <ruby>尊敬<rt>そんけい</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby> - raises them | <ruby>謙譲<rt>けんじょう</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby> - lowers you |
|---|---|---|
| いる | いらっしゃる／おいでになる | おる |
| <ruby>行<rt>い</rt></ruby>く | いらっしゃる／お<ruby>越<rt>こ</rt></ruby>しになる | <ruby>参<rt>まい</rt></ruby>る／<ruby>伺<rt>うかが</rt></ruby>う |
| <ruby>来<rt>く</rt></ruby>る | いらっしゃる／お<ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>えになる | <ruby>参<rt>まい</rt></ruby>る／<ruby>伺<rt>うかが</rt></ruby>う |
| する | なさる | いたす |
| <ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>う | おっしゃる | <ruby>申<rt>もう</rt></ruby>す／<ruby>申<rt>もう</rt></ruby>し<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>げる |
| <ruby>食<rt>た</rt></ruby>べる・<ruby>飲<rt>の</rt></ruby>む | <ruby>召<rt>め</rt></ruby>し<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がる | いただく |
| <ruby>見<rt>み</rt></ruby>る | ご<ruby>覧<rt>らん</rt></ruby>になる | <ruby>拝見<rt>はいけん</rt></ruby>する |
| <ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>く・<ruby>尋<rt>たず</rt></ruby>ねる | お<ruby>聞<rt>き</rt></ruby>きになる | <ruby>伺<rt>うかが</rt></ruby>う／<ruby>承<rt>うけたまわ</rt></ruby>る |
| <ruby>知<rt>し</rt></ruby>っている | ご<ruby>存<rt>ぞん</rt></ruby>じだ | <ruby>存<rt>ぞん</rt></ruby>じている／<ruby>存<rt>ぞん</rt></ruby>じ<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>げる |

---

## 敬語の動詞 · Formation (cont.)

| Plain verb | <ruby>尊敬<rt>そんけい</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby> - raises them | <ruby>謙譲<rt>けんじょう</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby> - lowers you |
|---|---|---|
| もらう | - | いただく／<ruby>頂戴<rt>ちょうだい</rt></ruby>する |
| あげる | - | さし<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>げる |
| くれる | くださる | - |
| <ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>う | お<ruby>会<rt>あ</rt></ruby>いになる | お<ruby>目<rt>め</rt></ruby>にかかる |
| <ruby>着<rt>き</rt></ruby>る | お<ruby>召<rt>め</rt></ruby>しになる | - |
| <ruby>寝<rt>ね</rt></ruby>る | お<ruby>休<rt>やす</rt></ruby>みになる | - |
| <ruby>借<rt>か</rt></ruby>りる | - | <ruby>拝借<rt>はいしゃく</rt></ruby>する |

Four of the honorific verbs conjugate irregularly before ます. This is the detail that most often gives a learner away:

---

## 敬語の動詞 · Formation (cont.)

| Dictionary | ます-form | Never |
|---|---|---|
| いらっしゃる | いらっしゃいます | ❌いらっしゃります |
| おっしゃる | おっしゃいます | ❌おっしゃります |
| なさる | なさいます | ❌なさります |
| くださる | くださいます | ❌くださります |

---

## 敬語の動詞 · Examples

デザートも**<ruby>召<rt>め</rt></ruby>し<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>がります**か。<br>*Will you be having dessert as well?*

お<ruby>名前<rt>なまえ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>何<rt>なん</rt></ruby>と**おっしゃいます**か。<br>*What is your name, please?*

お<ruby>写真<rt>しゃしん</rt></ruby>を**<ruby>拝見<rt>はいけん</rt></ruby>しました**。とてもきれいですね。<br>*I've had a look at your photographs. They're beautiful.*

<ruby>明日<rt>あした</rt></ruby>の<ruby>三時<rt>さんじ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>御社<rt>おんしゃ</rt></ruby>へ**<ruby>伺<rt>うかが</rt></ruby>います**。<br>*I'll come to your office at three tomorrow.*

---

## 敬語の動詞 · Examples (cont.)

<ruby>申<rt>もう</rt></ruby>し<ruby>訳<rt>わけ</rt></ruby>ございません、<ruby>担当<rt>たんとう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>者<rt>もの</rt></ruby>は<ruby>外出<rt>がいしゅつ</rt></ruby>して**おります**。<br>*I'm very sorry - the person in charge is out of the office.*

その<ruby>件<rt>けん</rt></ruby>については、<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>どもは<ruby>何<rt>なに</rt></ruby>も**<ruby>存<rt>ぞん</rt></ruby>じません**。<br>*We know nothing at all about that matter.*

<ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>が**おっしゃった**<ruby>通<rt>とお</rt></ruby>りに<ruby>準備<rt>じゅんび</rt></ruby>を<ruby>進<rt>すす</rt></ruby>めております。<br>*We're preparing exactly as the department head instructed.*

<ruby>昨年<rt>さくねん</rt></ruby>の<ruby>展示会<rt>てんじかい</rt></ruby>で<ruby>一度<rt>いちど</rt></ruby>**お<ruby>目<rt>め</rt></ruby>にかかった**ことがございます。<br>*I believe we met once at last year's exhibition.*

---

## 敬語の動詞 · Nuance & register

Hold the three-way system in mind and none of this is guesswork. <ruby>丁寧<rt>ていねい</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby>（です・ます）makes your speech polite to the listener. <ruby>尊敬<rt>そんけい</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby> raises the subject of the verb. <ruby>謙譲<rt>けんじょう</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby> lowers the subject of the verb, which raises whoever the action is aimed at. Choosing a form is therefore a question about *who is doing the verb*, not about how polite you feel.

Two refinements worth having early:

---

## 敬語の動詞 · Nuance & register (cont.)

**The humble column has two halves.** <ruby>伺<rt>うかが</rt></ruby>う, <ruby>申<rt>もう</rt></ruby>し<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>げる, <ruby>拝見<rt>はいけん</rt></ruby>する and お<ruby>目<rt>め</rt></ruby>にかかる need a specific person on the receiving end who deserves the respect. <ruby>参<rt>まい</rt></ruby>る, <ruby>申<rt>もう</rt></ruby>す and おる do not - they simply lower and formalise, which is why <ruby>電車<rt>でんしゃ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>参<rt>まい</rt></ruby>ります works on a platform announcement even though a train respects nobody. That second group is sometimes labelled <ruby>丁重<rt>ていちょう</rt></ruby><ruby>語<rt>ご</rt></ruby>, and it is the group you use for your own side in front of an outsider.

---

## 敬語の動詞 · Nuance & register (cont.)

**In-group before rank.** English speakers expect politeness to track seniority. Japanese tracks the boundary of your group first. Talking to a client, your own <ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby> is lowered exactly like you: not ❌<ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>がおっしゃっていました but <ruby>部長<rt>ぶちょう</rt></ruby>の<ruby>中村<rt>なかむら</rt></ruby>が<ruby>申<rt>もう</rt></ruby>しておりました - no `さん`, humble verb, and the title placed before the surname rather than after it. Inside the office, with only colleagues listening, おっしゃいました is right again. Nothing about the boss changed; the audience did.

Some smaller points:

---

## 敬語の動詞 · Nuance & register (cont.)

- `いただく` does double duty - humble "eat/drink" and humble "receive". The<br>*context separates them.*
- <ruby>存<rt>ぞん</rt></ruby>じ<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>げる is used about **people**<br>*（お<ruby>名前<rt>なまえ</rt></ruby>は<ruby>存<rt>ぞん</rt></ruby>じ<ruby>上<rt>あ</rt></ruby>げております）, and <ruby>存<rt>ぞん</rt></ruby>じる about **facts**.*
